papers.note: The origin paper for chain of thought prompting and the single most cited reasoning reference in the field.
papers.title: Chain of Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.explain_beginner: If you ask an AI model a hard math word problem and demand a direct answer, it often gets it wrong. If instead you ask it to work through the problem out loud, step by step, before giving a final answer, accuracy jumps sharply. This paper is the one that named that technique chain of thought prompting and proved the effect systematically across arithmetic, common sense, and symbolic logic problems. The surprising part is that this only works once a model is large enough, in smaller models, thinking out loud barely helps and can even make things slightly worse. The authors are upfront that this leaves an unresolved question, producing a plausible looking chain of reasoning does not guarantee the answer at the end is actually correct, and whether the model is genuinely reasoning in any meaningful sense remains an open question they explicitly decline to answer.
papers.explain_business: Before this paper, the standard assumption was that improving a model's performance on multi step problems required retraining or fine tuning it. Wei and colleagues showed you could get comparable or better gains purely by changing the prompt, at zero training cost, provided the underlying model was large enough, over roughly 100 billion parameters. That is the direct ancestor of every thinking or reasoning mode toggle now shipped in commercial AI assistants, and it means a business question like why is our AI bad at multi step calculations often has a cheap first fix, ask it to show its work, before an expensive one, retrain or replace the model entirely. The tradeoff businesses should weigh is real, this only works reliably on sufficiently large, capable models, and the paper's own caveat, that a plausible reasoning trace does not guarantee a correct answer, means chain of thought output should inform trust, not replace verification for high stakes decisions.
papers.explain_practitioner: Wei and colleagues show that few shot prompting with worked, step by step exemplars produces large accuracy gains over direct answer prompting on GSM8K, MultiArith, and symbolic reasoning benchmarks, and that this gain is an emergent property of scale rather than a smooth improvement, appearing reliably only around 100 billion parameters and larger. Their headline result, prompting a 540 billion parameter PaLM model with just eight chain of thought exemplars reached 58 percent accuracy on GSM8K math word problems, beating the prior best result of 55 percent from a fine tuned GPT-3 model equipped with an external verifier, without any additional training or weight updates. The authors state their own limitations plainly, the technique is costly to serve because it only works at large model scale, manually authoring worked exemplars is expensive at fine tuning scale even if cheap for a handful of few shot examples, there is no guarantee a correct looking reasoning chain leads to a correct answer, and whether the model is actually reasoning versus emulating the surface form of reasoning is a question the paper explicitly leaves open.

papers.note: The paper behind the main attention-free alternative, worth knowing when a client stack is not transformer based.
papers.title: Mamba: Linear-Time Sequence Modeling with Selective State Spaces
papers.explain_beginner: Most AI systems for language and other sequences use a design called the Transformer. The paper presents Mamba, a design that avoids attention. Mamba can decide what to keep or forget as it reads each item in a sequence, which helps with language and discrete data. It runs faster than Transformers, five times more work per second, and its cost grows steadily as inputs get longer, so long inputs become practical. It performs well on language, audio, and genomics. A 3 billion parameter Mamba does better than Transformers of equal size and equals Transformers with double the parameters. This matters because teams may not need attention models for every task.
papers.explain_business: For executives, Mamba is an alternative to systems built on Transformers, especially when long inputs or inference cost matter. The paper reports faster inference, five times more work per second than Transformers, and cost that rises with sequence length, so longer documents or signals do not become expensive. It works across language, audio, and genomics. In language, a 3 billion parameter Mamba beats Transformers of equal size and matches Transformers with double the parameters. The decision this informs is to evaluate Mamba for workloads where context length, latency, or throughput are constraints, rather than assuming every AI stack must use attention. It may reduce serving costs and expand use cases.
papers.explain_practitioner: This work addresses a weakness in subquadratic sequence models: they cannot reason from content. They make model parameters depend on the input, so the model can decide what information to carry forward and what to discard across the sequence. They design a hardware aware parallel method in recurrent form. These selective models form Mamba, a network design without attention or MLP blocks. Mamba gives inference five times faster than Transformers, cost that rises with sequence length, and gains on data up to million length sequences. It works across language, audio, and genomics. A 3 billion parameter Mamba beats Transformers of equal size and matches Transformers with double the parameters.

papers.note: Sampling many reasoning paths and taking the consensus is a cheap control an audit can recommend for high-stakes answers.
papers.title: Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models
papers.explain_beginner: The paper studies how to make language models better at reasoning. Instead of letting a model produce one line of thought and answer, the authors let it produce several different lines of thought. They then pick the answer that appears most often across those attempts. The idea is that a hard problem can be solved in different ways, but the correct answer should usually be the same. Tests on arithmetic and common sense tasks showed clear gains, such as 17.9 percent on GSM8K and 11.0 percent on SVAMP. This matters because a simple change can make model answers more reliable without training a new model.
papers.explain_business: This paper shows that a language model can answer complex reasoning questions more accurately if it is allowed to try several reasoning routes and then give the answer most of them support. The authors report large improvements on arithmetic and common sense tests, including 17.9 percent on GSM8K and 12.2 percent on AQuA. For executives, this suggests a practical reliability check: when an AI answer matters, ask for multiple attempts and use the consensus. The editor's note calls this a cheap control that an audit can recommend for high stakes answers. It informs decisions about how to review or deploy AI outputs in sensitive settings.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors introduce a decoding method for step by step prompting. Rather than taking only the single highest probability output, their approach generates many varied reasoning traces. It then chooses the answer that is most common after combining the evidence from those traces. This relies on the idea that different valid solution routes should converge on one correct answer. They tested the method on several arithmetic and common sense reasoning datasets. The reported gains over standard step by step prompting were 17.9 percent on GSM8K, 11.0 percent on SVAMP, 12.2 percent on AQuA, 6.4 percent on StrategyQA, and 3.9 percent on ARC challenge.

papers.note: A review of 146 studies from 2007 to 2018 finds AI in higher education concentrated in computer science and four application areas, with little critical reflection on risks or pedagogical theory, so educators remain largely absent from shaping how these tools affect teaching and learning.
papers.title: Systematic review of research on artificial intelligence applications in higher education – where are the educators?
papers.authors: Olaf Zawacki‐Richter, Victoria I. Marín, Melissa Bond, Franziska Gouverneur
papers.explain_beginner: This paper looked at many studies about artificial intelligence in universities, published between 2007 and 2018. The authors started with 2656 papers and narrowed them down to 146 for a close look. They found that most of this research comes from computer science and related fields, not from education. The tools studied mostly do four things: predict student success, grade or evaluate work, adapt to each learner, or act as tutoring systems. The paper warns that risks and ethics get little attention, and teachers are rarely involved in shaping these tools.
papers.explain_business: This review of 146 studies from 2007 to 2018 shows that AI in higher education is still driven mainly by computer science and STEM researchers, with little input from educators. The tools cluster around predicting student outcomes, assessment, personalisation, and tutoring. Risks, ethics, and pedagogical theory receive scant attention. For leaders, this signals that adoption decisions should not rely on technical research alone. Investment in AI should include educators in design and governance, and should fund evaluation of ethical and teaching impact, not just deployment of prediction, assessment, or tutoring systems.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors conducted a systematic review of AI in higher education, screening 2656 publications from 2007 to 2018 and synthesizing 146 articles using explicit inclusion and exclusion criteria. Descriptive analysis showed that computer science and STEM dominate the field, and empirical work relies mostly on quantitative methods. The synthesis identified four application areas: profiling and prediction, assessment and evaluation, adaptive systems and personalisation, and intelligent tutoring systems. The authors conclude that critical reflection on challenges and risks is largely absent, links to pedagogical theory are weak, and ethical and educational approaches need more exploration.

papers.note: The standard taxonomy of bias sources and fairness definitions, which an audit needs before it can test anything.
papers.title: A Survey on Bias and Fairness in Machine Learning
papers.explain_beginner: This survey looks at how artificial intelligence can treat people unfairly. It gathers examples from real uses where such unfairness appeared. It sorts the reasons bias can enter AI systems. It also organizes the different ways researchers define fairness, so people can compare ideas. The paper reviews many areas of AI and describes unfair results researchers found and attempts to fix them. It says more work is needed. This matters because AI often helps make important choices, so unfair treatment can harm groups. The survey gives a shared starting point for spotting and discussing bias.
papers.explain_business: This survey explains that AI systems can make important decisions and may treat groups unfairly. It gathers real cases where bias appeared, identifies where bias can enter, and organizes the ways fairness is defined. It also reviews how different AI areas have shown unfair results and what researchers tried. For an executive, the practical message is that fairness needs attention during design and engineering. The paper provides a shared vocabulary and map of bias sources, which can guide how organizations discuss and review fairness. It also shows the field still lacks complete solutions, so more work is needed.
papers.explain_practitioner: This 2019 survey by Mehrabi and colleagues reviews bias and fairness in machine learning. It collects real applications where bias has appeared and lists where bias can come from. It builds a taxonomy of how fairness is defined proposed by machine learning researchers. It then examines several AI domains and subdomains, reporting unfair outcomes seen in leading methods and approaches used to address them. The main contribution is a structured map of bias sources and fairness concepts, plus a review of problems in specific domains and fixes. It notes that many open problems remain. For engineers, it offers a reference for framing audits and comparing fairness choices before testing.

papers.note: The most cited education position paper, and the source of the competency and literacy framing now used in policy.
papers.title: ChatGPT for good? On opportunities and challenges of large language models for education
papers.explain_beginner: This is not a study that tested ChatGPT in real classrooms, it is a position paper, meaning a group of researchers laid out their reasoned argument about what large language models could mean for education, both the good and the bad, based on the technology's known capabilities rather than new classroom data. Written by a large interdisciplinary group of researchers spanning education, computer science, and psychology, the paper asks what changes for students and teachers once tools like ChatGPT can write essays, explain concepts, and answer questions on demand. It argues these tools could genuinely help by creating educational content, increasing student engagement, and personalizing how material is presented to individual learners. But it argues just as strongly that using them well requires new skills, both students and teachers need to learn to understand what the tool is actually doing, where it fails in unpredictable ways, and how to fact check its answers rather than trust them by default. It does not claim these problems are unique to education, the authors note bias and misuse risks apply to AI broadly, but it does argue education is a uniquely good place to teach people, early, how to think critically about AI systems in general.
papers.explain_business: For an education company or a school system deciding how to approach generative AI, the direct takeaway is that this influential, widely cited paper frames the central risk as a skills gap rather than a technology gap, meaning the practical need is training teachers and students in AI literacy and fact checking habits, not primarily restricting or banning access to the tools. This reframes procurement questions, a school evaluating an AI powered classroom product should ask whether it includes support for building these literacy skills, not just whether the underlying model is capable. The paper's point that bias, oversight needs, and misuse risk are generic to AI rather than education specific also matters operationally, since it means an education focused compliance review can reuse general purpose AI risk assessments rather than needing something entirely bespoke to the classroom setting. Because this is a position paper and not a study of outcomes, it does not tell a buyer whether a specific product actually improves learning, that would require the classroom outcome research this paper explicitly calls for and which, as of its publication, had not yet been done. It is most useful right now for shaping policy and training priorities rather than for evaluating any specific AI education vendor.
papers.explain_practitioner: As a position paper rather than an empirical study, the paper's contribution is a structured argument rather than a dataset or experiment, authored by twenty three researchers across computer science, education, and cognitive science departments. It organizes its analysis around dual perspectives, opportunities and challenges from the student side and from the teacher side, covering content generation, engagement, and personalized learning as the main opportunity categories. On the challenge side, it specifies that large language model brittleness, the tendency to fail or produce confident but wrong answers in ways that are hard to predict, requires both groups to build new AI literacy skills before the models can be safely integrated into curricula. The paper explicitly states that bias in model output, the need for continuous human oversight, and potential for misuse are not unique to educational applications of AI, distinguishing genuinely education specific challenges from generic AI risks that any deployment context would face. Because it is argumentative and forward looking rather than data driven, its own implicit limitation is that none of its specific recommendations were tested against real classroom outcomes at the time of publication, the paper is explicitly framed as guidance for future work and policy rather than a report of findings.

papers.note: The founding sparse expert paper, worth citing when an audit has to date the origin of a design choice.
papers.title: Outrageously Large Neural Networks: The Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts Layer
papers.explain_beginner: Neural networks can only learn so much because their size limits how much information they hold. This paper shows a way to make a network much larger while keeping the work per input fairly small. It uses many small forward processing parts and a learned gate that picks only a few of them for each example. The authors tested this on language prediction and translation, building models with up to 137 billion parameters placed between stacked LSTM layers. These models beat earlier best results while using less computation. The finding matters because it shows very large models can be practical, not just theoretical.
papers.explain_business: This paper shows that a model can be made far larger without making every input use the whole model. A learned gate sends each example through only a few small expert subnetworks. In tests on language prediction and translation, models with up to 137 billion parameters gave better results than earlier best systems while using less computation. The authors report over a thousand times more capacity with only minor efficiency losses on graphics processor clusters. For an executive, this supports choosing sparse expert designs when scaling language AI, because it can improve quality while controlling compute cost. It informs decisions about model architecture and infrastructure spending.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors built a mixture of experts layer for selective activation at scale. It contains up to thousands of forward processing subnetworks. A trainable gate selects a sparse group of experts for each example, so only part of the layer runs. They inserted this layer between stacked LSTM layers in a convolutional setup for language prediction and translation. The largest model reached 137 billion parameters. On large benchmarks, it outperformed prior best results while costing less computation. They also report over a thousand times more capacity with only small efficiency losses on modern graphics processor clusters. Sparse expert routing can deliver much larger models without proportional compute.

papers.note: The most cited general LLM survey, covers pre-training, post-training, utilisation and evaluation in one frame.
papers.title: A Survey of Large Language Models
papers.explain_beginner: If you wanted one long reading list to understand how something like ChatGPT is actually built, this is it. A large language model is the technology, trained on huge amounts of text, that lets a computer generate humanlike writing and answer questions. This survey, one of the most cited papers in the entire field, walks through the whole pipeline, how these systems learn from raw text in the first place, how they get fine tuned afterward to follow instructions and stay safer, how people actually use them day to day through prompting and step by step reasoning, and how researchers test whether they work at all. It does not report new experiments of its own, it organizes and explains what hundreds of other papers found, and the authors are candid that basic questions like why scaling up model size improves performance are still not theoretically well understood.
papers.explain_business: This survey is most useful to an executive as a map of where competitive advantage in the LLM industry actually sits, because it separates building a competitive model into four distinct capability areas, acquiring and cleaning enough training data and compute, running the alignment and safety tuning that turns a raw model into something usable, building the application layer that turns model output into a product, and running the evaluation infrastructure that proves it works reliably. Few vendors are strong across all four, so this framing is directly useful for build versus buy decisions, since a company evaluating an AI vendor can ask which of these four stages that vendor actually controls versus buys in from someone else. It is a synthesis paper, not new research, so it carries no new regulatory or safety claims on its own, its value is organizing existing knowledge for faster onboarding into a fast moving field.
papers.explain_practitioner: Zhao and colleagues organize the LLM literature into four stages, pre training, covering data curation, architecture choices, and self supervised objectives, post training, covering supervised fine tuning and reinforcement learning from human feedback for alignment, utilization, covering in context learning, prompt engineering, and agentic tool use, and evaluation, covering benchmarks for language ability, reasoning, and safety. Because it is a synthesis rather than original experimental work, its evidentiary basis is the cited literature itself, and the authors have issued repeated revisions to keep pace with a field that moves faster than a single publication cycle. They flag open problems they consider unresolved rather than solved, the theoretical basis for why scale improves capability, how to make training and inference more computationally efficient, how to reliably align model behavior with human intent, and how to build genuinely agentic systems that plan and act reliably. Its main practitioner value is as a citation map into primary sources, not a standalone technical reference on its own.

papers.note: The MultiMedQA and Med-PaLM paper, and the origin of the multi axis human evaluation framework used since.
papers.title: Large language models encode clinical knowledge
papers.explain_beginner: The question, can a large language model, the same basic technology behind general purpose chatbots, actually answer medical exam style questions and open ended clinical questions accurately enough to be useful, or even safely, in medicine. Researchers cared because language models were improving fast on general tasks, but medicine has a much higher bar for being wrong, an answer that sounds fluent and confident but contains a factual error could mislead a patient or clinician, so they needed to test not just whether these models could answer medical questions but whether the answers were actually safe compared with those from real clinicians. The team built a broad medical question benchmark combining professional exam questions, research questions, and real consumer health searches, and found a large language model tuned for this task answered US medical licensing exam style questions correctly about two out of three times, comfortably beating the previous best model, and that with additional tuning aimed at safer long form answers, the rate of answers a human reviewer judged as potentially harmful dropped dramatically, down near the rate seen in answers written by actual clinicians. What it does not settle, the models were still tested mostly on curated exam style questions rather than messy real clinical conversations, and the authors are clear their models remained less reliable overall than clinicians.
papers.explain_business: This paper is the technical proof point that large language models can approach, though not yet match, clinician level safety on written medical question answering, and it is the evidence base that later, more product oriented medical AI assistants were built on. The dramatic gap between the earlier model's 29.7 percent potentially harmful answer rate and the tuned model's 5.9 percent shows that model choice and specific safety tuning matter enormously, a generic large language model without this kind of medical safety tuning should be assumed to produce fluent but wrong answers at a meaningfully higher rate. A 67.6 percent score on licensing exam style questions is good enough to beat prior specialist medical models, but is not the same as being ready for autonomous clinical use, since the authors themselves stress multiple choice questions are easier than real practice. Nothing about this paper constitutes regulatory clearance, it is foundational research, so any product built on this line of work still needs its own separate clinical validation and approval pathway before deployment. This is relevant mainly to teams building or vetting medical question answering or documentation assistants, as a benchmark for what strong safety tuning can achieve.
papers.explain_practitioner: Method, introduced the MultiMedQA benchmark, combining six existing medical question answering datasets spanning professional exams, biomedical research, and consumer queries, plus a newly created dataset of real world consumer health search questions, and evaluated Google's PaLM, an instruction tuned variant called Flan-PaLM, and a further instruction prompt tuned version called Med-PaLM. Flan-PaLM reached 67.6 percent accuracy on MedQA, the US Medical Licensing Exam style multiple choice benchmark, beating the prior best model, a 2.7 billion parameter system called PubMedGPT, by more than 17 percentage points. On human graded long form answers, Med-PaLM cut the rate of answers judged potentially harmful to 5.9 percent, down from 29.7 percent for the earlier Flan-PaLM version, approaching the 5.7 percent rate measured for answers written by actual clinicians, and Med-PaLM's rate of answers reflecting incorrect comprehension of the question fell to 2.1 percent versus 14.3 percent for Flan-PaLM. The authors state clear limitations, MultiMedQA, while broad, is not exhaustive, multiple choice question answering is inherently easier than real clinical workflows, the evaluation covered English language data only, their bias assessment was limited and not a comprehensive audit, and each answer in the human evaluation was judged by only a single clinician or layperson rather than multiple independent raters.

papers.note: Finds that even strong models cannot predict what their own generated code will do, a limitation worth citing in any audit of AI-assisted development.
papers.title: Program Synthesis with Large Language Models
papers.explain_beginner: The paper tested AI systems that can write text on writing short Python programs from plain English requests. It used two sets of tasks, one for beginners and one with harder math word problems. Bigger models solved more tasks, and the best solved about six in ten beginner tasks without extra training. Training on examples helped further. However, even the best models usually could not say what a program would output for a given input. This matters because AI can help write code, but people still need to check whether the code actually behaves correctly.
papers.explain_business: The paper shows that AI systems can turn plain English into short Python programs, and that larger models perform better. Fine tuning on examples improves results, and feedback from people can cut errors by half. The best fine tuned model reached 83.8 percent on harder math problems. However, even strong models generally could not predict what their generated code would output for a given input. For executives, this means AI coding tools can help write code but should not be trusted without review and testing. It informs decisions about where to use AI assisted development, how much human oversight to require, and what validation to build into audits.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors tested language models from 244 million to 137 billion parameters on two new Python benchmarks, MBPP and MathQA-Python, using few shot prompting and fine tuning. MBPP has 974 tasks while MathQA-Python has 23,914 harder text to code problems. Performance improved log linearly with model size. Their largest model reached 59.6 percent on MBPP with a carefully chosen few shot prompt and no code fine tuning. Fine tuning on a reserved dataset part added about ten points for most sizes and the largest fine tuned model reached 83.8 percent on MathQA-Python. Feedback from a person in ordinary language cut errors by half. Models generally could not predict program outputs.

papers.note: The reference mixture of experts design that made sparse trillion parameter models practical.
papers.title: Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity
papers.explain_beginner: The question here is whether a language model can be made dramatically bigger, meaning it holds far more learned parameters, without making it proportionally slower or more expensive to run. Standard transformer models use every single parameter for every word they process, so doubling the model size roughly doubles the computation needed. Fedus, Zoph and Shazeer instead built a model that activates only a small piece of itself for each word, called a sparse mixture of experts, so the total parameter count can grow into the trillions while the actual computation per word stays close to that of a much smaller dense model. They found this approach trained noticeably faster than the standard dense recipe for a given compute budget, and worked consistently across text in 101 different languages. What the paper does not settle is whether such enormous sparse models are worth the engineering cost, they still need enough memory across many machines to hold all the experts even though they only use a few per word, and training a first trillion parameter model of this kind exposed instability problems that took real engineering effort to fix.
papers.explain_business: For an organization deciding how to spend a fixed training compute budget, this paper's practical claim is that sparse expert routing can turn the same GPU or TPU hours into a model that reaches a given quality level up to 4 to 7 times faster than a standard dense model of comparable pretraining setup, or into a substantially more capable model for the same wall clock time. That is a real lever for teams training their own foundation models rather than only fine tuning existing ones. The condition to know before betting on this approach is that the savings are in compute time, not hardware footprint, a trillion parameter sparse model still needs enough combined memory across a cluster to hold every expert, so it suits organizations that already run multi accelerator training clusters more than those hoping to shrink a single server's footprint. It is also now the reference design that later mixture of experts production models built on and refined, so its tradeoffs are a reasonable baseline for evaluating any vendor claiming mixture of experts efficiency.
papers.explain_practitioner: Switch Transformer replaces the standard Mixture-of-Experts routing, which sends each token to multiple experts, with a simplified top-1 router that sends each token to exactly one expert, cutting communication and routing overhead. Built on the T5 pretraining recipe and evaluated against T5-Base, T5-Large and T5-XXL baselines, the switch routed models delivered up to a 7x pretraining speedup over T5-Base and T5-Large under matched compute, and a 4x speedup over T5-XXL, while scaling a sparsely activated model to a trillion parameters on the Colossal Clean Crawled Corpus. On multilingual mT5-Base comparisons the approach improved results across all 101 languages tested, not just a subset. A key engineering contribution the authors report is stabilizing training enough to use lower precision bfloat16 arithmetic for large sparse models, something earlier Mixture-of-Experts work could not do reliably. The tradeoff the authors acknowledge is that these gains come from wall clock and sample efficiency during pretraining, not from a smaller footprint, the trillion parameter model still requires distributed memory across many accelerators to store its experts.

papers.note: Organises evaluation into what, where and how, which is a workable skeleton for the testing section of an audit programme.
papers.title: A Survey on Evaluation of Large Language Models
papers.journal: ACM Transactions on Intelligent Systems and Technology
papers.explain_beginner: This paper reviews ways to test large language models. It groups testing around three questions: what abilities or areas to check, in what situations or uses, and with which techniques and test sets. It covers many areas such as general language tasks, reasoning, medicine, ethics, education, science, social science, and agent uses. It also collects examples where models did well and where they failed. The authors argue testing should be a serious field of its own, because better testing helps build better models and understand risks to society. Open problems remain.
papers.explain_business: This paper reviews how large language models are tested. It groups testing into what should be checked, in which settings, and with which techniques and test sets. It covers many uses, from language and reasoning to healthcare, ethics, education, science, and agents. It notes both successes and failures. For leaders, the practical message is that model evaluation should be planned as an ongoing discipline, not a one time check. That informs decisions about where models are used, how their risks are understood, and how evaluation supports development. Remaining difficulties exist.
papers.explain_practitioner: This survey reviews how large language models are evaluated. It sorts the field into three questions: which abilities or domains are tested, in which situations testing happens, and which techniques and test sets are used. It covers broad language work, reasoning, healthcare, moral questions, learning, physical and social sciences, and tool using agents. It reports both successful and unsuccessful cases across tasks. The key result is a call to treat evaluation as a central discipline that supports better model development. The authors also identify remaining difficulties and keep related open source materials available.

papers.note: The primer most clinicians have actually read, which makes it the right shared reference in client conversations.
papers.title: Large language models in medicine
papers.explain_beginner: The question, stepping back from any one specific model, what is the realistic role for large language models in medicine as a whole, what can they genuinely help with right now, and what makes them risky to lean on. This review appeared at a moment when language models were suddenly capable of passing medical licensing style exam questions, which understandably generated a great deal of excitement, but passing a written exam is a different thing from being safe to use with real patients, and the authors wanted to draw that distinction clearly for a broad medical readership. The authors describe genuine near term value in tasks like turning free text radiology reports into structured, standardized reports, pulling relevant information out of a patient's clinical notes, and drafting discharge summaries, while also documenting specific hazards, models that state false information fluently and confidently, models that reproduce harmful stereotypes absorbed from training text, and a lack of transparency in how any given answer was reached. What it does not settle, performing well on exam style questions does not tell you how a model will behave with an ambiguous, messy real patient case, and the review does not resolve who is accountable when a language model contributes to a bad clinical outcome.
papers.explain_business: This review supports prioritizing documentation and information extraction tasks, structuring radiology reports, drafting discharge summaries, pulling facts from clinical notes, as the safer near term entry point for adopting language models in a clinical setting, over direct diagnostic or treatment decision use. The point that these models cannot meet standard authorship or accountability criteria is directly relevant to liability planning, since if a language model contributes to an error, responsibility still has to rest with the supervising clinician or institution rather than the model itself, and organizations should make that chain of accountability explicit before any deployment. Strong performance on licensing exam questions should not be read by a buyer as evidence of general clinical readiness, since the review explicitly treats exam performance as a weaker signal than real world task performance under ambiguous conditions. Data privacy handling for any tool trained on or processing patient records needs separate legal review, since the paper flags this as a live, unresolved concern rather than something existing tools have already solved. This is relevant now for organizations piloting documentation support, treating the model as an aid a clinician reviews rather than a decision maker.
papers.explain_practitioner: Method, a narrative review of large language model capabilities and limitations for clinical use, covering education, documentation, information extraction, and research support applications, built from the published literature available in 2023 rather than new original benchmarking. The review highlights strong performance on medical licensing style exam questions as an early proof point of capability, and specific practical applications including converting unstructured radiology report text into structured formats and extracting relevant information from electronic health records and clinical notes to support documentation tasks like discharge summaries. Exam question performance is treated explicitly as a weak proxy for real clinical readiness, since exam questions are a controlled, simplified task compared with the ambiguity of live patient care, a distinction the authors draw deliberately rather than treating exam scores as the headline result. The authors identify hallucination, the generation of fluent but factually false content, as a central risk, alongside bias where models have been shown to associate certain demographic groups with negative stereotypes including violence, a black box lack of explainability that makes it hard to trace how an answer was produced, data privacy concerns tied to processing sensitive health information, and an accountability gap since language models cannot fulfill standard authorship or responsibility criteria.

papers.note: The paper argues that combining cognitive psychology and artificial intelligence now makes computer tutors as effective as human tutors, showing working systems for geometry proofs and LISP programming, which matters because it grounds AI in education in tested learning theory.
papers.title: Intelligent Tutoring Systems
papers.authors: John R. Anderson, C. Franklin Boyle, Brian J. Reiser
papers.explain_beginner: This paper says that computers can now teach students as well as human tutors can. The authors built tutoring programs using ideas from psychology about how people learn. One program helped students with geometry proofs, and another helped them write computer programs in LISP. The paper argues that combining thinking research and artificial intelligence makes this possible. This matters because it shows computer tutors can be grounded in tested learning theory, not just guesswork, so students might get effective teaching from machines.
papers.explain_business: This paper indicates that computer-based tutoring can now match human tutors in effectiveness. The authors built working tutors for geometry proofs and LISP programming, using principles from cognitive psychology and artificial intelligence. For decision makers, this means investing in AI tutoring systems grounded in learning theory could deliver quality instruction at scale, potentially reducing reliance on human tutors for certain subjects. It informs choices about where to apply AI in education and supports prioritizing tools built on validated cognitive models rather than ad hoc software.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors argue that cognitive psychology, artificial intelligence, and computer technology have matured enough to build computer tutors matching intelligent human tutors. They developed tutors based on pedagogical principles from the ACT theory of cognition. These systems were built for two domains: teaching students to do geometry proofs and teaching them to write LISP programs. The key result is that such tutors are feasible and effective, demonstrating that grounding instructional design in a cognitive theory can produce working tutoring systems for real tasks.

papers.note: The standard reference on why clinical AI stalls between research and practice, still the clearest statement of the gap.
papers.title: Key challenges for delivering clinical impact with artificial intelligence
papers.explain_beginner: This paper asks why so many impressive sounding results for AI in medicine, models that can supposedly spot cancer or eye disease as well as expert doctors, so rarely turn into something patients actually benefit from in a real hospital. It matters because by 2019 there was already a flood of papers claiming human level performance for medical AI, and this paper's authors, from a leading AI research lab's health division, wanted to explain the specific gap between a model doing well on a test dataset and that same model actually helping patients get better care. They found several concrete reasons for the gap, models trained on old data can quietly get worse as real world clinical practice shifts, models can accidentally learn to rely on irrelevant details in images rather than the medical signal itself, most studies never test whether the model works on patients and equipment from a different hospital than the one it was trained on, and many studies never even measure whether patients ended up healthier as a result. It does not offer a technical fix for these problems, it is a diagnosis of the field's shortcomings, and it stops short of predicting how quickly the field will actually close these gaps.
papers.explain_business: For a hospital, health system, or health tech investor evaluating a diagnostic AI product, the single most actionable fact from this widely cited paper, now with well over a thousand citations, is the external validation statistic, only about 6 percent of published medical imaging AI studies tested performance outside the original training site, so a vendor's headline accuracy number should be treated as unproven for your specific patient population and equipment until validated locally. The ruler artifact example is a concrete illustration of a real procurement risk, a model can post excellent benchmark accuracy while actually keying off an irrelevant correlated detail rather than genuine medical signal, which only shows up once you test on your own different data. The INFANT trial example is the compliance relevant fact for anyone tempted to approve a tool based on accuracy alone, higher measured accuracy did not produce better patient outcomes in that real trial, meaning outcome data, not just accuracy scores, should be a contractual requirement before wider deployment. This applies now, in 2026, to essentially any clinical AI purchase, the specific fix the paper calls for, independent external validation and prospective outcome trials before rollout, remains the standard a buyer should insist on since these problems were structural to the field rather than specific to any one now outdated model.
papers.explain_practitioner: Written as a narrative synthesis surveying dozens of existing studies of medical AI, the paper identifies specific and named failure modes rather than staying abstract. It documents dataset shift, where a model's performance degrades as clinical practice or patient populations change after training, and confounding, citing a memorable concrete example where an image classification algorithm partly relied on the presence of a ruler in dermatology photos, which correlated with malignant lesions being measured, rather than on the lesion itself. It reports that in a survey of 516 published medical imaging AI studies, only about 6 percent performed any external validation on data from outside the original training site, meaning the vast majority of published accuracy claims had not been tested against a genuinely independent population. It also cites a randomized clinical trial, the INFANT trial, as a cautionary case where a system with measurably higher diagnostic accuracy did not translate into better patient outcomes once deployed in an actual clinical trial, directly undercutting the assumption that better benchmark accuracy automatically means better care. The authors state plainly that most published evidence for medical AI comes from retrospective studies rather than prospective trials, and that algorithmic bias, including underperformance on darker skin tones in melanoma detection tools, remains inadequately measured across the field.

papers.note: Documents that social bias can rise with scale in ambiguous contexts, a finding an audit can use to challenge the assumption that bigger models are safer.
papers.title: Beyond the Imitation Game: Quantifying and extrapolating the capabilities of language models
papers.explain_beginner: Researchers built a large test called BIG-bench to check what language models can and cannot do. It has 204 tasks from many fields, created by hundreds of people. They tested several model families and compared them with human experts. Bigger models generally scored better and judged their own confidence better, but still did poorly overall and far below people. Different model types behaved similarly, though sparse models helped. Some skills improved steadily, often when memorized knowledge mattered. Other skills appeared suddenly, often when tasks needed several steps. Social bias grew with size in unclear situations, but prompting could reduce it. This helps researchers prepare for new abilities and harmful effects.
papers.explain_business: Executives should not treat model size as a guarantee of safety or quality. A large benchmark with 204 tasks from many fields tested several model families, from millions to hundreds of billions of parameters, against human experts. Larger models improved, but their absolute performance and confidence estimates stayed weak and below people. Different model types performed similarly, though sparse designs helped. Some abilities grew steadily from memorized knowledge, while others appeared suddenly and depended on multi-step tasks or fragile measures. Social bias increased with scale in unclear contexts, but prompting could reduce it. This informs decisions to fund evaluation, human baselines, and bias testing rather than assuming scale is enough.
papers.explain_practitioner: Researchers assembled BIG-bench, a 204-task suite contributed by 450 authors from 132 institutions. Tasks span linguistics, child development, math, common sense, biology, physics, social bias, software. They evaluated OpenAI GPT models, Google dense transformers, and sparse transformers in the Switch style across sizes from millions to hundreds of billions of parameters. Human experts completed every task as a baseline. Results show scores and confidence estimates rise with size but stay weak and below human raters. Model classes behave similarly, with sparse models helping. Gradual, predictable improvements involve knowledge or memorization. Sudden breakthroughs involve multiple steps, components, or brittle metrics. Social bias rises with scale in ambiguous contexts, though prompting helps.

papers.note: A widely cited overview for clinical staff, useful as background reading to issue before an audit interview round.
papers.title: Revolutionizing healthcare: the role of artificial intelligence in clinical practice
papers.explain_beginner: This review examines how artificial intelligence is used in clinical care. It says AI can help doctors identify illnesses, choose treatments, and support patients. By studying large amounts of health data, AI can spot patterns and sometimes do better than people on certain tasks. The paper reports possible gains such as greater accuracy, lower costs, saved time, and fewer mistakes. It also mentions care tailored to individuals, better medicine amounts, health planning for groups, online helpers, emotional and mental care, and teaching patients. However, data privacy, unfair bias, and the need for skilled people must be handled. This matters because hospitals need to adopt AI carefully and responsibly.
papers.explain_business: For executives, this review suggests AI can support clinical operations by improving identifying illnesses, choosing treatments, and lab tests. It may raise accuracy, cut costs, save time, and reduce human errors. Practical uses include care tailored to individuals, setting medicine amounts, managing health across groups, guidelines, online helpers, emotional and mental care, and teaching patients. The paper notes effects on trust between patients and doctors. Adoption is not just automation, it should enhance care. The decision it informs is whether and how to introduce AI responsibly. Leaders should plan for data privacy and unfair bias controls, retain skilled people, and equip staff with the knowledge and tools needed for implementation.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors reviewed indexed literature from PubMed/Medline, Scopus, and EMBASE. They included English articles. Their question was how AI affects healthcare settings and what outcomes follow. The review reports that AI can improve identifying illnesses, choosing treatments, and lab tests. Using large datasets to find patterns, AI may exceed human performance. Reported benefits include higher accuracy, lower costs, time savings, and fewer human errors. Uses include care tailored to individuals, setting medicine amounts, managing health across groups, guidelines, online helpers, emotional and mental care, and teaching patients. The authors conclude AI can assist diagnosis and clinician decisions, but data privacy, unfair bias, and the need for skilled people remain challenges.

papers.note: The paper argues universities should respond to ChatGPT with clear policies, staff training and detection methods rather than bans, because the tool offers real benefits alongside cheating risks, which matters as institutions decide how to govern AI in teaching and assessment.
papers.title: Chatting and cheating: Ensuring academic integrity in the era of ChatGPT
papers.authors: Debby Cotton, Peter A. Cotton, J. Reuben Shipway
papers.explain_beginner: This paper looks at ChatGPT in universities and asks whether it helps or hurts learning. It says the tool can get students more involved, working together, and able to access help more easily. But it also makes cheating and copying easier to do. The authors argue that banning ChatGPT is not the best answer. Instead, universities should make clear rules, train staff, and use ways to spot cheating. The main point is that schools can handle the risks if they act early and focus on honest use.
papers.explain_business: For leaders in education, this paper says ChatGPT brings real benefits and real risks, so a simple ban is not the right move. The authors recommend clear policies, staff training, and detection methods to support honest use. This informs decisions about how to govern AI in teaching and assessment. Instead of blocking the tool, institutions should set rules, build staff capability, and put checks in place. That way they can protect academic integrity while still allowing the engagement, collaboration, and accessibility benefits the paper describes.
papers.explain_practitioner: The paper reviews both the upsides and downsides of ChatGPT in higher education. It notes benefits such as student engagement, collaboration, and accessibility, alongside concerns about academic honesty and plagiarism. The authors examine why detecting and preventing dishonest use is hard, then propose strategies for ethical use. These include creating policies and procedures, offering training and support, and applying detection and prevention methods. The conclusion is that a proactive, ethical approach lets universities manage the challenges while still gaining the opportunities the tool provides.

papers.note: This review found that human tutoring helps students far less than commonly believed, and that intelligent tutoring systems are nearly as effective, which matters because it suggests schools can rely on software for tutoring gains at much lower cost.
papers.title: The Relative Effectiveness of Human Tutoring, Intelligent Tutoring Systems, and Other Tutoring Systems
papers.explain_beginner: This review looked at studies that compared students who received tutoring with students who learned the same material without tutoring. People often assume human tutors are far better than computer programs. The review found this is not true. Human tutoring produced a moderate improvement, and computer tutoring systems designed to respond step by step produced almost the same improvement. This matters because it suggests schools may get similar learning benefits from software as from human tutors, which could make extra help available to more students at lower cost.
papers.explain_business: Leaders often assume that only human tutors deliver strong learning gains and that software is a weak substitute. This review of comparison studies found otherwise. Human tutoring improved outcomes by a moderate amount, and intelligent tutoring systems achieved almost the same result. The practical implication is that software based tutoring can deliver learning benefits close to those of human tutors, likely at much lower cost and with easier scaling. This informs decisions about where to invest limited instructional budgets, suggesting that intelligent tutoring software deserves serious consideration alongside human tutoring programs.
papers.explain_practitioner: The author reviewed experiments comparing human tutoring, computer tutoring, and instruction covering the same content without tutoring. Computer systems were grouped by interaction granularity: answer-based, step-based, and substep-based. Intelligent tutoring systems typically use step or substep interaction, while other systems use answer-based interfaces. The common belief was that finer granularity yields larger effects, with expected effect sizes of 0.3, 1.0, and 2.0 for answer-based systems, intelligent tutoring systems, and adult human tutors. The review did not confirm this. Human tutoring measured 0.79, and intelligent tutoring systems measured 0.76, nearly equal.

papers.note: A survey of 399 Hong Kong university students found generally positive views of generative AI for personalized learning and writing support, but also concerns about accuracy, privacy, ethics and career impact, so educators and policymakers should address these worries when integrating such tools.
papers.title: Students’ voices on generative AI: perceptions, benefits, and challenges in higher education
papers.authors: Cecilia Ka Yuk Chan, Wenjie Hu
papers.explain_beginner: This paper asked 399 university students in Hong Kong how they feel about generative AI tools like ChatGPT. Most students had a positive view. They saw these tools as helpful for learning in ways suited to them, for writing, for sharing ideas, and for research and analysis. At the same time, students worried about whether the tools give correct information, about privacy, about ethics, and about how the tools might affect their personal growth, their future jobs, and society's values. The paper matters because it shows that students are open to these tools but also have real concerns that schools and policymakers should take seriously.
papers.explain_business: This study surveyed 399 Hong Kong university students and found broad openness to generative AI in learning, with students valuing personalized support, writing help, and research assistance. However, students also flagged risks around accuracy, privacy, ethics, and impacts on personal development, careers, and societal values. For executives in education or edtech, the practical message is that adoption can move forward, but trust and safeguards matter as much as features. The decision this informs is how to roll out generative AI: invest in accuracy checks, privacy protections, and clear ethical guidelines, and involve students in shaping policy, rather than treating the technology as a simple add-on.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors surveyed 399 undergraduate and postgraduate students across disciplines in Hong Kong to map their perceptions of generative AI in higher education. The study examined familiarity, willingness to engage, perceived benefits and challenges, and views on effective integration. Students were generally positive, citing personalized learning support, writing and brainstorming help, and research and analysis capabilities. They also raised concerns about accuracy, privacy, ethics, and effects on personal development, career prospects, and societal values. Framing the findings through Biggs' 3P model, the authors argue that student perceptions shape learning approaches and outcomes, so educators and policymakers should use these insights to design responsible integration guidelines.

papers.note: The foundational indirect injection paper with a security taxonomy, still the clearest reference for explaining the risk to a client.
papers.title: Not What You've Signed Up For: Compromising Real-World LLM-Integrated Applications with Indirect Prompt Injection
papers.journal: Proceedings of the 16th ACM Workshop on Artificial Intelligence and Security
papers.explain_beginner: This paper explains a new risk for apps that use large language models. Normally people think the user gives the instructions. The authors show that an attacker can instead place hidden instructions inside information the app later looks up, such as a webpage or document. Because the model may treat that data as commands, the attacker can affect the app without ever talking to it directly. The paper sorts these dangers into categories, including stealing data, spreading itself, and polluting information. It also tested real systems like Bing Chat and code helpers. The main point is that many current systems lack good defenses, so builders and users need to be careful.
papers.explain_business: For executives, this paper warns that adding an LLM to a product creates a new security exposure. If the system reads outside content, such as web pages or documents, an attacker can hide instructions in that content and influence the application without direct access. The authors show this can lead to stealing data, attacks that spread themselves, polluted information, and control over app actions or API calls. They demonstrated the problem on real services, including Bing Chat, and on synthetic GPT-4 applications. Because effective defenses are still lacking, leaders should treat LLM integrations as risky and decide whether to deploy or rely on them before robust protections exist.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors study LLM integrated applications where retrieved content can be interpreted as instructions, not just data. They examine indirect prompt injection, where an adversary plants prompts in material likely to be fetched during inference, so no direct user interface is needed. They build a security taxonomy covering stealing data, self-spreading, polluted information, and other risks. They then test attacks on real systems, including Bing Chat and code completion engines, plus GPT-4 synthetic applications. The key result is that retrieved prompts can act like executable code, alter application behavior, and control whether and how other APIs are called. The paper notes effective mitigations remain scarce.

papers.note: Shows two model families are closely related, which matters when an audit has to decide whether architecture-specific controls transfer.
papers.title: Transformers are SSMs: Generalized Models and Efficient Algorithms Through Structured State Space Duality
papers.explain_beginner: The paper tests a network security tool that reads raw packet bytes and predicts the next byte. It compares two model designs, a Transformer and a Mamba-2 state space model, using the same benign data and attack families. The Transformer caught 15.0% of zero-day attack windows with very few false alarms, while Mamba-2 caught 14.1% with more false alarms. So swapping attention for a state space design did not improve detection here. Its benefit is efficiency: similar results with fewer parameters, linear processing, and constant memory streaming. Threshold choice mattered more than model choice. Limits include low recall, blindness to encrypted payloads, and one training corpus.
papers.explain_business: This paper evaluates a raw-byte network anomaly detector for zero-day attacks. It compares a Transformer with a Mamba-2 state space model. Detection is modest, 15% or 14% of zero-day windows, with few false positives. The state space model does not detect better, but it uses fewer parameters, linear time, and constant memory. The bigger operational lever is alert threshold selection, not model family. EVT thresholds depend only on the benign tail, so they remain stable across labelled attack families, unlike Youden. Because the two model families are closely related, architecture-specific controls may transfer, which matters for audits. Decisions should weigh efficiency against recall, encrypted payload blindness, and one training corpus.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors built a detector that does not tokenize, treating raw packet bytes as a next-byte prediction. Per-window surprise becomes alerts. They compared a causal Transformer against a smaller Mamba-2 selective state space model. At the EVT point, the Transformer detected 15.0% of zero-day windows at 0.038% false positives, while Mamba-2 detected 14.1% at 0.1%. Replacing self-attention with a state space backbone did not improve detection. Its advantage was architectural: comparable detection at 57% of parameters, linear scaling in sequence length, and streaming with constant memory. Threshold selection affected deployed behaviour more than backbone choice. EVT thresholds, fitted on the benign tail, were invariant to labelled attack families, unlike Youden.

papers.note: The paper argues that AI is becoming embedded in university teaching, learning, support and administration, and that institutions must address adoption challenges to shape how higher education evolves, which matters to anyone tracking AI's growing role in education.
papers.title: Exploring the impact of artificial intelligence on teaching and learning in higher education
papers.explain_beginner: This paper looks at how artificial intelligence is starting to appear in universities, not just in one area but across teaching, learning, student support, and administration. The authors ask what this means for how students learn and how universities operate and change over time. They note that new technology is arriving quickly and being adopted faster than before. The main point is that universities face real challenges in adopting AI well, and that these choices will shape what higher education becomes. This matters because AI is becoming a normal part of university life.
papers.explain_business: For executives, this paper signals that artificial intelligence is spreading through universities in teaching, learning, student support, and administration, and that adoption is speeding up. The authors argue that institutions must actively address the challenges of adopting these technologies, because those choices will influence how higher education develops. In practice, this means leaders should treat AI adoption as a strategic issue that touches many parts of the institution, not a single department's project. The decision it informs is whether and how to plan for AI adoption deliberately, so the institution helps shape its future rather than reacting to it.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors examine the emergence of artificial intelligence in higher education and its educational implications for student learning and institutional teaching and evolution. They consider recent technological advances and the accelerating adoption of new technologies in universities, then use these trends to anticipate the future character of higher education where AI is embedded throughout the institution. The paper identifies challenges that institutions and student learning face when adopting these technologies across teaching, learning, student support, and administration, and it outlines directions for further research. The key contribution is framing adoption challenges and a research agenda rather than reporting experimental results.

papers.note: This review found ChatGPT's accuracy varies by subject, strong in economics but weak in maths, and can assist teaching while risking fake information and plagiarism, so schools should update assessments, policies and training now.
papers.title: What Is the Impact of ChatGPT on Education? A Rapid Review of the Literature
papers.explain_beginner: A review looked at early research on ChatGPT in education, covering December 2022 to February 2023. It found the chatbot's accuracy depends on the subject. It did very well in economics, was okay at programming, and struggled with mathematics. ChatGPT can help teachers create materials and give students a virtual tutor for questions and group work. But it can also produce false information and let students avoid plagiarism checks. The review says schools and universities should act quickly to change how they assess students, update their rules, and train both teachers and students.
papers.explain_business: This review shows ChatGPT's reliability depends on the subject, strong in economics, weaker in maths, which matters for any organization using it in training or education products. It can support instructors and learners, but it can also generate false information and help users evade plagiarism checks. The practical implication is that schools and universities should not wait. Leaders should update assessment methods and institutional policies now, and invest in training for instructors and students. This informs decisions about adopting AI tools, managing academic integrity risk, and funding staff and student readiness programs.
papers.explain_practitioner: This rapid review analyzed 50 articles from relevant databases and Google Scholar, published December 2022 to February 2023, using open, axial, and selective coding. It examined ChatGPT's capabilities across subjects, educational uses, and researcher-identified issues. Performance ranged from outstanding in economics to satisfactory in programming to unsatisfactory in mathematics. The tool can assist instructors with course materials and suggestions, and act as a virtual tutor answering questions and supporting collaboration. Challenges include incorrect or fake information and bypassing plagiarism detectors. The author recommends immediate updates to assessment methods and institutional policies, plus instructor training and student education.

papers.note: A continuously refreshed coding benchmark, the working model for contamination free evaluation.
papers.title: LiveCodeBench: Holistic and Contamination Free Evaluation of Large Language Models for Code
papers.explain_beginner: Coding benchmarks used to grade AI models are usually created once and then reused for years, which creates a problem, if a model's training data happens to include the exact test questions or extremely similar ones, that model looks like a better programmer than it actually is. Jain and coauthors built LiveCodeBench to sidestep this by continuously pulling in new programming problems from live coding contest sites, LeetCode, AtCoder, and CodeForces, dated after a known cutoff, so the questions are guaranteed to postdate a model's training data. The benchmark also expands what measuring coding ability means, beyond generating code from a description it also tests whether a model can predict what a piece of code will output, catch and fix its own mistakes, and actually execute logic correctly, not just produce plausible looking syntax. Testing 52 different language models this way, the authors found evidence that some models perform noticeably better on older, likely seen benchmark problems than on freshly collected ones, a sign those older scores were inflated. The paper stops short of naming a fix for contamination in existing benchmarks, its contribution is a live, continuously refreshed alternative.
papers.explain_business: For a business selecting a code generation model based on public benchmark leaderboards, this paper's practical warning is that scores on long standing static benchmarks like HumanEval should be treated with real skepticism, since the underlying test problems are old enough that some models may have effectively seen them during training. LiveCodeBench offers a more trustworthy alternative for comparing models because its problem set only includes contest problems dated after public knowledge cutoffs, and because it also measures whether a model can execute and self-correct code, not just produce code that looks right, which is closer to how a coding assistant is actually used in practice. The practical action for a team evaluating coding assistants is to check whether a vendor's reported benchmark numbers come from a contamination controlled source like this one, and to weight self-repair and execution prediction performance alongside raw code generation scores, since those better predict real world debugging and iteration usefulness in a development workflow.
papers.explain_practitioner: LiveCodeBench sources 400 problems published between May 2023 and May 2024 from LeetCode, AtCoder, and CodeForces, tagging each with its release date so evaluation can be restricted to problems released after any given model's training cutoff, directly addressing benchmark contamination rather than trying to detect it after the fact. Beyond standard code generation, the benchmark evaluates three additional capabilities, self-repair, where a model must fix code that failed its own tests, code execution, predicting a program's runtime behavior, and test output prediction, predicting what a given input produces without running the code, giving a more holistic capability profile than pass or fail generation scores alone. Across 18 base and 34 instruction tuned models, 52 total, the authors report empirical evidence of contamination and overfitting to older static benchmarks such as HumanEval, models that score unusually well on older benchmarks relative to their LiveCodeBench performance are treated as a signal of prior exposure. The authors release all prompts, model completions, and an evaluation toolkit, but the comparison is necessarily a moving target, since the live problem set keeps growing and scores from different evaluation dates are not perfectly comparable.

papers.note: This early review argues ChatGPT can produce human-like prose that threatens traditional assessment, so universities should rethink how they evaluate learning, weighing both opportunities and risks for students, teachers and institutions.
papers.title: ChatGPT: Bullshit spewer or the end of traditional assessments in higher education?
papers.authors: Jürgen Rudolph, Samson Tan, Shannon Tan
papers.explain_beginner: This paper looks at ChatGPT, a chatbot that can write surprisingly human-like text in seconds. The authors reviewed existing research and tried the tool themselves. They found that ChatGPT could make traditional ways of testing students, like essays and exams done at home, much harder to trust. The paper says universities need to rethink how they check what students have learned. It also points out both possible benefits and risks for students, teachers and schools. The main message is that assessment must change because AI writing tools are here to stay.
papers.explain_business: For executives in higher education, this paper signals that AI chatbots like ChatGPT can produce convincing written work, which undermines conventional assessment such as take-home essays. The authors recommend that institutions rethink how they evaluate learning and consider both opportunities and risks for students, teachers and the organisation. The decision this informs is whether to invest in new assessment methods, staff training and policies around AI use. It also highlights OpenAI's shift from non-profit to commercial business, showing that AI tools will keep advancing, so institutions should act rather than wait.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors conducted an extensive literature review and hands-on experiments with ChatGPT, a variant of OpenAI's GPT language model. They describe its functionality, strengths and limitations, then position it within Artificial Intelligence in Education research. They examine student-facing, teacher-facing and system-facing applications and analyse opportunities and threats. The paper is among the first peer-reviewed journal articles on ChatGPT in higher education. It concludes with recommendations for students, teachers and institutions, many focused on assessment. The key result is that ChatGPT's human-like prose threatens traditional assessment, so evaluation methods need rethinking.

papers.note: Added because a reader's question on this site drew on it (1 time so far). The page exists so the next reader finds it in the answer.
papers.title: Chain-Of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.authors: Jason Wei, Xuezhi Wang, Dale Schuurmans, Maarten Bosma, Brian Ichter, Fei Xia, Ed Chi, Quoc V Le, Denny Zhou

papers.note: This review of 138 studies from 2016 to 2022 finds AI in higher education growing fast, led by China and education departments, mostly used for assessment, prediction, tutoring and managing learning, which shows where the field is heading and what remains unstudied.
papers.title: Artificial intelligence in higher education: the state of the field
papers.explain_beginner: This paper reviewed 138 studies about artificial intelligence in higher education from 2016 to 2022. It found that publications grew very quickly in 2021 and 2022, rising two to three times above earlier years. Research happened on six continents, and China replaced the US as the leader. Education departments became the main source of researchers. Most studies focused on undergraduate students and on language learning. AI was mostly used for assessment, prediction, tutoring, helping as an assistant, and managing student learning. The review also points to gaps, including newer tools like ChatGPT, showing where future research could go.
papers.explain_business: This review of 138 studies shows AI in higher education is expanding fast, especially in 2021 and 2022, with China now leading research output. Most work targets undergraduate students and language learning, and the main uses are assessment, prediction, tutoring, AI assistance, and managing learning. For executives, this signals where adoption and investment are concentrating, and it highlights that instructors and managers are studied far less than students. The identified gaps, including newer tools such as ChatGPT, suggest areas where current evidence is thin, which can inform planning, procurement, and research priorities.
papers.explain_practitioner: This systematic review followed PRISMA principles and protocol, identifying 138 articles from 2016 to 2022 for full examination. Data were extracted and coded using a priori and grounded coding. Publications rose nearly two to three times in 2021 and 2022 compared with prior years. Research spanned six continents, with leadership shifting from the US to China, and education departments becoming the dominant researcher affiliation. Undergraduates were the most studied group at 72 percent, and language learning was the most common subject. Five usage codes emerged: assessment or evaluation, predicting, AI assistant, intelligent tutoring system, and managing student learning.

papers.note: Preregistered experiment, 40 percent time reduction and 18 percent quality gain on professional writing tasks.
papers.title: Experimental evidence on the productivity effects of generative artificial intelligence
papers.explain_beginner: This study asks whether letting a professional use ChatGPT for a real writing task makes that task faster and better, and whether the benefit is the same for everyone or mostly helps people who were struggling before. The researchers recruited college educated professionals, people who write for a living in roles like marketing, HR, consulting, and grant writing, and had each of them complete two writing tasks specific to their own occupation, randomly letting some use ChatGPT and not others. This matters because a lot of early claims about AI boosting productivity came from surveys or small demos rather than a controlled test with real professional tasks and independent grading. The study found that ChatGPT access cut the time spent on a task substantially and raised the graded quality of the output, and the people who benefited most were those who had been the weakest writers beforehand, essentially closing much of the gap between strong and weak performers. It does not tell us what happens when this scales across an entire labor market, including whether demand for these writing services changes, and the authors note that real world adoption outside the lab was still far from universal even among people who had just been shown how useful it was.
papers.explain_business: The direct business relevance is a specific, experimentally measured range, roughly 40 percent faster task completion and 18 percent higher quality scores for professional writing tasks, which gives a concrete benchmark against which to judge an internal generative AI writing pilot rather than relying on anecdote. The equity relevant finding is that these tools appear to help weaker or newer writers the most, narrowing performance gaps across a team, which is relevant to how a manager might target training or access rather than assuming senior staff benefit equally. The important caveat for planning is the adoption gap the study itself surfaces, even after being shown the tool's benefit in a controlled setting, a large share of participants were not using it on the job weeks later, which points to a real friction between demonstrated capability in a study and actual daily use, often due to unfamiliarity or workplace access restrictions rather than the tool's capability. This applies now to any organization with knowledge workers doing occupation specific writing, and the harder question the study leaves open, how the whole labor market and pricing for these services shifts once adoption is widespread, is not one a single company's pilot can answer on its own.
