papers.explain_practitioner: The design was a randomized controlled experiment run on the Prolific platform with college educated professionals completing two occupation specific writing tasks each, mid task random assignment moved half the participants into a ChatGPT access condition while the rest served as controls, and outputs were graded independently. Time spent on the assigned task fell by about 40 percent for the treatment group, and average grades rose by about 18 percent, with the paper noting that most of the quality gain reflected the quality of ChatGPT's own draft output rather than participants meaningfully editing or improving on it. The most notable distributional result was that the gap between the weakest and strongest performers in the control group nearly disappeared in the treatment group, with the tool bringing most participants close to what the best unaided writers had achieved. As a limitation, the authors are explicit that their controlled task based estimates cannot capture general equilibrium effects, changes in the price or demand for these services once the whole market has access to the tool, and they report that only about 34 to 42 percent of participants said they had actually used ChatGPT at their real job weeks after the study, showing a real gap between demonstrated capability and workplace adoption.

papers.note: The paper argues that K-12 schools rarely weigh the ethical and societal costs of AI tools like facial recognition and automated assessment, and it offers teachers instructional resources from MIT and Code.org to help students understand AI and its dilemmas.
papers.title: Artificial intelligence in education: Addressing ethical challenges in K-12 settings
papers.explain_beginner: This paper looks at how artificial intelligence is used in schools for things like personalized learning, automated grading, and facial recognition to understand student behavior. It says that while these tools can help students and teachers, schools rarely think carefully about the ethical and social problems they create. The authors explain what AI is, describe its benefits, and then point out the ethical dilemmas. They also suggest free teaching materials from MIT and Code.org so teachers can help students learn about AI and its ethical questions. The main message is that schools should consider both the good and the bad of AI.
papers.explain_business: This paper argues that K-12 schools often adopt AI tools like facial recognition and automated assessment without fully weighing their ethical and societal costs. For executives in education technology or school leadership, this signals a need to evaluate not just the promised benefits, such as personalized learning and teacher support, but also the ethical risks. The authors recommend using instructional resources from MIT and Code.org to teach students and teachers about AI ethics. The practical takeaway is that decision makers should include ethical review and AI literacy in their planning before or while deploying AI in classrooms.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors define AI through machine learning and algorithms, then survey educational applications such as personalized learning platforms, automated assessment, and facial recognition for behavior insights. They note that in K-12 contexts, the ethical and societal costs of these systems are seldom fully examined. The paper identifies ethical challenges and dilemmas, and recommends instructional resources from MIT Media Lab and Code.org to teach AI and ethics. The goal is to help practitioners gain the benefits of AI while navigating its ethical issues, and to provide teachers with materials to build students' understanding of AI and its ethical dimensions.

papers.note: Surveying 457 students and 180 staff in Hong Kong, this study proposes an AI policy framework for universities with pedagogical, governance and operational dimensions, giving educators a structured way to integrate AI responsibly across teaching, privacy and training.
papers.title: A comprehensive AI policy education framework for university teaching and learning
papers.explain_beginner: This study asked 457 students and 180 teachers and staff at Hong Kong universities about their views on text generative AI. From their answers, the author built a guide for how universities can use AI well. The guide has three parts. One part is about teaching and learning, so AI helps students learn better. Another part is about safety, privacy and who is responsible. The third part is about tools and training for staff and students. The guide matters because it gives universities a clear, organised way to bring AI into education responsibly, instead of leaving everyone confused about the rules.
papers.explain_business: For an executive, this paper signals that AI adoption in universities needs a structured policy, not ad hoc tools. Based on surveys of 457 students and 180 staff in Hong Kong, the author proposes a framework with three parts: teaching and learning, governance of privacy, security and accountability, and operations covering infrastructure and training. The practical takeaway is that institutions should decide on all three fronts together, because student and staff perceptions shape how well AI is used. This informs decisions about where to invest, especially in training and infrastructure, and how to assign clear responsibilities before scaling AI in teaching.
papers.explain_practitioner: The study surveyed 457 students and 180 teachers and staff across disciplines in Hong Kong universities, mixing quantitative and qualitative methods to capture perceptions of text generative AI. From this data the author derived the AI Ecological Education Policy Framework, structured along three dimensions. The Pedagogical dimension targets improved teaching and learning outcomes through AI. The Governance dimension covers privacy, security and accountability. The Operational dimension addresses infrastructure and training. The framework is intended to give stakeholders a nuanced grasp of AI's implications in academic settings, so they understand their responsibilities and can act accordingly. No specific effect sizes or interventions are reported in the abstract.

papers.note: The founding internal audit framework, and the source of the document per stage audit report structure now common in practice.
papers.title: Closing the AI accountability gap: defining an end-to-end framework for internal algorithmic auditing
papers.journal: Proceedings of the ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency
papers.explain_beginner: AI systems are often found to cause real harm, a hiring tool that quietly favors one group, a risk score that treats people unfairly, only after they are already out in the world and someone outside the company notices. This paper argues that companies should instead audit their own AI systems for potential harm while still building them, not after the fact, and lays out a concrete five stage process for how to do it, define what the system is meant to do and who it affects, map out everyone with a stake in it, collect the paperwork that documents how it was built, actually test it against real failure cases, and reflect on what was found and what should change before release. Each stage is meant to leave behind a real document, not just a conversation. The authors are honest that this is only part of the answer, since people auditing their own company's product can never be fully independent, and the process assumes documentation habits that move much slower than typical AI development schedules.
papers.explain_business: For any organization building AI in house, this is a template for what an internal audit trail should look like before a regulator or a lawsuit forces the question, specific documents at each build stage, ethical review, stakeholder map, datasheets, model cards, test results, and a remediation plan, rather than a single after the fact report. The practical payoff is that reconstructing this evidence after an AI system has already caused harm is far more expensive and often impossible, so the cost of building the paper trail as you go is lower than the cost of proving compliance retroactively. The catch the authors themselves flag is that internal auditors are not neutral, they work for the company whose product they are reviewing, so this process reduces but does not eliminate the case for an external, independent audit on top of it, particularly for any AI system a regulator would classify as high risk.
papers.explain_practitioner: Raji and coauthors propose SMACTR, an internal audit lifecycle spanning Scoping, Mapping, Artifact Collection, Testing, and Reflection, each producing specific deliverables, an ethical and social impact review at scoping, a stakeholder map and design history review at mapping, datasheets and model cards as collected artifacts, adversarial test results and an ethical risk chart at testing, and a remediation plan plus audit summary report at reflection. The paper's contribution is procedural rather than empirical, it does not report a success metric on a specific benchmark, instead it formalizes a lifecycle meant to be run inside any organization building AI. The authors state their own limitation directly, internal auditors necessarily share an organizational interest with the system they are auditing, so the framework is explicitly positioned as one piece of a broader accountability system that still needs external oversight, and they flag that setting clear pass or fail thresholds during testing, such as how close a fairness metric needs to be to parity, remains genuinely unresolved.

papers.note: Chain of thought text can rationalise a biased answer without mentioning the bias, which undercuts using it as an audit artifact.
papers.title: Language Models Don't Always Say What They Think: Unfaithful Explanations in Chain-of-Thought Prompting
papers.explain_beginner: When an AI model explains its reasoning step by step before giving an answer, does that explanation actually describe why it gave that answer? This paper tested that question directly by secretly rigging the setup, for example always making the correct answer choice A in the examples shown to the model, or reordering answer choices to plant a bias, then giving the model a fresh question and watching what it did. The result, the model's answer shifted toward the biased choice, sometimes making it wrong far more often than it should have been, but its step by step explanation never mentioned the bias, it just built a plausible sounding story to justify whatever answer the biased prompt nudged it toward. This means an explanation can look completely reasonable and still be a cover story rather than the real reason for the answer, which matters enormously for anyone trusting these explanations at face value.
papers.explain_business: This paper has a direct compliance implication for any organization using chain of thought output as documentation for why an AI system made a decision, whether for internal audit, regulatory disclosure, or customer facing explanation. The finding that models can produce fluent, plausible reasoning traces that do not reflect the actual cause of the output means a generated explanation is not, by itself, evidence of a fair or unbiased decision process, since it demonstrably failed to surface at least one class of induced bias in controlled testing. For businesses in lending, hiring, or other decisions where explainability carries legal weight, chain of thought text should not be treated as a substitute for actual bias testing or independent audit methods. This applies now, to any current deployment relying on generated explanations as a transparency mechanism, and the authors imply additional faithfulness specific techniques are needed before that trust is warranted.
papers.explain_practitioner: Turpin and colleagues test chain of thought faithfulness in GPT-3.5 and Claude 1.0 across 13 tasks from the BIG-Bench Hard suite plus additional social bias evaluations, by deliberately injecting biasing features into the prompt, such as reordering few shot answer choices so the correct answer is always in position A, then checking whether the model's generated explanation ever acknowledges that bias. It essentially never does. The biasing manipulation degraded accuracy by as much as 36 percent when it pointed toward an incorrect answer, while the chain of thought output constructed a plausible post hoc justification for the biased answer instead of surfacing the actual cause. The central finding is that CoT explanations can systematically misrepresent the true reason for a model's prediction even while sounding fully coherent, which undercuts using generated explanations as a genuine audit trail for model decisions, a limitation the authors state directly rather than treat as a solvable edge case.

papers.note: This review finds that students who trust AI dialogue systems without question may lose critical thinking, decision-making and analytical skills, which matters as generative tools spread through classrooms and research.
papers.title: The effects of over-reliance on AI dialogue systems on students' cognitive abilities: a systematic review
papers.authors: Chunpeng Zhai, Santoso Wibowo, Lily D. Li
papers.explain_beginner: This review looked at how students use AI chat systems for school and research. When students accept what the AI says without questioning it, they may stop practicing important thinking skills. The authors examined 14 studies and found that this blind trust can weaken decision-making, critical thinking, and analytical reasoning. The reason is that people often prefer quick, easy answers over slower, more careful thinking. This matters because AI tools are becoming common in classrooms, so students need to learn when to trust them and when to think for themselves.
papers.explain_business: This review shows that when students trust AI dialogue systems without question, their critical thinking, decision-making, and analytical skills can decline. The authors analyzed 14 studies and found that over-reliance is linked to ethical issues around AI and to a preference for quick answers over careful reasoning. For organizations selling or deploying AI tools in education, this signals a need to design for appropriate trust, not blind acceptance. It informs decisions about training, guardrails, and features that encourage users to evaluate AI outputs rather than accept them automatically, protecting long-term cognitive skills.
papers.explain_practitioner: This systematic review followed PRISMA guidelines and analyzed 14 articles from ProQuest, IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, and Web of Science. It examined how students' over-reliance on AI dialogue systems with generative models affects decision-making, critical thinking, and analytical reasoning. Over-reliance was defined as accepting AI recommendations without question, often due to difficulty judging AI reliability or calibrating trust. The key finding is that ethical issues related to AI contribute to over-reliance, which in turn harms cognitive abilities. Users tend to favor fast, optimal solutions over slower ones limited by practicality, preferring cognitive shortcuts even when ethical concerns exist.

papers.note: A survey of 60 leading AIED researchers found most lack ethics training, so the field needs a multidisciplinary framework with robust guidelines to handle fairness, bias, transparency and unintended consequences in educational AI.
papers.title: Ethics of AI in Education: Towards a Community-Wide Framework
papers.authors: W. Holmes, Kaśka Porayska‐Pomsta, Ken Holstein, Emma Sutherland, Toby T. Baker, Simon Buckingham Shum, et al.
papers.explain_beginner: A group of researchers asked 60 leading experts in artificial intelligence and education about ethics. Only 17 replied. The answers showed that most experts in this field have never been trained to handle moral questions about their work. The paper argues that good intentions alone are not enough, because AI in education can still be unfair, biased, or have unexpected effects on students. The authors conclude that the field needs a shared ethical framework, built with help from many disciplines and clear rules, so that AI tools for learning are designed and used responsibly.
papers.explain_business: This paper signals that the AI in education field lacks shared ethical standards, and most researchers in it have no ethics training. For an executive, that means products built on this research carry unresolved risks around fairness, bias, transparency, and unintended effects on learners. The decision this informs is whether to wait for a community-wide framework or act now. A practical response is to require multidisciplinary ethics review and clear internal guidelines before deploying educational AI, rather than assuming good intentions are enough. This can reduce reputational, legal, and trust risks.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors surveyed 60 leading AIED researchers on ethics in educational AI, covering fairness, accountability, transparency, bias, autonomy, agency, and inclusion, and distinguishing between doing ethical things and doing things ethically. Seventeen responded. Their contributions surfaced complex issues, including the finding that most AIED researchers lack training to address emerging ethical questions. The paper frames this as a critical gap and proposes that a well-designed framework combining a multidisciplinary approach with robust guidelines is vital. The key result is the identified need for community-wide ethical infrastructure rather than relying on individual intentions.

papers.note: 5,172 support agents, 15 percent productivity gain concentrated in less experienced workers, the most cited field study of AI at work.
papers.title: Generative AI at Work
papers.explain_beginner: This study asks a very concrete version of a big question, does giving workers access to a generative AI assistant actually make them more productive on the job, measured in a real workplace rather than a lab. The researchers studied a large software company's customer support operation, where thousands of agents, most of them based in the Philippines, handle live chats with customers, and where the company rolled out a GPT based tool that suggests responses to agents in real time as they type. Because the tool was rolled out to different teams at different times, the researchers could compare agents who had it against similar agents who did not yet have it, holding time and individual differences roughly constant. What they found is that access to the AI assistant raised the number of issues resolved per hour, but the gain was extremely uneven, brand new agents improved dramatically while the most experienced agents barely changed. It does not tell us whether these gains hold up over years, whether they change how many agents a company needs to hire, or whether wages eventually rise to reflect the higher output, because the study window was too short to observe any of that.
papers.explain_business: For any company running a large customer service or similar structured knowledge work operation, the actionable takeaway is that generative AI assistants deliver their biggest and most measurable return on newer and lower performing staff, not on your best people, which should directly shape where a pilot program is targeted and how its success is measured. A rollout evaluated only on average productivity gains, roughly 14 percent here, would understate the tool's effect on ramping new hires and understate that senior staff may see little direct benefit from the same deployment. The cost side is that this was a build, not a buy, the company constructed a purpose built tool trained on its own best agent conversations, so the 14 to 34 percent figures are not guaranteed to transfer to an off the shelf chatbot plugged into an unrelated workflow. This applies now to any structured, high volume text based service role, and the open question this study leaves for a business to answer on its own is whether faster ramping of new hires should change hiring plans, training budget, or headcount, since the paper itself does not extend far enough in time to say.
papers.explain_practitioner: Using data from roughly 5,179 customer support agents and about 3 million chat conversations, the authors exploit a staggered rollout of an internal GPT based assistant to estimate causal effects with a difference in differences design, comparing treated and not yet treated agents over time. The average effect was a 14 percent increase in issues resolved per hour, driven by shorter average handling time and the ability to manage more simultaneous chats, with resolution rates and customer satisfaction essentially flat. The distribution behind that average masked a much sharper pattern, novice and lower skilled agents gained roughly 34 percent, while the most tenured, highest performing agents saw little to no measurable improvement, and treated agents with about two months of tenure performed on par with untreated agents who had six months of experience. That compression toward the top performer's skill level, rather than a uniform boost, is the paper's central empirical result, and it argues the tool functions partly as a channel for transferring the practices of the best agents to everyone else. The authors are explicit that their design cannot speak to longer run effects on staffing levels, wages, or whether these gains persist once agents fully adapt, since the observation window covers only a few months after rollout.

papers.note: A review of 100 papers from 2010 to 2020 maps how AI in education moved from classification and recommendation toward adaptive, immersive and gamified learning, and warns that inappropriate use, shifting teacher and student roles, and ethical issues matter as much as the technology itself.
papers.title: A Review of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Education from 2010 to 2020
papers.authors: Xuesong Zhai, Xiaoyan Chu, Ching Sing Chai, Morris Siu–Yung Jong, Andreja Istenič Starčič, Michael Spector, et al.
papers.explain_beginner: This paper looked at 100 studies about artificial intelligence in education, published between 2010 and 2020. The authors sorted the research into three groups: tools that classify or recommend things, tools that give feedback or adapt to learners, and tools that involve emotions, role play, immersive learning, or games. They found the field is moving toward more personal and interactive learning. They also warn that problems like misuse of AI, changing roles for teachers and students, and ethical concerns matter just as much as the technology. This helps readers understand both the promise and the risks of AI in classrooms.
papers.explain_business: This review of 100 papers from 2010 to 2020 shows that AI in education has shifted from simple sorting and recommending toward adaptive, immersive, and gamified learning. For leaders, the key message is that the technology alone is not enough. Inappropriate use, changing roles of teachers and students, and social and ethical concerns are just as important as the tools. This informs decisions about investing in AI for training or education, and it argues for pairing technology adoption with clear policies on ethics, teacher support, and student roles rather than treating AI as a purely technical purchase.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors performed a content analysis of 100 papers from the Social Sciences Citation Index education category, covering 2010 to 2020. Of these, 63 were empirical papers containing 74 studies, and 37 were analytic. Research questions were grouped into three layers: development (classification, matching, recommendation, deep learning), application (feedback, reasoning, adaptive learning), and integration (affection computing, role playing, immersive learning, gamification). Suggested future trends include the Internet of Things, swarm intelligence, deep learning, neuroscience, and assessment of AI in education. Reported challenges include inappropriate use of AI techniques, shifting teacher and student roles, and social and ethical issues.

papers.note: The paper maps international AI education policies and finds no single global consensus, proposing a synthesized set of ethical principles to guide students, teachers, developers and policymakers in building trustworthy AIED.
papers.title: Ethical principles for artificial intelligence in education
papers.authors: Andy Nguyen, Ha Ngan Ngo, Yvonne Hong, Belle Dang, Bich‐Phuong Thi Nguyen
papers.explain_beginner: This paper looks at the rules different countries and organizations have made for using artificial intelligence in schools. The authors compared these policies and found that there is no single global agreement on what counts as ethical. Because of this, they combined the ideas into one shared set of ethical principles. This matters because AI is being used more and more in education, and it can affect students' private data and their freedom to learn in their own way. The authors hope their combined principles will help everyone involved build AI tools that are trustworthy.
papers.explain_business: AI in education is spreading, and different regions follow different ethical rules, so there is no single global standard to rely on. This paper reviewed international policies and combined them into one set of ethical principles for AI in education. For executives, this means any AI learning product or institutional rollout should be checked against a shared ethical framework, not just local rules. The framework covers the interests of students, teachers, developers, policymakers, and institutional leaders. It informs decisions about which AI education tools to adopt, how to govern their use, and how to build trust with users and regulators.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors examined current policies and guidelines on ethical AI in education from international organizations to test whether a global consensus exists. They first reviewed the opportunities AIED offers and the ethical concerns it raises, such as issues around personal data and learner autonomy. They then applied thematic analysis to synthesize these policies into a conceptual set of ethical principles. The paper discusses each principle and its implications for students, teachers, developers, policymakers, and institutional decision makers. The resulting framework is intended to guide ethical and trustworthy development and deployment of AIED and to encourage future impact studies.

papers.note: A large urban school experiment found that an intelligent algebra tutor, built with teachers rather than imposed on them, raised student test scores well above comparison classes, showing that lab tutoring systems can work at real scale in ordinary high schools.
papers.title: Intelligent Tutoring Goes To School in the Big City
papers.authors: Kenneth R. Koedinger, John R. Anderson, William H. Hadley, Mary A. Mark
papers.explain_beginner: This paper describes a project that brought a computer tutor into real high school algebra classes in a big city. Teachers helped design the tutor and the curriculum, so it fit their goals and teaching style. In one school year, about 470 students used the tutor. These students scored 15 percent better than other classes on standard tests, and twice as well on tests about the specific topics they studied. The finding matters because it shows that computer tutoring can work in ordinary, busy city schools, not just in small experiments.
papers.explain_business: This study shows that a computer-based algebra tutor, developed with teachers rather than imposed on them, improved student performance in real urban high schools. Students using it scored 15 percent higher on standardized tests and twice as high on curriculum-specific tests. For decision makers, the lesson is that intelligent tutoring can be deployed at scale in ordinary classrooms and still produce measurable gains. It supports investing in tools co-designed with educators, and it suggests such systems can be a practical way to raise math achievement in large school districts.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors report a large-scale evaluation of an intelligent algebra tutor, PAT, embedded in the Pittsburgh Urban Mathematics Project curriculum, which emphasizes real world analysis and computational tools. The tutor was created through a client-centered design process, combining teacher curricular and classroom expertise with AI and cognitive psychology knowledge. PAT became part of regular 9th grade algebra in three Pittsburgh schools. In 1993-94, 470 experimental students outperformed comparison classes by 15 percent on standardized tests and 100 percent on PUMP-targeted tests, demonstrating technical and pedagogical scalability in urban high schools.

papers.note: The first widely cited demonstration of goal hijacking and prompt leaking, useful for dating when the risk became public knowledge.
papers.title: Ignore Previous Prompt: Attack Techniques For Language Models
papers.explain_beginner: In 2022, researchers studied whether people could misuse GPT-3, a widely used language model, by typing clever but simple instructions. They found that two kinds of attacks worked: one could change what the model was trying to do, and another could make it reveal hidden instructions. The team showed that even attackers with little skill could take advantage of the model's random behavior. This matters because GPT-3 was already used in many public applications, and few studies had looked at how malicious users might exploit it. The findings helped make these risks part of public discussion.
papers.explain_business: For executives, this paper is an early warning about using GPT-3 in public products. It shows that simple, manually written inputs from malicious users could redirect the model's purpose or expose hidden instructions. The attackers did not need advanced skills, and the model's random behavior made outcomes unpredictable. That combination creates rare but potentially serious risks. The work informs decisions about whether to deploy such models in public roles and how much weight to give malicious user input in risk planning. It also helps date when these risks became publicly known, which matters for risk assessments.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors introduced PromptInject, a framework for building attack prompts in repeated steps using masks. They used it to test GPT-3, then a leading model used in production, with manually written inputs. Their study covered two attack types: redirecting the model's intended goal and extracting its hidden prompt. The key result was that GPT-3 could be pushed away from intended behavior easily, and that attackers with limited skill but clear ill intent could exploit the model's random output behavior. This creates rare but serious risks. The authors released the PromptInject code, making it available for later security research.

papers.note: This survey maps how educational data mining and learning analytics have grown since 2013, cataloguing methods, tools, datasets and trends, so AI in education researchers can see the field's current state and where it is heading.
papers.title: Educational data mining and learning analytics: An updated survey
papers.explain_beginner: This paper looks at how researchers study data from education, such as information about students and how they learn. The authors updated an earlier survey from 2013 to show how much the field has grown. They describe the different names people now use for this work, the tools available, the free datasets, and the methods researchers apply. They also point to where the field is heading. It matters because it gives a clear picture of how data and AI are being used to understand and improve education, and it helps newcomers see the whole landscape in one place.
papers.explain_business: This survey shows that using data and AI in education has grown a lot since 2013 and now covers many areas, from academic and institutional analytics to teaching analytics and data driven decision making. It catalogues the tools, datasets, methods, and trends that define the field today. For an executive, this means the space is broad and maturing, so any investment or strategy in education technology should account for these many subfields and the free resources already available. The decision it informs is how to scope and prioritise AI in education initiatives using a clear map of the current landscape.
papers.explain_practitioner: This survey updates a 2013 review on data mining in education. The authors give a general overview of how Educational Data Mining and Learning Analytics are applied to educational data. They cover the main publications and milestones, the knowledge discovery cycle, educational environments, specific tools, freely available datasets, commonly used methods, main objectives, and future trends. They also note the many related terms now in use, such as Academic Analytics, Institutional Analytics, Teaching Analytics, and Educational Data Science. The key result is a current state of the art that maps the field's growth and direction since 2013.

papers.note: Automating exemplar construction removes a hidden human dependency, which is worth tracing when an audit asks who authored a prompt.
papers.title: Automatic Chain of Thought Prompting in Large Language Models
papers.explain_beginner: The paper looks at a way to help large language models solve reasoning problems by showing them example solutions. Normally, people must write those examples by hand, which takes time and task-specific effort. The authors tested letting the model create the examples itself, using a simple instruction to reason in steps. Because model-written examples can contain errors, they added variety when choosing questions. Their method, Auto-CoT, matched or beat the human-written example approach on ten public reasoning tests with GPT-3. This matters because it can reduce manual work and make prompting easier to reuse.
papers.explain_business: This research suggests companies can reduce human effort when using large language models for reasoning tasks. Instead of paying experts to write example solutions for each task, teams can let the model generate examples automatically. The method, Auto-CoT, selects varied questions and creates reasoning steps, then uses them as prompts. On ten public reasoning tests with GPT-3, it performed as well as or better than manually designed examples. For executives, this informs decisions about reducing manual prompt design, lowering prompt engineering costs, and auditing who or what authored prompts, while noting generated examples may contain mistakes.
papers.explain_practitioner: The paper addresses CoT prompting, where demonstrations include a question and reasoning chain. Manual demonstrations perform well but require hand-crafted task-specific examples. The authors propose Auto-CoT. It uses an LLM with a simple step-by-step prompt to generate reasoning chains for demonstrations one by one. Since generated chains can be wrong, Auto-CoT samples questions for diversity before generating chains. On ten public benchmark reasoning tasks with GPT-3, Auto-CoT consistently matched or exceeded manual CoT. The key result is that automatic demonstration construction can remove the need for manual, task-specific demonstration design while preserving or improving performance.

papers.note: The paper argues that educational data mining and learning analytics should collaborate more formally, sharing methods and tools, which matters because AI in education needs both communities working together to improve teaching and learning research.
papers.title: Learning analytics and educational data mining
papers.explain_beginner: This paper looks at two groups of researchers who study data in education. One group is called Educational Data Mining, the other is Learning Analytics and Knowledge. They grew up separately even though they work on similar problems. The authors say these two groups should talk to each other more and work together in a formal way. That way they can share their research, their methods, and their tools. This matters because better teamwork between them can lead to better research on teaching and learning, and stronger use of AI in education.
papers.explain_business: Rising interest in data and analytics across education has created demand for high quality research into models, methods, technologies, and impact. Two separate research communities, Educational Data Mining and Learning Analytics and Knowledge, have been serving that demand on their own. This paper argues they should collaborate formally and share research, methods, and tools. For an executive, the practical implication is that investments in education analytics may deliver more if they draw on both communities rather than one. The decision this informs is whether to support and fund collaboration between these groups instead of treating them as separate silos.
papers.explain_practitioner: The paper addresses two distinct research communities, Educational Data Mining (EDM) and Learning Analytics and Knowledge (LAK), which developed independently in response to growing interest in data and analytics in education. The authors argue that this separation limits progress. Their position is that the communities should establish increased and formal communication and collaboration. The proposed benefit is the sharing of research, methods, and tools for data mining and analysis. This sharing would serve the development of both fields, EDM and LAK, rather than one borrowing from the other informally.

papers.note: Balanced account of both democratised access and misinformation risk across practice, research and education.
papers.title: The future landscape of large language models in medicine
papers.explain_beginner: The question, looking ahead, what will large language models realistically be used for across patient care, medical research, and medical training, and what has to go right, or wrong, for that future to play out safely. This piece was written as ChatGPT style tools suddenly became available to any clinician or student, ahead of any real consensus on rules for using them, so the authors wanted to lay out a considered view of where the genuine opportunities were versus where hasty adoption could cause real harm. The authors argue real opportunity exists in cutting the roughly one quarter of a clinician's workday currently spent on documentation, in translating medical information across languages, and in personalized tutoring for medical students, but they pair every opportunity with a matched risk, such as models inventing plausible sounding but false medical information, a problem generally called hallucination, and models reproducing racial, gender, or socioeconomic bias absorbed from their training data. What it does not settle, this is a forward looking argument and set of recommendations, not a study with new data, so it cannot say how often these risks actually materialize in practice, and it leaves open who is accountable when a language model's suggestion contributes to patient harm.
papers.explain_business: For a healthcare organization thinking about where to first apply language models, this paper's own prioritization points toward documentation and administrative automation as the area with the clearest return, given the roughly 25 percent of clinician time the authors attribute to this work today. The warning against routing patient data through public consumer chat interfaces is directly actionable, any pilot should use an access controlled application built on the underlying model's own interface rather than a general public facing chat tool, given the data leakage and prompt injection risks named specifically. The call for documenting exact model versions used in any clinical or research application adds a real record keeping requirement, since the authors note model updates can silently change outputs in ways that break reproducibility if the version is not tracked carefully. The authors state plainly that the legal and liability framework for AI assisted clinical decisions did not yet exist at the time of writing, meaning organizations adopting these tools for decision support, as opposed to pure documentation support, are operating ahead of settled legal ground. This is most relevant now to organizations piloting documentation or research support, which the authors treat as lower risk and closer to ready than direct diagnostic use.
papers.explain_practitioner: Method, a perspective article synthesizing the literature available at the time and the authors' own analysis of large language model capabilities and risks across three domains, patient care, medical research, and medical education, rather than reporting new experimental results. The authors cite documentation and administrative work as consuming around 25 percent of a clinician's working day as the target opportunity for automation, and lay out paired risks including hallucinated, plausible sounding but false medical content, bias reproducing race, gender, and socioeconomic patterns found in training data, data leakage and prompt injection as security concerns specific to handling sensitive clinical information, and version to version inconsistency across model updates that undermines scientific reproducibility when a study's exact model version is not carefully documented. The authors state a direct limitation and recommendation together, a legal framework for handling liability and errors needs to be established before these tools are used for clinical decision making, and they separately caution that students risk treating these tools as a crutch that could undermine development of independent clinical reasoning, recommending secure, access controlled applications rather than routing patient information through public consumer interfaces.

papers.note: The most cited general survey of the field, covering the GPT, LLaMA and PaLM families, training datasets, and evaluation metrics. A reasonable first read for anyone needing the shape of the field rather than a single result.
papers.title: Large Language Models: A Survey
papers.explain_beginner: Large language models like the systems behind ChatGPT multiplied so quickly that it became hard to keep track of how they worked or how they compared to one another. This paper does not run a new experiment. Instead it steps back and maps the whole field in one place, explaining how the major model families were built, what data they were trained on, and how researchers judge whether one model is actually better than another. It walks through the lineages behind well known systems such as GPT, LLaMA, and PaLM, describing what each family contributed and where it fell short. It also lays out the common ways models get tested, from simple accuracy scores to broader benchmark suites, and shows how leading models stack up against each other on shared tasks. The paper does not argue for a single new idea. Its value is as an orientation guide, giving newcomers a shared vocabulary and a sense of the landscape before they dive into any one narrower piece of research.
papers.explain_business: This paper introduces no new capability, so it changes nothing about what an organization can build or buy today. Its practical use is as a map for people who need to choose between model families without becoming AI researchers first. Understanding that GPT, LLaMA, and PaLM descend from different design choices and training data helps a buyer ask sharper questions of a vendor, such as what a model was trained on, how it was evaluated, and which benchmarks actually resemble the buyer's own use case. The survey's comparison tables are a reasonable starting point for due diligence conversations, though they age quickly since new models ship constantly and the numbers here reflect only what existed at the time of writing. There is no cost, risk, or compliance finding to act on directly. The main business takeaway is procedural. treat any single benchmark score with caution, ask which evaluation methodology produced it, and expect today's leaderboard position to be temporary.
papers.explain_practitioner: The paper is a structured literature review rather than an empirical study. It groups modern large language models by lineage, walking through the GPT, LLaMA, and PaLM families and summarizing the architectural choices, scale, and training recipes that define each generation. It then surveys the pretraining corpora, instruction tuning sets, and alignment data typically used to build these models, alongside the metrics and benchmark suites researchers rely on for evaluation, spanning knowledge tests, reasoning tasks, and generation quality. A comparison section places several prominent models side by side on shared tasks so readers can see relative strengths rather than take vendor claims at face value. The authors are explicit that a survey like this is a snapshot. Because the field moves fast, any fixed comparison table risks going stale within months as new models and benchmarks appear, and the paper's own coverage stops at the models and datasets known at the time of writing. It closes by naming open problems, including evaluation reliability and how far current benchmarks generalize.

papers.note: Written for clinical safety professionals appraising AI, which is exactly the audience for a healthcare AI audit.
papers.title: Artificial intelligence, bias and clinical safety
papers.explain_beginner: The question here is simple to state. When a hospital starts using a computer program that learns from past cases, what people call machine learning or AI, to help make decisions, what new ways can that go wrong that don't apply to older, hand coded software. People cared about this because by 2019 hospitals were already piloting AI tools for reading scans and flagging risk, often based on nothing more than how well the software scored on a test dataset. The authors, a group of UK clinicians and informaticians, did not test one specific AI tool. Instead they laid out the failure patterns doctors and safety officers should watch for, split into problems that show up almost immediately, ones that emerge over months as the tool meets real patients, and ones that only appear over years as clinical practice changes around the tool. What the paper does not settle is how often these failures actually occur in deployed systems, since it is a reasoned argument and checklist, not a study of outcomes, and it names no single tool as unsafe.
papers.explain_business: For a hospital or vendor, this paper functions as an early checklist for procurement and safety review of any ML powered clinical tool, published years before formal regulatory guidance caught up to these questions. The risk it names concretely, a tool validated only on data resembling its training population can fail silently on your actual patient mix, and because neural network outputs are largely a black box, a wrong recommendation can look just as confident as a right one, so accuracy figures from a vendor's original study are not sufficient on their own. The quality control questions give a usable audit list, whether training data covers your demographics and care settings, and whether the vendor documents planned retraining and how it will be revalidated. The recommendation to test with randomized trial level rigor anticipated later FDA and MHRA expectations for AI as a medical device, which is now relevant to compliance planning. This matters at initial procurement and again at every model update, since a tool retrained on new data effectively becomes a new product needing fresh scrutiny, not a one time approval that covers all future versions.
papers.explain_practitioner: Method, a narrative review structured around named failure mechanisms rather than a systematic literature search. It illustrates its point with a well known example from outside medicine, a defense image classifier that learned to tell sunny days from cloudy days rather than tank from no tank, a case of what the authors call distributional shift. The paper's main output is a table of quality control questions covering training data provenance, population and site diversity, label quality, model interpretability, confidence reporting, and how findings are communicated to avoid automation complacency, where clinicians stop scrutinizing recommendations from a system they have learned to trust. The authors argue ML diagnostic tools should be validated with the same rigor as a new laboratory screening test, ideally through randomized trials against existing decision support, a higher bar than the internal validation most tools received at the time. A limitation the authors state directly, their framework offers no way to quantify how much any one failure mode will matter in a specific deployment, and they note that suboptimal decisions happen with or without ML support, so a bad outcome can be hard to attribute cleanly to the algorithm rather than ordinary clinical error.

papers.note: The paper argues that AI in education can make learning processes explicit and give every student personalised tutoring, while augmenting rather than replacing teachers, which matters because it could address achievement gaps as smart machines reshape work.
papers.title: Intelligence Unleashed: An argument for AI in Education
papers.explain_beginner: This paper explains what artificial intelligence in education is and what it could do for learning. The authors say AI can help make learning clearer and give every student one-on-one tutoring, in every subject, at a scale that was not possible before. It can also support students working in groups and in virtual settings. Importantly, the authors do not think AI should replace teachers. Instead, AI should work alongside teachers and make their expertise go further. The paper matters because this could help close achievement gaps and prepare people for a world where smart machines are changing jobs.
papers.explain_business: For executives, this paper signals that AI in education is not just a technology play, it is a strategy for improving learning outcomes at scale. The authors argue that well-designed AIEd can personalise learning, support teachers rather than replace them, and help address achievement gaps and teacher retention. It also responds to job displacement by smart machines, which raises the bar for what education systems must achieve. The practical decision this informs is to invest in collaborative, standards-based AIEd tools co-designed with educators, with funding focused on proven teaching and learning needs, not isolated experiments. The prize is better outcomes, but it requires new partnerships and ethical data use.
papers.explain_practitioner: The paper has two aims: explain AIEd to non-specialists and argue for its role in teaching and learning. The authors describe AIEd as systems with human-like capabilities and behaviours, and as a scientific effort to make implicit knowledge computationally precise and explicit, opening the black box of learning. They report that existing tools can already provide one-on-one tutoring at scale, support group work, and create authentic virtual environments. Near-future expectations include lifelong learning companions and real-time assessment. The key argument is augmentation, not replacement, of teachers, with progress requiring a component-based infrastructure, shared data standards, and attention to pedagogy, technology, and system change.

papers.note: Organises mitigation into eleven method areas and lists open source libraries, which is practical for recommending remediation.
papers.title: Fairness in Machine Learning: A Survey
papers.explain_beginner: This survey explains that machine learning can affect people in important ways, so companies and researchers must watch for unfair outcomes linked to gender, ethnicity, or disability. The fairness literature is large and difficult for newcomers, so the authors map the main ideas and remedies. They group fixes by when they happen, before training, during training, and after training, then split these into eleven areas. They also cover fairness beyond simple yes or no predictions, including regression, recommender systems, and unsupervised learning, and point to publicly available software tools. It matters because it gives a practical starting point for reducing bias.
papers.explain_business: This survey says that when machine learning affects people, leaders need confidence that it will not create unexpected social harm, such as bias related to gender, ethnicity, or disability. The fairness field is complex, so the authors provide a structured overview. They group remedies by when they are applied, before training, during training, and after training, with eleven method areas. They also cover settings beyond yes or no prediction and list publicly available software libraries. In practice, this helps executives decide how to assess and remediate fairness risks, where to look for tools, and why unresolved tensions require ongoing governance rather than a single fix.
papers.explain_practitioner: This survey reviews fairness approaches for machine learning. It organizes mitigation methods by the stage at which they act, before training, during training, and after training. Within that structure, it identifies eleven method areas. The authors note that most published work focuses on yes or no prediction, but they also discuss fairness for regression, recommender systems, and unsupervised learning. They list publicly available software libraries. The key result is a practical map of the field, plus five unresolved tensions that summarize open fairness challenges. This helps researchers choose remediation strategies and locate tools, while seeing where evidence remains limited.

papers.note: This position paper sorts AI in education into three paradigms, from AI directing learners to learners leading with AI, arguing the field is shifting toward learner agency and personalized, data-driven learning, which matters for anyone tracking how AI tools reshape teaching.
papers.title: Artificial intelligence in education: The three paradigms
papers.explain_beginner: This paper looks at how artificial intelligence has been used in education over time. The authors describe three stages. In the first, AI teaches and learners just receive. In the second, learners work together with AI. In the third, learners take charge and AI supports them. The paper argues that education is moving toward the third stage, where learners have more control and learning becomes more personal. This matters because it shows how AI tools may change teaching, shifting power from the system to the learner.
papers.explain_business: This paper argues that AI in education is moving through three stages, ending with learners in control and AI adapting to them. For leaders, the practical message is that products and strategies built around AI simply delivering content to passive students may become outdated. Instead, tools should support learner choice, personalization, and feedback loops where learner data informs the system. This informs decisions about where to invest in educational technology, how to design products, and how to prepare for a market that increasingly values learner agency and data-driven personalization.
papers.explain_practitioner: This position paper categorizes AI in education into three paradigms. Paradigm One uses AI to model knowledge and direct cognitive learning, with learners as recipients. Paradigm Two uses AI to support learning, with learners as collaborators. Paradigm Three uses AI to empower learning, with learners exercising agency. The authors argue the field is shifting toward the third paradigm, which emphasizes learner agency, personalization, reflection, and iterative, data-driven, learner-centered design. The key result is a framework describing this trend, not an experiment. It offers a lens for positioning AIEd systems and research.

papers.note: Extends chain of thought to image plus text and reports reduced hallucination, relevant to document and imaging workflows.
papers.title: Multimodal Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in Language Models
papers.explain_beginner: The question behind this paper is simple to state, can an AI system reason more reliably about a picture and a passage of text together than it does about text alone? Earlier chain of thought prompting had language models write out their reasoning step by step in words before giving an answer, which helped on math and logic questions, but it broke down on questions that needed a diagram or photo, because the model had nothing but text to reason over and often invented plausible sounding but wrong explanations, a failure researchers call hallucination. Zhang and coauthors built a two step system, called Multimodal-CoT, that first drafts a reasoning explanation using both the image and the text, then uses that explanation to choose a final answer. On the ScienceQA science quiz benchmark, their model, with under a billion parameters, beat the previous best result and also beat a much bigger text only model, GPT-3.5, coming close to the recorded human score. The paper does not show whether the same gains hold outside quiz style benchmarks, and the authors' own review of wrong answers found the model still fumbles basic commonsense tasks like counting objects in a picture or reading a map.
papers.explain_business: For any product that has to answer questions about a mix of documents and images, contracts with attached diagrams, product manuals with photos, medical charts with annotated scans, this paper shows that separating explain first from answer second measurably cuts down on confidently wrong answers, without needing a giant model. That matters for cost, the reported gains came from a sub billion parameter model, cheap enough to run at volume compared to frontier scale systems. The catch for deployment is that the benchmark here is a science quiz format with fairly clean, single images, and the authors' own failure analysis shows the technique still struggles with basic visual commonsense like counting or spatial reasoning, so a business use case that depends on precise visual counting or layout understanding should not assume this result transfers directly. Teams building document or image heavy assistants should treat this as evidence that rationale then answer pipelines reduce one specific, measurable failure mode, not as proof the system is reliable enough yet for unsupervised use in a workflow that requires exact visual detail.
papers.explain_practitioner: Multimodal-CoT is a two stage encoder-decoder pipeline built on T5 style transformers at 223 million and 738 million parameters, with frozen ViT-large image features fused into the text encoder. Stage one generates a rationale conditioned on both modalities, stage two conditions answer prediction on that generated rationale rather than the raw inputs. On ScienceQA, the 738M model reached 90.45 percent accuracy, above the prior best published result of 86.54 percent, above GPT-3.5 (text-davinci-003) at 76.47 percent, and just above the human benchmark of 88.4 percent, all using well under a billion parameters. The authors trace the gain to hallucination reduction, a baseline error analysis found 56 percent of wrong answers stemmed from hallucinated rationales, and vision grounding corrected 60.7 percent of those specific errors. Their own manual review of 50 remaining failures found the residual error pattern is not hallucination but commonsense reasoning gaps, roughly 80 percent involved tasks like map reading, object counting, or alphabetical ordering that the model's visual features are too coarse to support.

papers.note: This review finds AI can help teachers plan, give feedback and assess essays, while teachers also train and check these systems, so it matters for anyone weighing AI's real classroom benefits against implementation challenges.
papers.title: The Promises and Challenges of Artificial Intelligence for Teachers: a Systematic Review of Research
papers.authors: İsmail Çelik, Muhterem Dindar, Hanni Muukkonen, Sanna Järvelä
papers.explain_beginner: This review looked at how teachers use artificial intelligence in their work. It found that AI can help teachers in three main ways. It can help them plan lessons by showing what students need. It can help during teaching by giving feedback right away. It can also help grade essays automatically. The review also found that teachers are not just users of AI. They help train it by acting as examples, and they check whether the automatic grading is correct. The paper also points out that using AI in teaching comes with challenges, so schools should think carefully before adopting it.
papers.explain_business: This review suggests AI can support teachers with lesson planning, real time feedback, and automated essay scoring, which could ease workload pressures in these areas. It also shows that teachers remain essential to making these systems work, since they help train the algorithms and verify automated assessments. For leaders, the practical message is that AI adoption in classrooms is not purely a software purchase. It requires teacher time and involvement, plus attention to implementation challenges. This informs decisions about where to pilot AI, how to budget for staff involvement, and how to set realistic expectations for rollout.
papers.explain_practitioner: This systematic review examined research on teachers' use of AI applications and machine learning methods for analyzing teacher data. The authors report that AI supports three areas of teaching: planning, by identifying and communicating student needs, implementation, through immediate feedback and enabling teacher intervention, and assessment, via automated essay scoring. The review also identifies teacher roles in AI development, including serving as models for training algorithms and verifying the accuracy of automated assessment systems. Several implementation challenges in teaching practice are highlighted, and the authors present these as guidelines for future work in the field.

papers.note: The study develops an Intelligent-TPACK framework showing that teachers need both technological and pedagogical knowledge, plus ethics, to integrate AI well, since technical skill alone is insufficient for sound educational use.
papers.title: Towards Intelligent-TPACK: An empirical study on teachers’ professional knowledge to ethically integrate artificial intelligence (AI)-based tools into education
papers.explain_beginner: Teachers are starting to use AI tools in classrooms, but this study says knowing how to operate the technology is not enough. The researcher built a survey to measure what teachers know about using AI for teaching, adding ethical questions to an existing framework called TPACK. The findings show that teachers who understand AI tools better also see more clearly how AI can help students learn. Technical skill helps teachers judge AI decisions, but on its own it does not make AI use work well in class. Teachers need technical and teaching knowledge together, plus ethics, to use AI soundly.
papers.explain_business: For leaders planning AI adoption in education, this research indicates that buying AI tools and training staff on their features will not deliver good teaching outcomes by itself. The study developed a measure of teacher knowledge for AI use and found that technical skill matters mainly when paired with pedagogical understanding, and that teachers also need ethics to evaluate AI decisions. The practical implication is that professional development budgets should fund integrated training covering technology, teaching method, and ethical judgment together, rather than standalone technical courses. This informs decisions about hiring, training design, and how readiness for AI integration is assessed.
papers.explain_practitioner: The study addresses a gap in teacher knowledge for instructional AI use. The author developed a scale based on the TPACK framework, extended with ethical aspects, to measure knowledge for pedagogically and ethically sound AI integration. A model was then built to examine how TPACK components and ethics interact. Results show that greater knowledge of interacting with AI tools relates to better understanding of AI's pedagogical contributions. Technological knowledge (TK) supports assessing AI decisions, but TK alone is insufficient. TK becomes meaningful for efficient AI deployment when combined with pedagogical knowledge (PK), expressed as technological pedagogical knowledge (TPK). The proposed Intelligent-TPACK framework reflects this.

papers.note: This paper traces how AI in education has developed unevenly, missing key links between research and practice, and argues that understanding this history matters for judging current claims about AI's role in teaching and learning.
papers.title: Historical threads, missing links, and future directions in AI in education
papers.explain_beginner: This paper looks at how artificial intelligence has been used in education over time. The authors say this history has grown in an uneven way, and important connections between research and what actually happens in classrooms have been missed. They argue that knowing this past matters. It helps us judge the big claims people make today about AI in teaching and learning. So before believing that AI will transform education, it is worth understanding how it got here and what gaps still exist.
papers.explain_business: For executives, this paper is a caution about adopting AI in education based on hype. The authors show that AI's history in education has been uneven, with weak links between research and real practice. That means current promises about AI improving teaching and learning should be assessed with care. The decision this informs is whether to invest in or deploy AI tools now, and it suggests asking how past gaps between research and practice will be avoided. Understanding this history supports more grounded, evidence aware choices.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors examine the historical development of AI in education, describing it as uneven and noting missing links between research and practice. Rather than presenting new experiments or models, the paper traces how the field evolved and where connections broke down. Its key argument is that this history is essential for evaluating current claims about AI's role in teaching and learning. For engineers and researchers, the takeaway is that technical work should be read alongside its uneven past and the persistent gap between research outputs and classroom practice.

papers.note: This meta-analysis of 50 controlled evaluations found intelligent tutoring raised test scores by a median of 0.66 standard deviations, but gains were much larger on locally developed tests than standardized ones, so educators should weigh how test alignment and implementation quality shape reported effectiveness.
papers.title: Effectiveness of Intelligent Tutoring Systems
papers.authors: James A. Kulik, J. D. Fletcher
papers.explain_beginner: This paper looked at 50 studies of computer tutoring systems, which are programs that teach students and adjust to their needs. On average, students using these systems scored better than those in regular classes, moving from the middle of the pack to the top quarter. But the size of the improvement depended on the test used. Gains were bigger on tests made by the local school than on standard nationwide tests. The authors also note that poorly run programs or weak comparison groups led to smaller gains. So how well a system is used and how it is measured both matter.
papers.explain_business: This analysis of 50 controlled studies shows intelligent tutoring can raise test scores substantially, with a median gain of 0.66 standard deviations, roughly moving an average student to the 75th percentile. However, results depend heavily on how success is measured. Gains were much larger on locally made tests than on standardized ones, and weak implementations or unsuitable comparison groups produced little benefit. For decision makers, this means pilot results can look better than real world impact if tests are not independent. Invest in proper implementation and use standardized measures to judge whether a tutoring system truly works before scaling it.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors conducted a meta-analysis of 50 controlled evaluations of intelligent tutoring systems. The median effect was 0.66 standard deviations over conventional instruction, equivalent to a shift from the 50th to the 75th percentile. Effect size varied strongly with the outcome measure: locally developed tests showed larger gains than standardized tests, indicating that alignment between test content and instructional objectives shapes results. Two additional groups failing selection criteria were examined: six evaluations with nonconventional control groups and four with flawed implementations. Both showed small effects, suggesting control treatment design and implementation fidelity also influence reported effectiveness.

papers.note: Names three distinct error types in zero-shot reasoning, which gives an audit categories to count rather than a single pass or fail.
papers.title: Plan-and-Solve Prompting: Improving Zero-Shot Chain-of-Thought Reasoning by Large Language Models
papers.explain_beginner: AI language models can struggle with problems that need several reasoning steps. Earlier methods either gave hand-written examples or simply told the model to think step by step. The paper says simple step-by-step prompting often makes three mistakes: wrong arithmetic, skipped steps, and misreading the question. The authors propose Plan-and-Solve prompting. It first asks the model to plan by breaking the task into smaller parts, then asks it to complete those parts. A version called PS+ adds more detailed instructions. On ten datasets and three reasoning problems with GPT-3, this approach beat the simple step-by-step method and was competitive with other methods. It matters because it improves reasoning without examples.
papers.explain_business: This paper suggests a prompting choice for companies using AI language models on tasks that require reasoning steps. Instead of relying on hand-written examples or an instruction to think step by step, teams can ask the model to first plan how to break the problem into smaller parts, then carry out those parts. Adding detailed instructions, called PS+, can reduce arithmetic mistakes and improve reasoning quality. In tests on ten datasets and three reasoning problems with GPT-3, this zero-shot method beat the step-by-step baseline, was comparable to or better than Zero-shot-Program-of-Thought, and was comparable to 8-shot CoT on math. It informs decisions about which prompting strategy to deploy for applications.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors target zero-shot multi-step reasoning, where a model is prompted without hand-crafted demonstrations. They identify three failure modes in Zero-shot-CoT: arithmetic mistakes, omitted steps, and misinterpretation of meaning. Their Plan-and-Solve method first has the model create a plan that splits the task into smaller subtasks, then execute those subtasks. PS+ adds more detailed instructions to reduce arithmetic mistakes and improve the generated reasoning steps. They tested on ten datasets covering three reasoning problems using GPT-3. The zero-shot approach consistently outperformed Zero-shot-CoT across all datasets by a large margin, was comparable to or better than Zero-shot-Program-of-Thought, and was comparable to 8-shot CoT on math reasoning.

papers.note: A review of 118 papers finds 53 uses of large language models in education, from grading to feedback, but flags low readiness, poor transparency and weak privacy safeguards, so it urges open sourcing, newer models and human centred design.
papers.title: Practical and ethical challenges of large language models in education: A systematic scoping review
papers.authors: Lixiang Yan, Lele Sha, Linxuan Zhao, Yuheng Li, Roberto Martínez‐Maldonado, Guanliang Chen, et al.

papers.note: Explains why internal validation overstates performance, which is the single most common defect in evidence a client presents.
papers.title: Methodologic Guide for Evaluating Clinical Performance and Effect of Artificial Intelligence Technology for Medical Diagnosis and Prediction.

papers.note: Peer reviewed architecture taxonomy covering training pipelines, datasets and deployment issues in one place.
papers.title: A Review on Large Language Models: Architectures, Applications, Taxonomies, Open Issues and Challenges
papers.authors: Mohaimenul Azam Khan Raiaan et al.
papers.explain_beginner: This paper does not run a new experiment, instead it asks a mapping question, given how fast large language models have multiplied since ChatGPT's release, can one document pull together how they are built, trained, used, and where they still fall short, in a way a newcomer or a busy practitioner can actually use? Raiaan and coauthors trace the history of these text generating AI systems from earlier language models up through the transformer based systems in wide use today, explain the standard pipeline of pretraining then fine tuning then alignment with human feedback, and catalog real applications across fields including healthcare, education, agriculture, and business. The review found that despite the pace of progress, unresolved problems, like factual errors the model states confidently, high computational cost, and difficulty adapting safely to sensitive domains, show up repeatedly across nearly every application area they surveyed. As a review rather than new research, it does not itself resolve any of these open problems, it organizes and names them so future work has a clearer target.
papers.explain_business: For a team trying to get oriented before making an AI investment decision, this kind of review is useful as a single reference point that lays out what current large language models can plausibly do well, translation, summarization, question answering, code assistance, against the practical constraints, inference cost, hallucination risk, and domain adaptation difficulty, that determine whether a specific use case is ready to deploy now or needs more groundwork first. It is explicitly not a source of new performance numbers or a comparison of specific vendor models, so it should not be used to pick between competing products. Its business value is in scoping conversations, helping a team new to this technology understand which problems, like factual reliability or high serving cost, are known, active, unsolved research areas rather than something a vendor's product update will quietly fix, and which application domains, per the survey's own examples in healthcare and education, already have documented deployment patterns worth learning from before committing budget.
papers.explain_practitioner: This is a structured survey rather than an empirical study, it synthesizes the large language model literature along five threads, historical evolution from earlier neural language models to current transformer architectures, the mechanics of the transformer itself, the standard three stage training pipeline of pretraining, supervised fine tuning, and reinforcement learning from human feedback, the datasets and compute resources that pipeline depends on, and deployment patterns across domains including biomedical and healthcare, education, agriculture, and general business use. Because it is a review, there is no single benchmark result or baseline comparison to report, its contribution is the taxonomy itself and the systematic cataloging of open issues, which the authors group by technical causes, hallucination, high inference and training cost, limited context handling, and by practical deployment barriers, data privacy, domain adaptation, and evaluation gaps. The authors' own framing acknowledges the review's core limitation, a field moving this fast means any single snapshot taxonomy risks being outdated by the time newer architectures or training techniques become standard practice.

papers.note: Trains a diffusion model rather than an autoregressive one at 8B scale and reaches comparable results, challenging the assumption that core language-model capability depends on next-token prediction.
papers.title: Large Language Diffusion Models
papers.explain_beginner: Almost every well known AI language model, including ChatGPT, generates text by predicting one word at a time, left to right. This paper asked whether that particular method is actually necessary for a model to become fluent and capable, or whether a very different training approach could work just as well. The researchers built LLaDA, an 8 billion parameter model trained with a diffusion method borrowed from image generating AI, where the model learns by having words randomly hidden and then practicing filling them back in, eventually learning to generate whole passages by repeatedly cleaning up a mostly blanked out draft. Tested on reasoning, math, and coding tasks, it performed close to, and on some tasks better than, a similarly sized model built the standard way. It also handled a known weakness of standard models, called the reversal curse, noticeably better. This does not mean diffusion will replace the standard approach, only that the standard approach is a choice, not the only path to a capable language model.
papers.explain_business: For organizations making long term bets on model architecture, this paper is evidence, not yet a product recommendation, that the autoregressive next word prediction approach underlying almost every commercial LLM today is not the only viable path to a competent language model. That matters strategically because it widens the field of plausible future architectures rather than confirming any current alternative is ready to deploy. As the authors note, LLaDA still lacks the inference speed optimizations, RLHF based alignment for safety and instruction following, and multimodal support that production systems require, so it is not something a business should adopt directly today. The realistic near term relevance is for teams tracking the research frontier on inference cost and architecture diversity, since a maturing diffusion based alternative could eventually offer different speed or robustness trade offs, but that is a multi year horizon, not an immediate deployment consideration.
papers.explain_practitioner: LLaDA is an 8 billion parameter language model trained from scratch using a diffusion objective rather than next token prediction. Training randomly masks tokens at rate t and trains a Transformer to predict the masked tokens by optimizing a variational lower bound, while generation starts from a fully masked sequence and iteratively unmasks it using a low confidence remasking schedule. Against LLaMA3 8B, LLaDA base scored 65.9 versus 65.4 on MMLU, 35.4 versus 34.8 on HumanEval, and notably 70.3 versus 48.7 on GSM8K, and it surpassed LLaMA2 7B across 15 benchmarks overall.
