That said, the review itself warns that these results come from research benchmarks, not live traffic, and rarely say what accuracy or user experience is given up to get them, so a defense that looks strong in a paper still needs to be piloted against an organization's own inputs before being trusted in production. This matters immediately for anyone deploying an LLM that processes content from outside parties, since prompt injection is already an active attack class, not a theoretical future one, and the choice of defense affects both security exposure and ongoing model performance.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors systematically reviewed 88 studies on prompt injection and jailbreak defenses for large language models and extended NIST's adversarial machine learning taxonomy with additional categories, including character, token, and sentence level input perturbation, self reflection checks, decoding steering, defensive pruning, and expanded input and output filtering. Where studies reported numbers, results include Jatmo style fine tuning cutting prompt injection success from as high as 87 percent down to nearly zero while keeping over 98 percent of task performance, and a dual LLM architecture called CaMeL driving attack success to zero against indirect injection on several commercial models. The review's own stated limitation is that these numbers are not comparable across studies, because papers use different datasets, model versions, and settings such as temperature, many do not report the accuracy cost of their defense, and no study in the set tested a defense that combines every strategy the taxonomy now lists.

papers.note: Ranks which high risk requirements companies find hardest, with Article 10 data governance first and Article 15 second.
papers.title: AI Act high-risk AI compliance challenge and industry impact: A multiple case study
papers.explain_beginner: This study asks a simple question: when companies affected by Europe's new AI Act have to follow strict rules for high-risk AI systems, what parts of that process do they actually find hardest, and how does the law affect business overall. To find out, the researchers talked in depth with people from six companies and three independent experts, sixteen people in total, about their real experience trying to comply. They found that some requirements are much harder to meet than others, and identified four things that make compliance easier or harder for a given company, its industry and brand reputation, whether it already deals with other regulations, how mature its AI practices are, and simply how big the company is. People generally had mixed views on whether the regulation helps or hurts business, but they were notably positive about voluntary codes of conduct as a lighter-touch way to show compliance. Because the study is based on a small number of companies, its findings are a useful early signal rather than a definitive industry-wide verdict.
papers.explain_business: For a company that will need to comply with the EU AI Act's high-risk provisions, this study is a useful early warning about where the real friction is likely to show up, not in the law's broad principles but in specific documentation, risk management, and oversight requirements that practitioners rank as most burdensome. It also finds that four factors predict how hard compliance will feel, industry and brand exposure, whatever other regulation the company already handles, how mature its AI governance already is, and company size, which businesses can use to gauge their own likely compliance burden ahead of time. A practical takeaway is that voluntary codes of conduct were viewed favorably by practitioners as an interim way to demonstrate good faith before full high-risk certification is complete, which may be worth exploring as a lower-cost first step. Because the underlying sample is only six companies, treat these as directional signals for budgeting and planning conversations, not as a substitute for a formal compliance gap assessment of your own AI systems.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors use a multiple case study design covering six companies plus three independent experts, sixteen respondents overall, to explore how organizations experience compliance with the EU AI Act's high-risk requirements. Rather than measuring outcomes numerically, qualitative interviews were used to build a ranked view of which high-risk obligations practitioners find most demanding, and to surface four contextual factors, industry and brand values, the existing regulatory environment, an organization's AI maturity, and company size, that shape how difficult compliance feels. The result that matters most for adoption is the consistently positive attitude toward voluntary codes of conduct as a practical bridge toward full compliance, alongside a mixed but documented set of arguments for and against the regulation's broader industry impact. The main limitation is sample size, sixteen respondents across six companies is not enough to generalize across sectors or company sizes, and the authors themselves call for further validation with industry partners and for turning the findings into concrete operational tools rather than treating them as final conclusions.

papers.note: Audits 2,385 traces and finds reward hacking in about two thirds of two benchmark families, which is a concrete figure an audit can cite.
papers.title: Do Agent Benchmarks Measure Capability? Protocol Validity in the Age of Agentic AI

papers.note: Converting an existing model to a hybrid architecture is a substantial modification, which raises re-assessment questions under the AI Act.
papers.title: Priming: Hybrid State Space Models From Pre-trained Transformers
papers.explain_beginner: This paper introduces a way to build a new kind of AI model without starting from zero. Normally, making a hybrid model, which mixes two memory styles, means expensive training from scratch. The authors instead take an already trained Transformer and convert it, using a small amount of extra training. The result keeps quality while running faster and using less memory. They compared three memory layer types and found one clearly best. This matters because it makes powerful, efficient AI models cheaper to create and easier to study.
papers.explain_business: This research shows you can convert an existing Transformer into a faster, more memory-efficient hybrid model without paying for full pre-training. The conversion uses a tiny fraction of the original training budget and works across model families and sizes. In practice, a 32B hybrid model outperformed its source on reasoning, matched a comparable Transformer, and decoded up to 2.3 times faster. The decision this informs is whether to keep serving standard Transformers or convert them to hybrids for lower inference cost. It also flags a governance point: converting a model is a substantial modification, which raises re-assessment questions under the AI Act.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors present Priming, which initializes a Hybrid State-Space model from a pre-trained Transformer rather than training from scratch. Short alignment and post-training phases recover downstream quality using under 0.5% of the source model's pre-training token budget. The method works across Transformer families, dense and Mixture-of-Experts classes, and scales. This enabled a controlled comparison of SSM layer types under identical conditions: Gated KalmaNet, Gated DeltaNet, and Mamba-2. Their expressiveness hierarchy, GKA over GDN over Mamba-2, predicted long-context reasoning performance. A Hybrid GKA 32B beat its Qwen3-32B source by 3.8 average reasoning points, stayed within 1% of a Transformer post-trained on the same data, and delivered up to 2.3x higher decode throughput.

papers.note: Addresses when an updated system is still the same system, which decides whether re-assessment is triggered and is rarely documented by clients.
papers.title: High-Risk AI Systems and the Problem of Identity in the European AI Act
papers.explain_beginner: The European Union has rules for high-risk AI systems. These rules assume we can tell when an updated system is still the same system, because that decides whether it must be checked again. The paper says the law does not clearly explain how to make that call. The author proposes a way to judge identity using what a system is meant to do and how trustworthy it is. This matters because without a clear test, companies and regulators may disagree about when new checks are needed.
papers.explain_business: Under the EU AI Act, high-risk systems face checks before launch, monitoring after launch, and fresh assessment when substantially modified. Each step requires deciding whether an updated system is still the same system, yet the law gives no clear internal test. This paper offers a practical lens based on intended function and trustworthiness, plus a simple decision flow for audits and disputes. For executives, it signals that identity decisions should be documented and defensible. It informs investment in precise intended purpose reporting and standardized trustworthiness reporting, which support comparability across time and deployments.
papers.explain_practitioner: The paper examines identity judgments under the EU AI Act, which requires conformity assessment, post-market monitoring, and re-assessment after substantial modification. The author applies the function+ framework, individuating systems by intended function plus context-sensitive trustworthiness criteria. The analysis finds the Act lacks an internal auditable test for synchronic identity, meaning sameness at a single point in time, and defers this to sectoral or harmonization instruments. The contribution maps AIA lifecycle obligations to function+ components and offers a minimal decision flow for audits and disputes, plus recommendations for testable intended purpose and standardized trustworthiness reporting.

papers.note: Added because a reader's question on this site drew on it (1 time so far). The page exists so the next reader finds it in the answer.
papers.title: Consulting the Digital Doctor: Efficacy of ChatGPT-3.5 in Answering Questions Related to Diabetic Foot Ulcer Care
papers.authors: Rachel N. Rohrich, Karen R. Li, Christian X. Lava, Isabel Snee, Sami Alahmadi, Richard C. Youn, John S. Steinberg, Jayson N. Atves, Christopher E. Attinger, Karen K. Evans
papers.explain_beginner: This study asked whether a popular AI chatbot gives good answers about caring for diabetic foot ulcers, which are serious wounds linked to diabetes. Doctors asked the chatbot 11 common questions and then rated the replies. The answers were mostly accurate and easy to understand, but some contained wrong information, and most left out important details. The chatbot also wrote at a reading level too hard for many adults. The takeaway is that AI can help patients learn general information and feel more involved in their care, but it should not replace a doctor, and patients should check important advice with their medical team.
papers.explain_business: This evaluation of ChatGPT-3.5 for diabetic foot ulcer questions shows the tool can deliver generally accurate, understandable information but also produces occasional errors and frequent omissions, and it writes at a reading level above the average American adult. For healthcare organizations, this signals both opportunity and risk. Patients will use AI for wound care guidance, so leaders should decide how to guide that use, for example by offering vetted educational content, training staff to discuss AI limits, and monitoring for misinformation. The findings support treating AI as a supplement to clinical care rather than a trusted standalone source, and they inform investments in patient education and safety protocols.
papers.explain_practitioner: Researchers queried ChatGPT-3.5 with 11 frequently asked diabetic foot ulcer care questions in December 2023, covering wound care, concerning symptoms, and surgical management. Four plastic surgeons rated each response on a 10-point scale for accuracy, comprehensiveness, and danger, and gave qualitative feedback. Ten readability indexes assessed reading level. Mean scores were 8.7 for accuracy, 8.0 for comprehensiveness, and 2.2 for danger. Responses averaged an 11.9 grade level. Reviewers praised simplicity in all 11 cases and general information value in 4. Three responses contained incorrect information, and 10 omitted key details such as deep vein thrombosis symptoms and comorbidities affecting limb salvage.

papers.note: Considers how people change behaviour in response to a model, which means fairness at the prediction alone is not enough.
papers.title: Strategic Best-Response Fairness Framework for Fair Machine Learning
papers.explain_beginner: Machine learning systems often make decisions about people, like who gets a loan or a job. Usually, fairness is checked only by looking at the predictions themselves. This paper says that is not enough, because people change their behavior based on those predictions. For example, if a system seems biased, people might give up trying. The authors introduce a new idea called strategic best-response fairness. It asks whether two groups that start out the same end up putting in the same effort and getting the same results. They found that many common fairness methods do not achieve this, but one method, equalized odds, does, though it has practical problems. The paper argues that fairness must consider how people react, not just the prediction.
papers.explain_business: This research shows that fair predictions alone may not prevent discrimination. People change their behavior based on how algorithms treat them, so a model that looks fair can still lead to unequal effort and outcomes. The paper introduces strategic best-response fairness, which checks whether groups that start out identical end up with the same behavior and results. It finds that common fairness methods like demographic parity do not guarantee this, while equalized odds does but with practical drawbacks. For executives, this means fairness audits should include behavioral responses, not just prediction metrics. Decisions about deploying ML should consider whether the system encourages equal effort and outcomes across groups, and may require designing algorithms specifically for this goal.
papers.explain_practitioner: The paper proposes strategic best-response fairness (SBR-fairness) as a framework for fair machine learning. It moves beyond fairness in prediction alone, arguing that individuals may alter their behavior in response to algorithmic decisions. The key question is whether an algorithm trained on potentially biased data leads to identical equilibrium behaviors across subpopulations that are ex ante identical. The authors evaluate common fair-ML algorithms. They find that color-blindness and demographic parity criteria do not always achieve SBR fairness, meaning disparities in effort and outcomes can persist. Equalized odds does achieve SBR fairness, but it has several practical limitations. The work suggests SBR fairness is a necessary condition for breaking discrimination cycles and offers a complementary assessment tool.

papers.note: Compares NIST, ISO 42001 and the AI Act and adds sovereignty as a risk dimension, useful for clients with data location constraints.
papers.title: AI Risk Governance for Advancing Digital Sovereignty in Data-Driven Systems: An Integrated Multi-Layer Framework
papers.explain_beginner: The paper looks at how rules for artificial intelligence should also protect who controls data and systems. It compares three well-known governance approaches, then proposes a new framework with four layers, from laws down to daily operations. It groups risks into five kinds, including one for sovereignty, meaning a country or institution keeps meaningful control over its digital systems. The authors analyze the idea in healthcare, finance, and critical infrastructure. They conclude that good governance depends on all layers working together, not just one. The framework is still a theoretical proposal, not yet proven in real organizations, so it needs testing.
papers.explain_business: For executives, this paper argues that AI governance should include control over where data and systems reside, not just compliance with standard risk rules. It compares NIST, ISO/IEC 42001, and the EU AI Act, then offers a four-layer model that connects policy, oversight, technical controls, and operations. The model treats sovereignty as a distinct risk area alongside technical, ethical, security, and systemic risks. It is analyzed in healthcare, finance, and critical infrastructure. The practical decision is whether to adopt a governance approach that is tailored to local control needs and institutional capacity. However, the framework is conceptual, so it should guide planning, not replace validation.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors conducted a systematic literature review and synthesized existing AI governance approaches, including NIST, ISO/IEC 42001, and the EU AI Act. They built the Integrated AI Risk Governance Framework, or IARGF, with four layers: policy and regulations, institutional oversight, technical controls, and operational execution. It organizes risks into technical, ethical, security, systemic, and sovereignty-related categories. The framework uses recursive feedback across layers and is examined in healthcare AI, financial services, and critical infrastructure. Key findings are that governance effectiveness is a system property, sovereignty is both a goal and a risk dimension, and governance must scale to context and institutional capacity. The model remains conceptual and lacks empirical validation.

papers.note: Notes most imaging evidence comes from retrospective or controlled conditions, which limits what a deployer can claim.
papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare: From Diagnosis to Rehabilitation
papers.explain_beginner: This review looked at how artificial intelligence is used in healthcare, from diagnosis to rehabilitation. The authors examined recent studies from major medical databases. They found that AI can match health professionals on some specific tasks, especially in medical imaging, such as radiology and mammography, but mostly in retrospective or controlled settings. AI also helps in labs, rehabilitation, and chatbots for patient support. However, evidence varies, and issues like bias, ethics, regulation, and generalizability remain. It matters because AI may support care, not replace clinicians, and more real world testing is needed.
papers.explain_business: This review suggests AI can support healthcare operations in several areas, including imaging diagnosis, laboratory workflows, rehabilitation, and patient communication through chatbots. However, most imaging evidence comes from retrospective or controlled conditions, and rehabilitation evidence is uneven with limited prospective validation. For executives, the practical implication is that AI should be treated as a decision support tool that assists clinicians, not as a replacement. Investment and deployment decisions should require real world effectiveness data, checks for bias and generalizability, clear regulatory oversight, and governance led by clinicians. The paper informs a cautious adoption strategy, prioritizing validated use cases and measurable outcomes before scaling across care pathways.
papers.explain_practitioner: This narrative review searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and Embase, focusing on recent influential studies. The authors qualitatively synthesized evidence across diagnostic imaging, laboratory medicine, rehabilitation technologies, and conversational agents. The key result is that AI can perform comparably to clinicians on selected specific tasks, especially in imaging fields such as radiology, mammography, ophthalmology, dermatology, and digital pathology, but mostly under retrospective or controlled conditions. Laboratory tools aid workflow and decision support. Rehabilitation systems, including robotics, motion analysis, and large language models, show promise but have uneven evidence and limited prospective validation. Chatbots may help as clinician adjuncts. Generalizability, bias, ethics, and regulation remain unresolved.

papers.note: Produces tamper-evident evidence bundles and decision dossiers, which is the form of artefact an audit most wants to find already in place.
papers.title: XAI-Compliance-by-Design: A Modular Framework for GDPR- and AI Act-Aligned Decision Transparency in High-Risk AI Systems
papers.explain_beginner: The paper presents a way to make high-risk AI decisions easier to check. Instead of adding explanations only after a model is built, it combines explanation tools, compliance rules, and careful machine learning operations from the start. The system has two connected parts: one handles data, models, explanations, and monitoring, while the other handles policy, human oversight, audits, and decisions. A test using a made-up intrusion detection example produced records that can show how a decision was made and whether the records were changed. This matters because organisations using AI in sensitive areas need evidence for regulators, auditors, and accountability.
papers.explain_business: For executives, this paper suggests that high-risk AI used in security and privacy settings can be governed with evidence, not just model performance. The proposed framework ties technical explanations, monitoring data, and compliance records to specific rules in GDPR, the AI Act, and ISO/IEC 42001. Its test showed that even a small example can produce verifiable records for audits and accountability. In practice, this supports decisions about whether to invest in a governance pipeline built around evidence, how to prepare for audits, and how to reduce reliance on one-off explanations. It does not claim a new detection algorithm, so the value is in compliance readiness and oversight.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors propose a modular architecture for high-risk AI, called XAI-Compliance-by-Design. It combines explainable AI methods, compliance-by-design ideas, and trustworthy MLOps. Two connected flows are used: one technical flow covers data, models, explanations, and monitoring, while a governance flow covers policy, human oversight, audit, and decisions. An engine for compliance by design and a matrix mapping technical items to regulations connect these flows to GDPR, the AI Act, and ISO/IEC 42001. The Python proof of concept uses a synthetic intrusion-detection-inspired anomaly scenario, a Random Forest classifier, SHAP, LIME, drift indicators, and records designed to reveal tampering, plus decision files. It systematically produced verifiable artefacts supporting auditability and accountability.

papers.note: Explains how to calibrate controls to risk severity, and treats NIS2 and DORA as risk multipliers on the same system.
papers.title: Risk, Reasonableness and Residual Harm under the EU AI Act: A Conceptual Framework for Proportional Ex-Ante Controls
papers.explain_beginner: Europe's AI Act sorts AI systems into risk categories, from banned uses down to ones needing almost no oversight, but turning that sorting into real rules that companies can actually follow is not simple. This paper asks how regulators and companies should decide when an AI system's remaining risk, the risk left over after taking safety precautions, is acceptable. Rather than reporting an experiment, the author builds a conceptual framework borrowing ideas from older safety fields like engineering and workplace safety, where a similar question has long been asked. The answer proposed is that companies should be expected to reduce risk until further improvement would be clearly out of proportion to the benefit gained, a standard resembling reasonably achievable safety. It also stresses that a system counts as reasonably safe partly based on how predictable its misuse is and on what current best practice, or the state of the art, allows at the time. The paper concludes this approach makes the law workable, but only if technical standards keep pace with fast-moving AI technology.
papers.explain_business: For a company classifying its AI systems and building a compliance program under the EU AI Act, this paper's practical message is that compliance is not a one-time checklist but an ongoing judgment call, providers of high-risk systems are expected to reduce risk until doing more would be clearly out of proportion to the benefit, not to eliminate risk entirely. That means documenting what was considered reasonably foreseeable misuse, what safeguards were judged proportionate to the risk level, and how the system compares to current state-of-the-art practice, since these three tests are likely to matter in any compliance review or dispute. Following harmonized European standards, once they exist for a given use case, gives a legal presumption of compliance, so tracking which standards apply to a product is a genuinely useful shortcut rather than a formality. The unresolved risk for businesses is that no numeric bar for acceptable residual risk exists yet, so what counts as compliant may keep shifting as EU bodies issue further guidance, meaning compliance programs should be built to adapt.
papers.explain_practitioner: This is a conceptual and legal analysis rather than an empirical study, aiming to operationalize the EU AI Act's four-tier risk model, unacceptable, high-risk, limited-risk, and minimal-risk, by connecting it to established risk-regulation theory. The framework rests on three tests familiar from product safety law, reasonably foreseeable misuse, which asks providers to anticipate predictable user error or integration problems, appropriate measures, which calibrates safeguards to the severity of risk, and state of the art, a technological benchmark that shifts over time. The author argues the Act effectively imports the engineering concept of "as low as reasonably practicable," requiring high-risk AI providers to keep reducing risk until further reduction becomes grossly disproportionate to the benefit gained, and that harmonized standards give providers a presumption of legal compliance once followed. The limitation the author names most directly is that the Act sets no numeric threshold for how much residual risk to fundamental rights is acceptable, leaving that judgment to evolving standards bodies and regulators, which introduces normative ambiguity that only active governance, particularly by the European AI Office, can resolve over time.

papers.note: Compares adoption and obstacles across four sectors, useful for benchmarking a client against its own industry.
papers.title: Generative AI Adoption in Enterprise: A Comprehensive Case Study Analysis of Implementation Strategies and Outcomes Across Diverse Sectors
papers.journal: 2025 6th International Conference on Recent Advances in Information Technology (RAIT)

papers.note: Addresses the common client case of using pretrained or off the shelf models, and ties actions to ISO 27090 and OWASP.
papers.title: Compliance Made Practical: Translating the EU AI Act into Implementable Security Actions
papers.journal: IEEE/ACM International Workshop on Responsible AI Engineering
papers.explain_beginner: The EU AI Act requires AI systems to be secure, but most companies today do not build their AI models from scratch, they take an existing pretrained model and adapt it, which raises a specific practical question this paper tackles, whose job is it to secure a system built on someone else's model, and what exactly do they need to do. The paper looks at the technical guidance that already exists, official reports from ISO and Europe's cybersecurity agency ENISA that describe AI security risks thoroughly but read more like textbooks than checklists, and contrasts them with industry resources like OWASP's AI security guides, which are more hands on but were not written with the AI Act's specific legal requirements in mind. The author's contribution is connecting these two worlds specifically for the pretrained model scenario, translating the law's general security mandate into concrete actions, tied to a data security standard for AI that was still being finalized at the time.
papers.explain_business: Most organizations deploying AI today are exactly the audience this paper targets, teams using a vendor's foundation model, an open weights model, or an API rather than training from scratch, and the practical message is that AI Act security compliance still applies to them even though they did not build the underlying model, with responsibility landing on how the model is deployed, configured, and monitored rather than on how it was originally trained. The actionable path the paper offers is to use OWASP's AI Exchange and LLM Top 10 as the practical checklist and treat the ISO/IEC technical reports as the underlying risk rationale regulators will expect referenced. Because part of this guidance was tied to ISO/IEC 27090 before that standard was finalized, teams building a compliance program around it now should confirm they are working from the standard's final published version rather than the draft state this paper described.
papers.explain_practitioner: Bunzel's paper addresses AI Act security compliance specifically for the common case of organizations deploying pretrained or off the shelf models rather than training their own, arguing that existing technical guidance, ISO/IEC technical reports 24028 and 24029 and ENISA's Securing Machine Learning Algorithms report, comprehensively covers relevant risks and mitigations but lacks actionable, hands on implementation steps. The paper positions OWASP's AI Exchange and OWASP LLM Top 10 as filling that practical gap, and its contribution is mapping AI Act security obligations onto concrete actions organizations can take when they do not control the base model, tied specifically to the then upcoming ISO/IEC 27090 standard. As a synthesis and mapping paper rather than an empirical study, it reports no test results or dataset, and its clearest limitation is timing, part of its practical guidance is anchored to ISO/IEC 27090 while that standard was still being finalized, meaning organizations following it needed to track the standard's final text rather than treating the paper's mapping as permanently fixed.

papers.note: Prices fairness breaches against the AI Act fine tiers using 12.4 million real underwriting records, a rare quantified case.
papers.title: Algorithmic Bias Under the EU AI Act: Compliance Risk, Capital Strain, and Pricing Distortions in Life and Health Insurance Underwriting
papers.explain_beginner: Insurance companies increasingly use computer models to decide how much people pay for life and health coverage. This paper asks whether those pricing models are unfair to certain groups, and if so, what it would cost insurers to fix that unfairness under Europe's new AI Act. Using millions of real insurance records from four European insurers, the researchers found that people in the lowest income group were charged noticeably more than a fair calculation would justify, about 5.8 percent more for life insurance and 7.2 percent more for health insurance, which breaches an informal regulatory tolerance level. Digging into why, they found the overcharging usually was not caused directly by protected traits like income itself, but by indirect stand-ins for them, such as certain job categories or living in a poorer neighborhood. The good news is that available bias-correction techniques closed most of this unfair gap, while adding only a modest amount to the extra capital insurers must hold to stay financially safe under EU solvency rules.
papers.explain_business: For insurers, and for regulators or investors watching them, this study puts a number on something usually discussed only in the abstract, unfair AI-driven pricing carries a measurable capital cost, not just a reputational or legal one. The paper estimates roughly 22 basis points of extra required capital tied to biased pricing outcomes, but shows that applying a bias-correction technique called adversarial debiasing removes most of the unfairness while adding a comparatively small amount, about 14 basis points, to that capital requirement, at an estimated cost near 4.8 million euros for a mid-sized carrier. That makes proactive fairness testing look like a reasonable investment compared with the alternative, since the authors also calculate that fines become more expensive than fixing the problem once the chance of getting caught passes about 8.9 percent. The catch is that the underlying unfairness often comes from indirect variables, like job category or neighborhood, rather than obviously protected attributes, so insurers cannot assume removing protected fields from their models is enough to comply.
papers.explain_practitioner: Using 12.4 million quote-bind-claim records from four pan-European insurers spanning 2019 to 2024, the authors compare XGBoost and elastic-net GLM pricing models for mortality, morbidity, and lapse risk, then use SHAP values and an instrumental-variable approach based on night-shift timing to isolate which features drive unfair pricing outcomes, measured through statistical parity difference, disparate impact ratio, and equalized odds gap. The result that matters most is quantifying the compliance-to-capital link directly, unfair pricing in the bottom income quintile exceeds fair benchmarks by 5.8 percent for life and 7.2 percent for health products, translating into roughly 22 basis points of extra Solvency II underwriting capital. Applying adversarial debiasing closes 65 to 82 percent of that pricing gap while adding only about 14 basis points to capital, an estimated 4.8 million euros for a mid-sized insurer. A limitation the authors flag is that the study covers only four large carriers, so results may not generalize to smaller insurers, non-life products, or firms using internal capital models rather than the Solvency II standard formula.

papers.note: Finds only six empirical studies of real deployments, which is worth citing when a client asks for industry evidence.
papers.title: BRIDGING THE EXPERIENCE GAP: STRATEGIC COLLABORATIONS IN THE AGE OF GENERATIVE AI
papers.journal: Scientific Papers of Silesian University of Technology. Organization and Management Series

papers.note: Classifier-based detection with explanation of features, relevant where an audit needs evidence that a filter can be reviewed.
papers.title: Towards Secure AI: Detection of Prompt Injection Attacks with Explainability
papers.journal: 2025 2nd International Conference on Trends in Engineering Systems and Technologies (ICTEST)

papers.note: Criticises one-shot assessments and absent corrective action, which is a fair description of what most audits currently deliver.
papers.title: A systematic review of algorithm auditing processes to assess bias and risks in AI systems
papers.journal: Journal of Infrastructure, Policy and Development
papers.explain_beginner: The paper reviews recent research on how people check AI systems for bias and risk. It looked at 22 studies from technology, law, and social sciences. Audits often test models, inspect them, challenge them, or involve affected people, in areas such as medical forecasts, loan approvals, and hiring checks. The review finds current audits are usually too technical, ignore real-life experiences, do not explain whose values matter, happen only once, rarely include affected communities, and seldom lead to fixes. It suggests audits should become ongoing, inclusive, and connected to decisions. This matters because AI increasingly affects important life opportunities.
papers.explain_business: For executives, this review warns that checking AI for bias and risk is often treated as a one-time technical exercise. The paper examined 22 studies across technology, law, and social sciences and found that audits frequently miss real-world context, do not make value trade-offs clear, exclude affected communities, and rarely lead to corrective action. In practice, leaders should not treat an audit report as proof that a system is fair or low-risk. They should fund ongoing, inclusive reviews tied to clear accountability and follow-up fixes. This informs decisions about AI governance, deployment in high-impact areas such as lending, hiring, and medical forecasting, and investment in continuous auditing capabilities.
papers.explain_practitioner: The author performed a structured review of published research on methods for auditing bias and risk in opaque AI. The search covered technology, law, and social science sources and selected 22 recent applied studies. The reviewed work includes numeric comparisons, model checks, stress tests, and stakeholder involvement, with examples in medical forecasting, loan approvals, and hiring checks. The analysis reports recurring weaknesses: overly technical framing, unclear value choices, single-time assessments, little involvement from affected groups, and few corrective actions after audits. Promising directions include subsidiarity analysis, people-focused tools, and corrective coding. The main result is that auditing should become ongoing, whole-system, inclusive, and tied to governance actions.

papers.note: Shows a hiring model looking fair on standard measures while carrying a ten point disparity when measured properly, a direct warning about method choice.
papers.title: The Illusion of Fairness: Auditing Fairness Interventions in Algorithmic Hiring with Audit Studies

papers.note: Sets out 69 control considerations with a maturity model, which is close to directly reusable as an audit control bank.
papers.title: The Development of a Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) Governance Framework

papers.note: Reports that none of fifteen agent benchmarks score safety or cost, a gap an audit should expect to find unaddressed in client testing.
papers.title: From benchmarks to deployment: a comprehensive review of agentic AI evaluation
papers.explain_beginner: This review looks at how we test AI agents, which are systems that can plan several steps, use tools, and interact with their surroundings. It examines 15 widely used tests and finds a big gap. Agents can score well on these tests yet still fail in real work. The tests mostly check whether a task was finished, not whether the agent was safe, affordable, easy to maintain, or fits into existing workflows. None of the 15 scored safety or security, and none included cost in their main scoring. The authors conclude that better testing methods, not just stronger models, are needed for reliable use.
papers.explain_business: For leaders, this review warns that strong benchmark scores do not prove an AI agent is ready for business use. The authors studied 15 major agent tests and found they focus on finishing tasks while missing safety, security, cost, maintainability, and workflow fit. None of the 15 scored safety or security, and none included cost in their main scoring. That means current test results can hide operational, financial, and compliance risks. The practical decision is to require broader evaluations before deployment, covering cost, safety, integration, and reliability, rather than relying on benchmark rankings alone.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors reviewed evaluation methods for agentic systems that plan, use tools, and interact with environments. They analyzed 15 benchmarks, including AgentBench, WebArena, GAIA, ToolBench, and others, comparing their metrics, datasets, and domains, with software development as the main case. The key finding is that evaluation design, not model ability, is the main barrier to dependable deployment. Finishing tasks and simple pass or fail results hide code quality, security flaws, integration difficulty, planning coherence, resource use, and safety issues. None of the 15 benchmarks scored safety or security, none included cost in primary scoring, and 13 used only simple success or failure. They propose frameworks that score entire action sequences.

papers.note: Matches a dense Mamba needing 2.3x more active parameters, a concrete efficiency number for the state space line.
papers.title: Routing Mamba: Scaling State Space Models with Mixture-of-Experts Projection
papers.explain_beginner: State space models like Mamba are a newer, more efficient alternative to the standard attention-based design used in most AI language models, but making them bigger and more capable without a huge added cost is tricky. Simply adding mixture-of-experts, a popular trick for scaling up other AI models cheaply, does not work well when bolted onto Mamba in the obvious way, it can actually make performance worse. This paper introduces a new method called Routing Mamba that fixes this by having a single shared decision-maker choose which specialized expert components to use across several parts of the model at once, rather than each part deciding independently. Tested at a scale of about 1.3 billion actively used parameters, this approach matched the performance of a standard Mamba model more than twice its effective size, while saving on the computation needed, cutting required calculations by roughly a quarter in one hybrid setup. The tradeoff is that the researchers are not yet sure how well the exact design will carry over to every future variant of these models.
papers.explain_business: Routing Mamba is a research result rather than a shipped product, but it signals a path toward materially cheaper long-sequence language models, matching a dense model's quality with less than half its effective active-parameter cost, and cutting training compute by about 23 percent in one hybrid configuration tested. For organizations evaluating alternatives to standard transformer-based models, especially for use cases involving very long inputs where Mamba-style architectures already have an efficiency edge, this suggests mixture-of-experts scaling can be added to state space models without the performance penalty earlier naive attempts produced, so it is worth watching whether commercial model providers adopt this kind of shared-routing design. Nothing here changes near-term buying decisions directly, since the method was tested only up to 1.3 billion active parameters and has not been validated at the scale of today's leading commercial models, nor across the full range of competing architectures. The practical takeaway for now is to treat efficient mixture-of-experts variants of state space models as a promising but still maturing option, worth revisiting as larger-scale results appear.
papers.explain_practitioner: Routing Mamba (RoM) addresses a documented failure mode, naive mixture-of-experts integration into Mamba's projection layers degrades rather than improves performance. The method's key idea is a shared router, one routing decision applied jointly across the Conv, Gate, and Output projection layers of a Mamba block, rather than separate independent routers per layer, which the authors argue avoids conflicting expert selections and encourages coordinated specialization. Models were pretrained on 20 billion tokens of SlimPajama at sequence lengths of 4K, 8K, and 16K, and evaluated by perplexity plus downstream accuracy on LAMBADA, HellaSwag, PIQA, ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, and WinoGrande, across scales from 115 million to 1.3 billion active parameters. The headline result is that a 1.3B-active, 10B-total RoM model matches the perplexity of a dense Mamba model needing over 2.3 times more active parameters, and RoM combined with FFN-based mixture-of-experts on a Mamba-attention hybrid architecture yields a 23 percent reduction in training compute for equivalent performance. The authors' stated limitation is uncertainty about RoM's optimal configuration and how well it generalizes to the fast-evolving landscape of other state space, attention, and linear-attention variants.

papers.note: Added because a reader's question on this site drew on it (1 time so far). The page exists so the next reader finds it in the answer.
papers.title: Global research trends in AI-related foot and ankle surgery research: A bibliometric and visualized study
papers.explain_beginner: This paper looks at how researchers have used artificial intelligence in foot and ankle surgery over time. The authors searched a large scientific database and found 2047 studies published between 1999 and 2024, with the number growing every year. China and the United States produced the most research. Early work focused on building the basic computer methods, and later work moved toward studying how legs move and treating real patients. The authors say two topics are likely to matter most going forward: diabetic foot ulcers and computer-aided diagnosis. This matters because it shows where medical AI is heading and who is leading the way.
papers.explain_business: This study maps the growth of artificial intelligence research in foot and ankle surgery, based on 2047 publications from 1999 to 2024. Output is rising every year, and China and the United States dominate, though the United States shows stronger research impact per paper. The field has moved from basic algorithms to clinical applications, and the authors flag diabetic foot ulcers and computer-aided diagnosis as the areas most likely to grow. For decision makers, this signals where clinical and investment interest is concentrating, and it suggests that partnerships or hiring in these two areas, plus awareness of Chinese and American leadership, should shape research and product strategy.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors performed a bibliometric analysis of AI research in foot and ankle surgery, retrieving publications from the Web of Science Core Collection through December 31, 2024. They analyzed 2047 papers spanning 1999 to 2024 and visualized the data with VOSviewer and CiteSpace. Publication output rose steadily each year. China led in volume with 581 papers and an H-index of 47, while the United States had 489 papers and a higher H-index of 53. Keyword co-occurrence showed a shift from foundational algorithms toward lower limb kinematics and clinical disease applications. Burst analysis identified diabetic foot ulcers and computer-aided diagnosis as emerging hotspots.

papers.note: Maps AI Act articles down to concrete verification activities by lifecycle stage, directly reusable as an audit programme.
papers.title: Assessing High-Risk AI Systems under the EU AI Act: From Legal Requirements to Technical Verification
papers.explain_beginner: Europe's AI Act tells companies that high risk AI systems must meet requirements like having a human able to intervene, being technically robust, and using well governed data, but the law states these requirements at a high level and does not say exactly how to check, in a lab or an audit, whether a specific system actually meets them. This paper turns those legal requirements into a concrete checklist. The authors broke eleven broad requirement areas from the law down into 48 more specific sub requirements, and then further into 66 individual, testable verification activities, each tied to a stage of building or running the AI system. An example activity is confirming that a human operator can actually take control of the system while it is running, not just that a manual says they can. The authors are careful to say this is one reasonable way to break the law down, not the only correct one, and that some of the technical standards this checklist depends on were still being finalized in Europe when the paper was written.
papers.explain_business: Any organization placing a high risk AI system on the EU market gets a reusable starting checklist from this paper rather than having to invent a compliance testing plan from the AI Act's legal text alone, 66 specific, lifecycle tagged verification activities mapped back to the law and to standards like ISO 42001 and the NIST AI RMF that many compliance teams already use elsewhere. The realistic caveat is that the authors themselves call this one reasonable interpretation rather than the definitive one, and note that the European harmonised standards this mapping anticipates were not yet finalized, so a compliance program built on this framework should expect to revise its testing plan once those standards land rather than treating this mapping as the final word. This is directly usable now for scoping an internal conformity assessment program, with the understanding that specific verification steps may shift as EU standards bodies finish their work.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors decompose eleven high level AI Act requirement categories, covering human oversight, technical robustness, data governance, transparency, fairness, accountability, quality management, risk management, technical documentation, and record keeping, into 48 operational sub requirements and 66 concrete verification activities, each classified by verification type and by lifecycle stage. The framework grounds these activities in an extensive set of existing standards, including multiple ISO and IEC standards, GDPR, NIST's AI Risk Management Framework, and ISACA's AI audit guidance, and demonstrates the approach on an automotive intrusion detection system using version controlled artifacts and logged detection events as evidence. The authors state their own limitation plainly, the decomposition is explicitly not an exhaustive or definitive reading of the law, deliberately excludes sector specific rules such as medical device or automotive safety standards, and trades fine grained precision for a technology agnostic mapping that will need revision once the European harmonised standards it anticipates are actually finalized.

papers.note: Names specification risk, where an agent faithfully optimises a stated objective that misses the intent, which is a distinct audit finding type.
papers.title: Governing agentic performance management: a sociotechnical framework for organisational effectiveness

papers.note: Turns the Act pillars into 22 metrics and shows accuracy and compliance can diverge, which is a useful result for scoring an engagement.
papers.title: Towards Quantifying Compliance with the EU AI Act
papers.journal: Proceedings of the Annual Hawaii International Conference on System Sciences
papers.explain_beginner: The EU AI Act sets ethical rules for AI in five areas: explainability, fairness, privacy, robustness, and social and environmental well-being. This paper turns those five areas into 22 measurable scores, so compliance can be checked in a repeatable way. The authors tested their scoring method on three standard classification tasks. They found that an AI can be very accurate yet still fail compliance expectations. Bigger datasets helped robustness but made privacy leakage worse. Some fairness and explainability scores overlapped, so they could be simplified, while social and environmental measures were the least developed.
papers.explain_business: This work offers a way to score AI systems against the EU AI Act using 22 concrete metrics across five ethical areas. For leaders, the key finding is that strong accuracy does not mean compliance, so accuracy alone is a poor proxy for regulatory readiness. Dataset size also involves a trade-off: it can improve robustness but raise privacy risk. The framework could inform build, buy, or audit decisions, and it suggests fairness and explainability reporting may be streamlined, while privacy and social and environmental measures need more investment before they can be trusted.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors propose a structured, score-based framework that operationalizes the EU AI Act's five pillars into 22 interpretable metrics, enabling reproducible, model-agnostic compliance assessment. They applied it to three benchmark tabular classification tasks using a standardized deep learning model. Results show dataset characteristics shape ethical performance: high predictive accuracy does not guarantee compliance, and larger datasets improve robustness while increasing privacy leakage vulnerability. Correlation analyses reveal redundancy among fairness and explainability metrics, suggesting simplification is possible, whereas privacy metrics remain essential and diverse. Social and environmental measures are least mature, indicating a need for novel, bounded metrics.

papers.note: Pairs governance with model risk management in financial services, which is the two-tier structure regulated clients already understand.
papers.title: Ai Governance and risk management

papers.note: Produces a risk-tiering matrix linking principles to auditable technical controls, which is the translation step most frameworks omit.
papers.title: AI Governance Risk Tiering for Sustainable Digital Infrastructure: A Systematic Review of Cybersecurity Frameworks
papers.explain_beginner: AI is being used more and more in public services and important infrastructure, and that brings real risks to privacy and fairness that today's rules do not handle well. This paper reviewed 450 research records and closely studied 95 of them. The authors found that current AI governance is scattered: some frameworks focus on ethics and privacy, others on rules and risk, and few combine both. Their main contribution is a model that sorts AI risks into tiers and links each tier to concrete technical checks, turning broad principles into steps organizations can actually audit and follow.
papers.explain_business: AI adoption across services and critical infrastructure is outpacing existing governance, which struggles with privacy, bias, transparency and accountability risks. This review of 95 studies shows the current landscape is fragmented, with most frameworks either ethics-focused or compliance-focused and few doing both. The practical takeaway is a risk-tiering matrix that connects principles to auditable technical controls, aligned with Sustainable Development Goal 9. For executives, this informs decisions about which governance model to adopt, how to prioritize controls by risk tier, and how to prepare for audits, supporting secure and sustainable AI deployment rather than one-off policy statements.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors conducted a systematic literature review following PRISMA 2020, screening 450 records from major databases and analyzing 95 high-quality studies. They applied principal component analysis and k-means clustering to map the governance landscape. Outputs include a heat map of frameworks, a theme co-occurrence network, a cluster analysis of framework coverage, and an integrated governance risk framework with a risk-tiering matrix. Results show a fragmented field split between ethics/privacy-centric and compliance/risk-focused approaches, with few integrated frameworks and tension between privacy and security. The matrix links ethical principles to auditable technical controls, addressing the translation step most frameworks omit.

papers.note: Places algorithmic auditing at the middle layer between governance and AI literacy, which is where an external audit actually sits.
papers.title: Navigating the AI Frontier: a holistic framework for algorithmic governance and responsible innovation in organizations

papers.note: Finds output reliability a stronger predictor of productivity than tool features, which supports making accuracy an audit priority.
papers.title: Generative AI Adoption and Productivity Outcomes in Small and Medium Enterprises
papers.journal: 2026 IEEE International Conference on Cybernetics and Innovations (ICCI)

papers.note: Sets out the interface problems between the AI Act and the medical device regulations, which is the first thing to resolve in a clinical audit.
papers.title: Risk-adjusted conformity assessment of AI systems in healthcare: A scoping review
papers.explain_beginner: The paper reviews 126 studies and reports about how the European Union checks whether healthcare AI is safe and compliant. Medical AI must follow both medical device rules and the AI Act, and the review finds this creates overlap and confusion. It also notes that many medical AI tools are treated as high risk, that systems which keep learning are hard to certify once and forget, and that monitoring after release is unclear. The authors say the legal framework is broad, but practical application is still debated. This matters because unclear duties could leave doctors responsible for AI performance they cannot easily verify.
papers.explain_business: For healthcare organizations and AI vendors, this review suggests that EU rules for medical AI are broad but not yet easy to apply consistently. The main practical issue is the overlap between the AI Act and medical device rules, plus uncertainty about how to monitor AI that changes after deployment. The paper points to limited shared evidence measures, strained review bodies, and unclear responsibility for after market performance. Executives should treat regulatory strategy as ongoing lifecycle governance, not a one time approval. Decisions should include who monitors performance, who owns accountability, and how to gather evidence that regulators and clinicians can use to verify performance.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors did a scoping review following Arksey and O'Malley and Levac and colleagues, reported with PRISMA-ScR. They searched bibliographic databases and grey literature for EU-focused work on risk-based compliance checks for healthcare AI. After screening and full text review, they included 126 publications from January 2022 to October 2025 and used thematic synthesis. Key findings were recurring problems: unclear boundaries between the AI Act and MDR or IVDR, broad high risk classification, weak lifecycle governance for adaptive systems, principle to practice gaps, few shared evidence metrics, limited notified body capacity, and unresolved after market evidence and accountability questions. The framework is comprehensive but uneven in practice.

papers.note: Models that change behaviour over time are the hardest case for static certification, which is a live problem for AI Act conformity.
papers.title: Dynamic State Space Models With Temporal Adaptation for Time-Varying Sequence Modeling
papers.journal: IEEE Transactions on Knowledge and Data Engineering

papers.note: Side by side comparison of ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini on metrics, capabilities and limits, useful when a buyer asks which model to pick.
papers.title: CAPABILITIES AND LIMITATIONS OF LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS
papers.explain_beginner: This paper takes stock of what today's large language models, the AI systems behind tools like ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini, can do well and where they still fall short, aimed at helping people choose and use these tools more wisely. Rather than running new experiments, the authors reviewed how these models evolved, explained how the underlying transformer architecture and its attention mechanism work, and then compared the three named chatbots directly. They describe the attention mechanism as a major breakthrough behind the recent leap in AI language capability, enabling real gains in productivity and in working with text-based tasks across many industries. At the same time, they caution that picking the right model for a specific job is genuinely difficult, given how complex these architectures are and how much training data they require, and that users need to stay cautious about trusting everything a model generates. Their practical suggestion is that open-source models or third-party integrations can sometimes be a more accessible or controllable alternative to the big commercial chatbots.
papers.explain_business: For a business deciding how to deploy chatbot-style AI, this paper's main practical value is a reminder, not a new capability, that ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini differ enough in behavior that a one-size-fits-all choice is likely to be suboptimal, so matching a specific model to a specific task is worth the evaluation effort rather than defaulting to whichever tool is most familiar. The authors explicitly flag output trustworthiness as a caveat that any deployment should account for, meaning human review remains necessary rather than optional for consequential tasks. They also point to open-source models or third-party integrations as viable alternatives worth considering, particularly where cost, customization, or data control matter more than using a leading commercial chatbot directly. Nothing in this paper indicates a new capability jump or new risk beyond what is already known about these three chatbots, it is best read as a grounding reference for teams new to evaluating LLM options, rather than as evidence for updating existing deployment or procurement decisions.
papers.explain_practitioner: This is a literature review and comparative analysis rather than an empirical study with a novel benchmark. The authors trace the evolution of large language models, walk through transformer architecture and the attention mechanism underlying it, review typical training pipelines including data collection, preprocessing, and neural network selection, and then compare three widely used chatbots, ChatGPT, Claude AI, and Gemini AI, on their practical behavior and characteristics. The result that matters most for practitioners is the framing of attention as a pivotal architectural advance enabling modern LLM capability, paired with a caution that no single model is universally best, each has distinct strengths and weaknesses that must be matched to the task at hand. The paper's own noted limitation is that selecting and configuring the right model for a given use case is a genuinely difficult process, complicated by architectural complexity and heavy training-data requirements, and that outputs still require caution regarding trustworthiness. As a secondary point, the authors suggest open-source models or third-party integrations as more practical or lower-risk alternatives to the major commercial systems in some situations.

papers.note: Proposes adversarial training plus input sanitisation, one of the mitigation patterns an audit would expect to see documented.
papers.title: Advances in AI-Driven Cybersecurity: Tackling Prompt Injection Attacks through Adversarial Learning
papers.explain_beginner: This paper looks at a new kind of online threat. Chatbots like ChatGPT follow instructions, and attackers can sneak in harmful instructions to make the chatbot say or do things it should not. The researchers studied how these tricks work and then built a defense. Their defense teaches the model to recognize sneaky prompts and also cleans up the text before it reaches the model. When tested, the chatbot resisted these attacks much better, while still working normally. This matters because more businesses and people rely on chatbots, so keeping them safe from manipulation is important.
papers.explain_business: Companies deploying chatbots and LLM tools face a real risk: attackers can manipulate these systems to leak data or produce harmful outputs. This paper shows a practical defense, combining adversarial training with input sanitization, that reduces that risk without noticeably slowing the model or hurting its usefulness. For executives, this supports investing in AI-specific security measures and treating prompt injection as a deployment concern, not an afterthought. It also informs decisions about vendor requirements, audit documentation, and security protocols that adapt as generative models change, helping protect brand trust and customer data.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors analyze prompt injection attacks against LLMs, covering how adversarial prompts bypass content filters, hijack model behavior, and extract sensitive data. They propose a defense framework combining adversarial training with input sanitization to detect and neutralize harmful prompts. Evaluation uses leading LLM platforms, benchmark datasets, and real-world scenarios. Results indicate improved resistance to both direct and indirect prompt injection, with minimal impact on model performance and responsiveness. The work argues for embedding adversarial robustness into the LLM deployment lifecycle and for AI-native security protocols that evolve with generative models.

papers.note: An attempt at statistical regularities in reasoning traces, early work but the direction an audit would need for quantitative assurance.
papers.title: Mean-Field Dynamics of Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in Large Language Models

papers.note: Gives a ten-step deployer roadmap including fundamental rights impact assessment, directly usable with a hospital client.
papers.title: The EU AI Act: implications and compliance guidance for healthcare facilities
papers.explain_beginner: The paper examines how European rules for artificial intelligence affect hospitals and clinics. It says the EU AI Act treats many medical AI tools as high risk, making healthcare a major focus. The authors studied what hospitals must do when they use these tools and built a ten step roadmap with four phases. Important duties include reviewing fundamental rights, checking each system locally, and keeping people meaningfully involved so staff do not trust automated advice too much. The main message is that hospitals should not buy AI as a one time product. They need ongoing partnerships with vendors and preparation before enforcement begins in August 2026.
papers.explain_business: For healthcare executives, this paper signals that using medical AI in Europe will require continuous compliance work, not just a one time purchase. Because most clinical AI systems are treated as high risk, hospitals must plan for fundamental rights impact reviews, local technical checks, supervision by people, and staff understanding of AI. The authors recommend a ten step roadmap and a four phase implementation approach. The practical decision is to treat AI vendors as long term partners, write lifecycle compliance duties into contracts, and fund governance and supervision before the August 2026 enforcement date. The administrative load is real, but it supports safe scaling and patient safety.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors reviewed the EU AI Act as a regulatory text, focusing on deployer duties in Articles 26, 27, and 50 for clinical settings. They compared those duties with established clinical governance standards, including MDR 2017/745 and FUTURE-AI. From this, they created a ten step compliance roadmap and illustrated it with a hypothetical high risk multimodal breast cancer AI system. They report that healthcare is a primary focus and most clinical AI tools are high risk. Their four phase framework covers governance, risk assessment, operational integration, and ongoing compliance. Key outputs include mandatory fundamental rights impact reviews, local technical checks, and structured supervision to reduce overreliance on automated advice.

papers.note: Ranks regulatory compliance and limited transparency as the most reported barriers, which matches what an audit usually surfaces.
papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare Practice: Validation, Fairness, and Regulatory Challenges: A Systematic Review
papers.journal: Inquiry: A Journal of Medical Care Organization, Provision and Financing
papers.explain_beginner: A 2026 review examined healthcare AI studies from 2020 to 2025. It found 20 studies that tested AI on future patients or in outside settings. Most used deep learning, especially for medical images. Imaging tools had a median score of 0.91 AUC, which the authors present as part of AI's strong potential, though the review did not combine results statistically. The main problems were rules and compliance, unclear AI reasoning, poor data, and fitting AI into clinical workflows. This matters because AI may help care, but these barriers must be addressed before widespread use.
papers.explain_business: This review suggests healthcare AI has promise, especially image based tools, but adoption is not just a technology purchase. Across 20 validated studies, the most common obstacles were rules and compliance, unclear AI reasoning, poor data, and workflow fit. The review reports strong potential for AI, with a median 0.91 AUC for imaging diagnostics, yet the evidence was too varied for a combined estimate. For executives, this means planning should include compliance review, explainability requirements, data governance, and clinical workflow testing before scaling. It informs decisions about where to invest, how to assess vendors, and why pilot validation and implementation support matter as much as model performance.
papers.explain_practitioner: This systematic review followed PRISMA 2020 and searched five databases for clinical AI studies published January 2020 through September 2025. It included original studies with validation on future patients or outside settings. Twenty studies qualified. Deep learning was most common at 60 percent, often convolutional neural networks for imaging. Radiology, oncology, and cardiology were leading areas. For imaging diagnostics, the descriptive median was 0.91 AUC, but varied study designs prevented a combined statistical analysis. Reported obstacles included rules and compliance at 55 percent, unclear AI reasoning at 40 percent, poor data at 35 percent, and workflow fit at 30 percent. The authors call for stronger validation and implementation focused research.

papers.note: National data showing services gaining while routine manufacturing did not, which tempers generalised productivity expectations.
papers.title: Generative AI and Uneven productivity gains: the political economy of sectoral asymmetry in South Korea

papers.note: Finds an automated checker useful before an audit but weak on cross-regulatory content, which marks the boundary of tooling.
papers.title: Evaluating GenAI for automated EU AI Act compliance against human experts
papers.explain_beginner: This paper looks at a computer tool that helps people check whether their artificial intelligence systems follow the new European Union AI Act. The tool uses a language model plus a search system over legal documents to explain the rules and spot possible risks. It was tested on real cases like hiring software, medical diagnosis, traffic management, and facial recognition in shops. The tool did well at identifying risk levels and suggesting fixes, but struggled with very technical or overlapping rules. Experts say it is useful before a formal audit, not as a replacement for one.
papers.explain_business: For executives, this research suggests an AI tool can help teams prepare for EU AI Act compliance before a formal audit. It was tested on real scenarios such as hiring, medical diagnostics, traffic management, and retail facial recognition. It performed well on core questions like risk levels and suggested improvements, but it was weaker on highly technical or cross-regulatory matters. The practical decision is to adopt such a tool as an early screening step to reduce audit preparation effort, while keeping human legal experts for complex or overlapping regulatory issues. It does not replace formal audits.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors built an AI compliance checker for the EU AI Act, combining a generative language model with retrieval over legal documents to produce structured, contextual analysis of obligations and risks. They evaluated it on real-world cases including algorithmic hiring, medical diagnostics, smart city traffic management, and retail facial recognition, using both automated analysis and expert review. The system reliably reconstructed core regulatory obligations, especially risk classification and improvement suggestions. Performance dropped on highly technical or cross-regulatory content. Experts judged it valuable as a pre-audit aid, citing legal reasoning depth, transparency, and contextual adaptability.

papers.note: Models validity degrading multiplicatively across pipeline stages, which gives an audit a way to argue a certification claim is overstated.
papers.title: Measurement Without Validity: The Compounding Reliability Problem in Agentic AI Evaluation
papers.explain_beginner: This paper looks at how AI systems are tested before they are trusted with important jobs. The author argues that each testing stage can lose some accuracy, and those losses multiply rather than add up. If three stages each keep 70 percent of their accuracy, the final result may be only about 34 percent trustworthy. The author checked 55 published AI evaluation papers and found most used weak or missing reliability checks. This matters because test scores often justify safety and deployment decisions, and those scores may be far less solid than they appear.
papers.explain_business: This research suggests that AI benchmark scores used for deployment, safety, and compliance may overstate real capability because validity losses compound across evaluation stages. An audit can use this framework to challenge certification claims, since a pipeline strong at each stage can still be only about one third valid overall. The practical decision is to require stage-by-stage validity evidence and reliability thresholds before accepting benchmark results, rather than treating a single score as proof. Leaders should treat evaluation quality as a measurable risk item and demand documentation of task validity, simulator calibration, and judge reliability before signing off.
papers.explain_practitioner: The paper proposes a three-layer model where total validity is bounded by the product of validity at task generation, human-simulator calibration, and automated judgment. With each stage at 0.70, the upper bound is 0.34, with a reported range of 0.22 to 0.54. The author validates this against a survey of 55 agentic evaluation papers, finding about 82 percent used mismatched, incomplete, or absent inter-rater reliability metrics, consistent with judgment-stage collapse. Evidence also includes task flaws in 7 of 10 benchmarks and up to 9 percentage point inter-simulator variance. Eight psychometric prescriptions and stratified ICC and alpha thresholds are provided.

papers.note: Codes 81 studies against MITRE ATLAS and shows research clusters at the prompt interface, leaving tool and memory boundaries uncovered.
papers.title: A Systematic Literature Review of Prompt Injection Attacks in LLM-Integrated Systems
papers.explain_beginner: This paper looks at how attackers can trick AI systems that use large language models. The problem is that these models cannot tell the difference between real instructions and sneaky text hidden in content they read. The authors reviewed 81 studies and sorted them using a standard security framework. They found that most research focuses on the first point of contact, the prompt, and on two common attack goals. Other parts of real AI systems, like tools and memory, get far less attention. This matters because real systems have many parts, so gaps in research leave real gaps in protection.
papers.explain_business: This review shows that current security research on AI prompt injection is heavily focused on one part of the system, the prompt, while other components like tools and memory are largely ignored. For executives, this means that published defences and threat models may not cover the full attack surface of production AI systems. The decision this informs is where to direct security investment and internal testing. Relying only on prompt-level protections is likely insufficient. Organisations deploying tool-augmented or memory-enabled AI should commission their own assessments of those less-studied boundaries and treat prompt injection as a system-level risk, not just a model-level flaw.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors conducted a PRISMA systematic review, searching IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, and ScienceDirect for peer-reviewed work from 2015 to October 2025. They included 89 publications and analysed 81. Each paper was coded against MITRE ATLAS version 5.4.0 along three axes: trust boundary, attacker objective, and research orientation. Attacker objectives were mapped to seventeen operational patterns. Results show a strong concentration on the prompt interface and on Instruction Hijack and Policy Bypass objectives. Tool and memory boundaries lack both attack characterisation and defence proposals. The authors attribute this to incentives favouring reproducible prompt-level experiments over complex architectural assessments.

papers.note: Maps which procedure applies to which system type and identifies blind spots, useful when advising a client which route they are on.
papers.title: Conformity assessment procedures under the AI Act
papers.explain_beginner: This paper looks at how high-risk AI systems are checked for safety and compliance under the AI Act. The authors map which checking procedure applies to which kind of AI system, so it is clearer which route a given system must follow. They find that the law borrows procedures from older European rules that were not designed with AI in mind. Because of this, the risk categories may miss dangers that are specific to AI, and some procedures may not really fit AI systems. The work matters because it points out gaps that regulators and companies need to address.
papers.explain_business: For executives, this paper clarifies which conformity assessment route a high-risk AI system will take under the AI Act, and warns that the rules lean on older European procedures not built for AI. In practice, the risk categories may not capture AI-specific dangers, and the chosen procedure affects what conformity assessment bodies must do. This informs decisions about compliance planning, budgeting, and which notified body or internal process to use. It also signals where regulatory expectations may shift, so leaders can build flexibility into product timelines and risk management rather than assuming current classifications are final.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors analyse conformity assessment procedures for high-risk AI systems under the AI Act. They first map the applicable procedures to different system types, providing structured implementation guidance. They then assess the Act's reliance on procedures from other Union harmonisation legislation, showing that this borrowing produces a risk classification that underweights AI-specific risks and questioning whether the procedures suit AI systems. They also examine how assigning these procedures shapes the obligations of conformity assessment bodies. The key contribution is a systematic analysis of the regulatory landscape that exposes systemic challenges and regulatory blind spots.

papers.note: Treats poisoning, drift and integrity as one governance problem, which matches how these failures actually present in production.
papers.title: AI governance under threat managing data poisoning, drift, and integrity challenges
papers.explain_beginner: This paper looks at three problems that can hurt AI systems used in business operations. Data poisoning is when bad information gets fed into the system on purpose. Data drift is when the real world changes and the data no longer matches. Data integrity means the data is trustworthy and complete. The authors say these problems are usually studied separately, but in real life they happen together and feed into each other.
