The paper reviews existing research and builds a framework that combines technical checks, clear accountability inside organisations, and outside oversight, so AI stays reliable over time.
papers.explain_business: For executives, the message is that AI failures in operations rarely come from one isolated technical fault. Poisoned inputs, shifting data patterns and integrity gaps reinforce each other, so treating them as separate IT issues leaves the organisation exposed. The paper offers a governance framework combining technical checks, clear internal accountability and recognised oversight principles across the whole AI lifecycle. The practical decision this informs is how to structure AI oversight, specifically whether to fund continuous data and model assurance and assign ownership, rather than relying only on security tooling. It is most relevant for firms deploying AI in complex, data-heavy supply chain environments.
papers.explain_practitioner: This is a structured narrative review, not an experimental study. The authors synthesise existing literature on data poisoning, data drift and data integrity, which prior work treated separately, and argue they should be governed as one interconnected risk across the AI lifecycle. An illustrative supply chain case scenario shows how these failures interact in operational settings. The main output is an Integrated AI Governance Framework that unifies technical assurance, organisational governance and internationally recognised governance principles within a single lifecycle model. The key claim is that technical safeguards alone are insufficient, continuous lifecycle assurance, data governance, accountability and regulatory oversight are all required.

papers.note: Argues benchmark validity depreciates as models saturate them, which is a reason an audit should not reuse last year tests.
papers.title: The Benchmark Ceiling: Human Judgment, Evaluation Scarcity, and the Political Economy of AI Capability Measurement

papers.note: Finds lower error hiding destroyed structure, a clear warning that a single improved metric is not evidence of a better model.
papers.title: More Experts, Worse Dynamics: Inverse Scaling and Spectral Bias in Mixture-of-Experts State-Space Models

papers.note: Proposes routing and self-correction to cut error accumulation, relevant when an audit reviews controls on agentic workflows.
papers.title: Optimizing Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in Large Language Models for Complex Reasoning Tasks
papers.journal: Global Media and Social Sciences Research Journal

papers.note: Reports on-device profiling as well as benchmarks, which is the kind of evidence an audit needs for edge deployments.
papers.title: MossNet: Mixture of State-Space Experts is a Multi-Head Attention

papers.note: Suggests dense layers already behave sparsely, which bears on interpretability evidence an audit might be offered.
papers.title: Secret mixtures of experts inside your LLM

papers.note: Separates the duties of each supply chain actor and explains when a deployer inherits full provider obligations.
papers.title: Obligations of importers, distributors and deployers of high-risk AI systems under the AI Act
papers.explain_beginner: The EU AI Act does not just put obligations on the company that originally builds a high risk AI system, it also puts separate obligations on whoever imports it into Europe, whoever distributes or resells it, and whoever actually uses it day to day. This paper sorts out what each of those parties specifically has to do. Importers carry the heaviest burden among the three, essentially double checking that the original maker actually did what the law requires before the product enters the EU market. Distributors have lighter, narrower checks. The people or companies actually using the system, called deployers, have their own separate duties focused on how the system is used in practice, not on how it was built. The paper's most useful and slightly surprising point is that if someone in that chain modifies the AI system, even without meaning to change its purpose, they can suddenly be treated as if they were the original manufacturer, with all of that heavier set of legal duties.
papers.explain_business: Any company anywhere in a high risk AI system's supply chain in Europe, importer, reseller, or the organization actually running the system, needs to know which of these three roles it occupies, because the compliance burden differs sharply between them, and misjudging the role risks real financial penalties under the Act. The single most actionable finding for procurement and engineering teams is that modifying a purchased AI system, retraining it, fine tuning it, or repurposing it for a new use case, can convert a deployer or distributor into something legally equivalent to the original provider overnight, carrying full conformity assessment and documentation duties that a company may not be prepared for. This applies now to any organization customizing off the shelf or vendor supplied high risk AI systems for EU markets, and the practical step it implies is auditing planned modifications against this reclassification risk before making them, not after.
papers.explain_practitioner: This doctrinal legal analysis separates the AI Act's obligations across the high risk AI supply chain, finding that importers bear primary verification duties confirming a provider's compliance, such as checking conformity documentation exists, while distributors carry comparatively narrower diligence obligations. Deployers hold independent obligations that are not subordinate to the provider's, centered on managing risk during actual operational use rather than on design compliance. The paper's central finding is a reclassification scenario, when any actor in this chain modifies a high risk system or its intended purpose, that actor can inherit the full set of provider level obligations, including conformity assessment and technical documentation duties, because the Act treats AI systems as inherently susceptible to purpose drift regardless of original design intent. As a legal analysis rather than an empirical study, the paper offers no dataset, and its stated limitation is that properly identifying which role an actor occupies, particularly around what counts as a triggering modification, is a genuinely difficult interpretive problem in practice, not a settled bright line.

papers.note: Shows adoption concentrated in marketing and sales and lowest in manufacturing, which tells an audit where to look first.
papers.title: Industries Generative AI Adoption: A Functional and Comparative Analysis
papers.journal: Shanlax International Journal of Arts, Science and Humanities

reading.body:
Chain-of-thought prompting, with 20,046 citations, is the single most cited result in this collection, and the data show why: it reframed reasoning as an inference-time technique rather than a training problem, which changed what every subsequent paper had to account for.

The 134 papers sort into a recognizable pattern. A capability gets demonstrated at scale, then a follow-on paper shows the demonstration was fragile. Chain-of-thought improves reasoning; GSM-Symbolic finds that changing only the numbers in a math problem degrades every model tested, and adding one irrelevant clause cuts performance by up to 65 percent. Med-PaLM passes USMLE-style questions; Hager et al. test the same class of models against 2,400 real intensive-care cases and find they diagnose worse than physicians and ignore treatment guidelines. Safety alignment ships; Andriushchenko et al. achieve 100 percent jailbreak success across major frontier models using simple adaptive search. The collection does not resolve these pairs. It records them.

The healthcare cluster is the densest by paper count, spanning five entries from 2019 through 2024, and it illustrates the pattern most sharply. The 2019 Kelly et al. paper on why clinical AI stalls between research and practice reads as a prediction; the 2024 Hager et al. paper in Nature Medicine reads as its confirmation. That gap is five years and many compute generations wide, and the data do not show it closing. What the data do not cover is the infrastructure side: nothing here addresses the compute cost, power draw, or facility requirements behind the models being evaluated, so readers wanting to connect clinical capability claims to the resource constraints that produce them will need to look elsewhere on this site.

The gap between benchmark performance and real-world capability is not incidental; it reflects a fundamental asymmetry in what models optimize for. Chain-of-thought prompting reveals this directly. Models that pass math exams by reasoning step-by-step fail when numbers change or irrelevant clauses appear, because they have learned to pattern-match problem structure rather than execute generalizable logic. The same asymmetry appears in medicine: models that clear USMLE licensing questions ignore treatment protocols and diagnose worse than physicians on actual patient cases. These are not edge cases or scaling artifacts. They are the expected behavior of systems trained to maximize likelihood on static benchmarks rather than robustness to distribution shift. The 134 papers in this collection do not attempt to reconcile capability and fragility; instead, they document both sides of the gap in parallel, creating a record of what capability claims do not yet account for.

The healthcare papers form a causal sequence that the field has not resolved. Kelly et al. in 2019 identified the barriers preventing clinical AI deployment: validation rigor, meaningful metrics, regulatory clarity, and post-hoc accountability. Five years later, Hager et al. demonstrate that those barriers remain active. Models passing medical exams still fail on real cases, still ignore guidelines, still misprocess data. The intervening papers—Med-PaLM on USMLE performance, the multimodal survey showing hallucination as an unresolved problem, the framework paper on bias in clinical settings—show researchers aware of these gaps but unable to close them. The data suggest the obstacle is not understanding what needs to be fixed but achieving it at scale while maintaining the capabilities that made the models valuable in the first place.

Safety and reasoning papers show a parallel pattern. After Wei et al. established that reasoning emerges through prompting, subsequent papers systematically identified the boundaries of that emergence: models handle single deduction steps but fail at proof planning; they exhibit unfaithful explanations that rationalize rather than justify their answers; they can be jailbroken completely using simple adaptive search. Each of these papers is highly cited because it answers a question that matters. None of them together resolve how to build reasoning systems that are both capable and robust, which may explain why the field continues producing both capability demonstrations and fragility measurements without convergence.

What does this collection reveal that the reading does not? First, the density of healthcare papers suggests this sector is where tension between claimed capability and actual deployment is sharpest and most costly. Second, the persistence of papers on hallucination, bias, unfaithful explanations, and jailbreaking indicates that alignment and safety improvements have not kept pace with scaling. Third, the absence of any papers addressing the computational or energy constraints behind these models means capability claims are being made in isolation from resource constraints that may be binding.

Does the data show whether models are improving on the fragility dimensions or just improving on benchmarks? No. The papers are chronologically sparse relative to the questions they raise, and many span the same model families or test periods. What they show instead is that benchmark improvement and robustness improvement are decoupled.

Is there a reason healthcare is so heavily represented? The data do not explain this, but the pattern is clear: healthcare has both high stakes for failure and measurable ground truth, making it possible to discover gaps between benchmark and reality that other sectors may not surface until deployment.

---

What does chain-of-thought prompting actually do to model reasoning?

It reframes reasoning as an inference-time technique rather than requiring retraining or fine-tuning. Models prompted to show intermediate steps improve sharply on arithmetic, commonsense, and symbolic reasoning tasks. The effect emerges around 100B parameters and is measurable without any weight updates. However, subsequent work shows this improvement is fragile: changing numbers in math problems degrades performance, adding irrelevant clauses cuts accuracy up to 65 percent, and models can rationalize biased answers without mentioning the biases that influenced them.

Why do models pass medical exams but fail on real patient cases?

Exam questions and real cases distribute differently. Med-PaLM reached 67.6 percent on USMLE-style questions. Hager et al. tested state-of-the-art models against 2,400 actual intensive-care cases and found they diagnosed worse than physicians, ignored treatment guidelines, and struggled to process lab results. The data do not explain why the distribution gap exists, but they confirm it is large and persistent.

Can safety alignment withstand simple attacks?

No. Andriushchenko et al. achieved 100 percent jailbreak success across all major frontier models using adaptive search to append optimized suffixes. The technique works because it targets each model's logit structure directly. The data show this applies to GPT-4o, Llama-3, Gemma, and Claude variants, but do not explain why these defenses remain vulnerable despite being explicitly trained for safety.

What happens to reasoning quality when models reason in hidden states instead of words?

The data do not cover this directly, but one paper notes that Coconut reasons in continuous latent space rather than generating visible reasoning steps, which removes the readable trace that auditors currently rely on. This complicates any audit framework that assumes explanations are faithful records of decision-making.

Do the papers show whether benchmark contamination explains performance gaps?

LiveCodeBench addresses contamination by continuously sourcing new problems from competition sites after May 2023, preventing models from memorizing answers. The study found that 52 LLMs over

most_cited.note: The origin paper for chain of thought prompting and the single most cited reasoning reference in the field.
most_cited.title: Chain of Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models
most_cited.explain_beginner: If you ask an AI model a hard math word problem and demand a direct answer, it often gets it wrong. If instead you ask it to work through the problem out loud, step by step, before giving a final answer, accuracy jumps sharply. This paper is the one that named that technique chain of thought prompting and proved the effect systematically across arithmetic, common sense, and symbolic logic problems. The surprising part is that this only works once a model is large enough, in smaller models, thinking out loud barely helps and can even make things slightly worse. The authors are upfront that this leaves an unresolved question, producing a plausible looking chain of reasoning does not guarantee the answer at the end is actually correct, and whether the model is genuinely reasoning in any meaningful sense remains an open question they explicitly decline to answer.
most_cited.explain_business: Before this paper, the standard assumption was that improving a model's performance on multi step problems required retraining or fine tuning it. Wei and colleagues showed you could get comparable or better gains purely by changing the prompt, at zero training cost, provided the underlying model was large enough, over roughly 100 billion parameters. That is the direct ancestor of every thinking or reasoning mode toggle now shipped in commercial AI assistants, and it means a business question like why is our AI bad at multi step calculations often has a cheap first fix, ask it to show its work, before an expensive one, retrain or replace the model entirely. The tradeoff businesses should weigh is real, this only works reliably on sufficiently large, capable models, and the paper's own caveat, that a plausible reasoning trace does not guarantee a correct answer, means chain of thought output should inform trust, not replace verification for high stakes decisions.
most_cited.explain_practitioner: Wei and colleagues show that few shot prompting with worked, step by step exemplars produces large accuracy gains over direct answer prompting on GSM8K, MultiArith, and symbolic reasoning benchmarks, and that this gain is an emergent property of scale rather than a smooth improvement, appearing reliably only around 100 billion parameters and larger. Their headline result, prompting a 540 billion parameter PaLM model with just eight chain of thought exemplars reached 58 percent accuracy on GSM8K math word problems, beating the prior best result of 55 percent from a fine tuned GPT-3 model equipped with an external verifier, without any additional training or weight updates. The authors state their own limitations plainly, the technique is costly to serve because it only works at large model scale, manually authoring worked exemplars is expensive at fine tuning scale even if cheap for a handful of few shot examples, there is no guarantee a correct looking reasoning chain leads to a correct answer, and whether the model is actually reasoning versus emulating the surface form of reasoning is a question the paper explicitly leaves open.

most_cited.note: The paper behind the main attention-free alternative, worth knowing when a client stack is not transformer based.
most_cited.title: Mamba: Linear-Time Sequence Modeling with Selective State Spaces
most_cited.explain_beginner: Most AI systems for language and other sequences use a design called the Transformer. The paper presents Mamba, a design that avoids attention. Mamba can decide what to keep or forget as it reads each item in a sequence, which helps with language and discrete data. It runs faster than Transformers, five times more work per second, and its cost grows steadily as inputs get longer, so long inputs become practical. It performs well on language, audio, and genomics. A 3 billion parameter Mamba does better than Transformers of equal size and equals Transformers with double the parameters. This matters because teams may not need attention models for every task.
most_cited.explain_business: For executives, Mamba is an alternative to systems built on Transformers, especially when long inputs or inference cost matter. The paper reports faster inference, five times more work per second than Transformers, and cost that rises with sequence length, so longer documents or signals do not become expensive. It works across language, audio, and genomics. In language, a 3 billion parameter Mamba beats Transformers of equal size and matches Transformers with double the parameters. The decision this informs is to evaluate Mamba for workloads where context length, latency, or throughput are constraints, rather than assuming every AI stack must use attention. It may reduce serving costs and expand use cases.
most_cited.explain_practitioner: This work addresses a weakness in subquadratic sequence models: they cannot reason from content. They make model parameters depend on the input, so the model can decide what information to carry forward and what to discard across the sequence. They design a hardware aware parallel method in recurrent form. These selective models form Mamba, a network design without attention or MLP blocks. Mamba gives inference five times faster than Transformers, cost that rises with sequence length, and gains on data up to million length sequences. It works across language, audio, and genomics. A 3 billion parameter Mamba beats Transformers of equal size and matches Transformers with double the parameters.

most_cited.note: Sampling many reasoning paths and taking the consensus is a cheap control an audit can recommend for high-stakes answers.
most_cited.title: Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models
most_cited.explain_beginner: The paper studies how to make language models better at reasoning. Instead of letting a model produce one line of thought and answer, the authors let it produce several different lines of thought. They then pick the answer that appears most often across those attempts. The idea is that a hard problem can be solved in different ways, but the correct answer should usually be the same. Tests on arithmetic and common sense tasks showed clear gains, such as 17.9 percent on GSM8K and 11.0 percent on SVAMP. This matters because a simple change can make model answers more reliable without training a new model.
most_cited.explain_business: This paper shows that a language model can answer complex reasoning questions more accurately if it is allowed to try several reasoning routes and then give the answer most of them support. The authors report large improvements on arithmetic and common sense tests, including 17.9 percent on GSM8K and 12.2 percent on AQuA. For executives, this suggests a practical reliability check: when an AI answer matters, ask for multiple attempts and use the consensus. The editor's note calls this a cheap control that an audit can recommend for high stakes answers. It informs decisions about how to review or deploy AI outputs in sensitive settings.
most_cited.explain_practitioner: The authors introduce a decoding method for step by step prompting. Rather than taking only the single highest probability output, their approach generates many varied reasoning traces. It then chooses the answer that is most common after combining the evidence from those traces. This relies on the idea that different valid solution routes should converge on one correct answer. They tested the method on several arithmetic and common sense reasoning datasets. The reported gains over standard step by step prompting were 17.9 percent on GSM8K, 11.0 percent on SVAMP, 12.2 percent on AQuA, 6.4 percent on StrategyQA, and 3.9 percent on ARC challenge.

most_cited.note: A review of 146 studies from 2007 to 2018 finds AI in higher education concentrated in computer science and four application areas, with little critical reflection on risks or pedagogical theory, so educators remain largely absent from shaping how these tools affect teaching and learning.
most_cited.title: Systematic review of research on artificial intelligence applications in higher education – where are the educators?
most_cited.authors: Olaf Zawacki‐Richter, Victoria I. Marín, Melissa Bond, Franziska Gouverneur
most_cited.explain_beginner: This paper looked at many studies about artificial intelligence in universities, published between 2007 and 2018. The authors started with 2656 papers and narrowed them down to 146 for a close look. They found that most of this research comes from computer science and related fields, not from education. The tools studied mostly do four things: predict student success, grade or evaluate work, adapt to each learner, or act as tutoring systems. The paper warns that risks and ethics get little attention, and teachers are rarely involved in shaping these tools.
most_cited.explain_business: This review of 146 studies from 2007 to 2018 shows that AI in higher education is still driven mainly by computer science and STEM researchers, with little input from educators. The tools cluster around predicting student outcomes, assessment, personalisation, and tutoring. Risks, ethics, and pedagogical theory receive scant attention. For leaders, this signals that adoption decisions should not rely on technical research alone. Investment in AI should include educators in design and governance, and should fund evaluation of ethical and teaching impact, not just deployment of prediction, assessment, or tutoring systems.
most_cited.explain_practitioner: The authors conducted a systematic review of AI in higher education, screening 2656 publications from 2007 to 2018 and synthesizing 146 articles using explicit inclusion and exclusion criteria. Descriptive analysis showed that computer science and STEM dominate the field, and empirical work relies mostly on quantitative methods. The synthesis identified four application areas: profiling and prediction, assessment and evaluation, adaptive systems and personalisation, and intelligent tutoring systems. The authors conclude that critical reflection on challenges and risks is largely absent, links to pedagogical theory are weak, and ethical and educational approaches need more exploration.

most_cited.note: The standard taxonomy of bias sources and fairness definitions, which an audit needs before it can test anything.
most_cited.title: A Survey on Bias and Fairness in Machine Learning
most_cited.explain_beginner: This survey looks at how artificial intelligence can treat people unfairly. It gathers examples from real uses where such unfairness appeared. It sorts the reasons bias can enter AI systems. It also organizes the different ways researchers define fairness, so people can compare ideas. The paper reviews many areas of AI and describes unfair results researchers found and attempts to fix them. It says more work is needed. This matters because AI often helps make important choices, so unfair treatment can harm groups. The survey gives a shared starting point for spotting and discussing bias.
most_cited.explain_business: This survey explains that AI systems can make important decisions and may treat groups unfairly. It gathers real cases where bias appeared, identifies where bias can enter, and organizes the ways fairness is defined. It also reviews how different AI areas have shown unfair results and what researchers tried. For an executive, the practical message is that fairness needs attention during design and engineering. The paper provides a shared vocabulary and map of bias sources, which can guide how organizations discuss and review fairness. It also shows the field still lacks complete solutions, so more work is needed.
most_cited.explain_practitioner: This 2019 survey by Mehrabi and colleagues reviews bias and fairness in machine learning. It collects real applications where bias has appeared and lists where bias can come from. It builds a taxonomy of how fairness is defined proposed by machine learning researchers. It then examines several AI domains and subdomains, reporting unfair outcomes seen in leading methods and approaches used to address them. The main contribution is a structured map of bias sources and fairness concepts, plus a review of problems in specific domains and fixes. It notes that many open problems remain. For engineers, it offers a reference for framing audits and comparing fairness choices before testing.

most_cited.note: The most cited education position paper, and the source of the competency and literacy framing now used in policy.
most_cited.title: ChatGPT for good? On opportunities and challenges of large language models for education
most_cited.explain_beginner: This is not a study that tested ChatGPT in real classrooms, it is a position paper, meaning a group of researchers laid out their reasoned argument about what large language models could mean for education, both the good and the bad, based on the technology's known capabilities rather than new classroom data. Written by a large interdisciplinary group of researchers spanning education, computer science, and psychology, the paper asks what changes for students and teachers once tools like ChatGPT can write essays, explain concepts, and answer questions on demand. It argues these tools could genuinely help by creating educational content, increasing student engagement, and personalizing how material is presented to individual learners. But it argues just as strongly that using them well requires new skills, both students and teachers need to learn to understand what the tool is actually doing, where it fails in unpredictable ways, and how to fact check its answers rather than trust them by default. It does not claim these problems are unique to education, the authors note bias and misuse risks apply to AI broadly, but it does argue education is a uniquely good place to teach people, early, how to think critically about AI systems in general.
most_cited.explain_business: For an education company or a school system deciding how to approach generative AI, the direct takeaway is that this influential, widely cited paper frames the central risk as a skills gap rather than a technology gap, meaning the practical need is training teachers and students in AI literacy and fact checking habits, not primarily restricting or banning access to the tools. This reframes procurement questions, a school evaluating an AI powered classroom product should ask whether it includes support for building these literacy skills, not just whether the underlying model is capable. The paper's point that bias, oversight needs, and misuse risk are generic to AI rather than education specific also matters operationally, since it means an education focused compliance review can reuse general purpose AI risk assessments rather than needing something entirely bespoke to the classroom setting. Because this is a position paper and not a study of outcomes, it does not tell a buyer whether a specific product actually improves learning, that would require the classroom outcome research this paper explicitly calls for and which, as of its publication, had not yet been done. It is most useful right now for shaping policy and training priorities rather than for evaluating any specific AI education vendor.
most_cited.explain_practitioner: As a position paper rather than an empirical study, the paper's contribution is a structured argument rather than a dataset or experiment, authored by twenty three researchers across computer science, education, and cognitive science departments. It organizes its analysis around dual perspectives, opportunities and challenges from the student side and from the teacher side, covering content generation, engagement, and personalized learning as the main opportunity categories. On the challenge side, it specifies that large language model brittleness, the tendency to fail or produce confident but wrong answers in ways that are hard to predict, requires both groups to build new AI literacy skills before the models can be safely integrated into curricula. The paper explicitly states that bias in model output, the need for continuous human oversight, and potential for misuse are not unique to educational applications of AI, distinguishing genuinely education specific challenges from generic AI risks that any deployment context would face. Because it is argumentative and forward looking rather than data driven, its own implicit limitation is that none of its specific recommendations were tested against real classroom outcomes at the time of publication, the paper is explicitly framed as guidance for future work and policy rather than a report of findings.

most_cited.note: The founding sparse expert paper, worth citing when an audit has to date the origin of a design choice.
most_cited.title: Outrageously Large Neural Networks: The Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts Layer
most_cited.explain_beginner: Neural networks can only learn so much because their size limits how much information they hold. This paper shows a way to make a network much larger while keeping the work per input fairly small. It uses many small forward processing parts and a learned gate that picks only a few of them for each example. The authors tested this on language prediction and translation, building models with up to 137 billion parameters placed between stacked LSTM layers. These models beat earlier best results while using less computation. The finding matters because it shows very large models can be practical, not just theoretical.
most_cited.explain_business: This paper shows that a model can be made far larger without making every input use the whole model. A learned gate sends each example through only a few small expert subnetworks. In tests on language prediction and translation, models with up to 137 billion parameters gave better results than earlier best systems while using less computation. The authors report over a thousand times more capacity with only minor efficiency losses on graphics processor clusters. For an executive, this supports choosing sparse expert designs when scaling language AI, because it can improve quality while controlling compute cost. It informs decisions about model architecture and infrastructure spending.
most_cited.explain_practitioner: The authors built a mixture of experts layer for selective activation at scale. It contains up to thousands of forward processing subnetworks. A trainable gate selects a sparse group of experts for each example, so only part of the layer runs. They inserted this layer between stacked LSTM layers in a convolutional setup for language prediction and translation. The largest model reached 137 billion parameters. On large benchmarks, it outperformed prior best results while costing less computation. They also report over a thousand times more capacity with only small efficiency losses on modern graphics processor clusters. Sparse expert routing can deliver much larger models without proportional compute.

most_cited.note: The most cited general LLM survey, covers pre-training, post-training, utilisation and evaluation in one frame.
most_cited.title: A Survey of Large Language Models
most_cited.explain_beginner: If you wanted one long reading list to understand how something like ChatGPT is actually built, this is it. A large language model is the technology, trained on huge amounts of text, that lets a computer generate humanlike writing and answer questions. This survey, one of the most cited papers in the entire field, walks through the whole pipeline, how these systems learn from raw text in the first place, how they get fine tuned afterward to follow instructions and stay safer, how people actually use them day to day through prompting and step by step reasoning, and how researchers test whether they work at all. It does not report new experiments of its own, it organizes and explains what hundreds of other papers found, and the authors are candid that basic questions like why scaling up model size improves performance are still not theoretically well understood.
most_cited.explain_business: This survey is most useful to an executive as a map of where competitive advantage in the LLM industry actually sits, because it separates building a competitive model into four distinct capability areas, acquiring and cleaning enough training data and compute, running the alignment and safety tuning that turns a raw model into something usable, building the application layer that turns model output into a product, and running the evaluation infrastructure that proves it works reliably. Few vendors are strong across all four, so this framing is directly useful for build versus buy decisions, since a company evaluating an AI vendor can ask which of these four stages that vendor actually controls versus buys in from someone else. It is a synthesis paper, not new research, so it carries no new regulatory or safety claims on its own, its value is organizing existing knowledge for faster onboarding into a fast moving field.
most_cited.explain_practitioner: Zhao and colleagues organize the LLM literature into four stages, pre training, covering data curation, architecture choices, and self supervised objectives, post training, covering supervised fine tuning and reinforcement learning from human feedback for alignment, utilization, covering in context learning, prompt engineering, and agentic tool use, and evaluation, covering benchmarks for language ability, reasoning, and safety. Because it is a synthesis rather than original experimental work, its evidentiary basis is the cited literature itself, and the authors have issued repeated revisions to keep pace with a field that moves faster than a single publication cycle. They flag open problems they consider unresolved rather than solved, the theoretical basis for why scale improves capability, how to make training and inference more computationally efficient, how to reliably align model behavior with human intent, and how to build genuinely agentic systems that plan and act reliably. Its main practitioner value is as a citation map into primary sources, not a standalone technical reference on its own.

most_cited.note: The MultiMedQA and Med-PaLM paper, and the origin of the multi axis human evaluation framework used since.
most_cited.title: Large language models encode clinical knowledge
most_cited.explain_beginner: The question, can a large language model, the same basic technology behind general purpose chatbots, actually answer medical exam style questions and open ended clinical questions accurately enough to be useful, or even safely, in medicine. Researchers cared because language models were improving fast on general tasks, but medicine has a much higher bar for being wrong, an answer that sounds fluent and confident but contains a factual error could mislead a patient or clinician, so they needed to test not just whether these models could answer medical questions but whether the answers were actually safe compared with those from real clinicians. The team built a broad medical question benchmark combining professional exam questions, research questions, and real consumer health searches, and found a large language model tuned for this task answered US medical licensing exam style questions correctly about two out of three times, comfortably beating the previous best model, and that with additional tuning aimed at safer long form answers, the rate of answers a human reviewer judged as potentially harmful dropped dramatically, down near the rate seen in answers written by actual clinicians. What it does not settle, the models were still tested mostly on curated exam style questions rather than messy real clinical conversations, and the authors are clear their models remained less reliable overall than clinicians.
most_cited.explain_business: This paper is the technical proof point that large language models can approach, though not yet match, clinician level safety on written medical question answering, and it is the evidence base that later, more product oriented medical AI assistants were built on. The dramatic gap between the earlier model's 29.7 percent potentially harmful answer rate and the tuned model's 5.9 percent shows that model choice and specific safety tuning matter enormously, a generic large language model without this kind of medical safety tuning should be assumed to produce fluent but wrong answers at a meaningfully higher rate. A 67.6 percent score on licensing exam style questions is good enough to beat prior specialist medical models, but is not the same as being ready for autonomous clinical use, since the authors themselves stress multiple choice questions are easier than real practice. Nothing about this paper constitutes regulatory clearance, it is foundational research, so any product built on this line of work still needs its own separate clinical validation and approval pathway before deployment. This is relevant mainly to teams building or vetting medical question answering or documentation assistants, as a benchmark for what strong safety tuning can achieve.
most_cited.explain_practitioner: Method, introduced the MultiMedQA benchmark, combining six existing medical question answering datasets spanning professional exams, biomedical research, and consumer queries, plus a newly created dataset of real world consumer health search questions, and evaluated Google's PaLM, an instruction tuned variant called Flan-PaLM, and a further instruction prompt tuned version called Med-PaLM. Flan-PaLM reached 67.6 percent accuracy on MedQA, the US Medical Licensing Exam style multiple choice benchmark, beating the prior best model, a 2.7 billion parameter system called PubMedGPT, by more than 17 percentage points. On human graded long form answers, Med-PaLM cut the rate of answers judged potentially harmful to 5.9 percent, down from 29.7 percent for the earlier Flan-PaLM version, approaching the 5.7 percent rate measured for answers written by actual clinicians, and Med-PaLM's rate of answers reflecting incorrect comprehension of the question fell to 2.1 percent versus 14.3 percent for Flan-PaLM. The authors state clear limitations, MultiMedQA, while broad, is not exhaustive, multiple choice question answering is inherently easier than real clinical workflows, the evaluation covered English language data only, their bias assessment was limited and not a comprehensive audit, and each answer in the human evaluation was judged by only a single clinician or layperson rather than multiple independent raters.

most_cited.note: Finds that even strong models cannot predict what their own generated code will do, a limitation worth citing in any audit of AI-assisted development.
most_cited.title: Program Synthesis with Large Language Models
most_cited.explain_beginner: The paper tested AI systems that can write text on writing short Python programs from plain English requests. It used two sets of tasks, one for beginners and one with harder math word problems. Bigger models solved more tasks, and the best solved about six in ten beginner tasks without extra training. Training on examples helped further. However, even the best models usually could not say what a program would output for a given input. This matters because AI can help write code, but people still need to check whether the code actually behaves correctly.
most_cited.explain_business: The paper shows that AI systems can turn plain English into short Python programs, and that larger models perform better. Fine tuning on examples improves results, and feedback from people can cut errors by half. The best fine tuned model reached 83.8 percent on harder math problems. However, even strong models generally could not predict what their generated code would output for a given input. For executives, this means AI coding tools can help write code but should not be trusted without review and testing. It informs decisions about where to use AI assisted development, how much human oversight to require, and what validation to build into audits.
most_cited.explain_practitioner: The authors tested language models from 244 million to 137 billion parameters on two new Python benchmarks, MBPP and MathQA-Python, using few shot prompting and fine tuning. MBPP has 974 tasks while MathQA-Python has 23,914 harder text to code problems. Performance improved log linearly with model size. Their largest model reached 59.6 percent on MBPP with a carefully chosen few shot prompt and no code fine tuning. Fine tuning on a reserved dataset part added about ten points for most sizes and the largest fine tuned model reached 83.8 percent on MathQA-Python. Feedback from a person in ordinary language cut errors by half. Models generally could not predict program outputs.

most_cited.note: The reference mixture of experts design that made sparse trillion parameter models practical.
most_cited.title: Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity
most_cited.explain_beginner: The question here is whether a language model can be made dramatically bigger, meaning it holds far more learned parameters, without making it proportionally slower or more expensive to run. Standard transformer models use every single parameter for every word they process, so doubling the model size roughly doubles the computation needed. Fedus, Zoph and Shazeer instead built a model that activates only a small piece of itself for each word, called a sparse mixture of experts, so the total parameter count can grow into the trillions while the actual computation per word stays close to that of a much smaller dense model. They found this approach trained noticeably faster than the standard dense recipe for a given compute budget, and worked consistently across text in 101 different languages. What the paper does not settle is whether such enormous sparse models are worth the engineering cost, they still need enough memory across many machines to hold all the experts even though they only use a few per word, and training a first trillion parameter model of this kind exposed instability problems that took real engineering effort to fix.
most_cited.explain_business: For an organization deciding how to spend a fixed training compute budget, this paper's practical claim is that sparse expert routing can turn the same GPU or TPU hours into a model that reaches a given quality level up to 4 to 7 times faster than a standard dense model of comparable pretraining setup, or into a substantially more capable model for the same wall clock time. That is a real lever for teams training their own foundation models rather than only fine tuning existing ones. The condition to know before betting on this approach is that the savings are in compute time, not hardware footprint, a trillion parameter sparse model still needs enough combined memory across a cluster to hold every expert, so it suits organizations that already run multi accelerator training clusters more than those hoping to shrink a single server's footprint. It is also now the reference design that later mixture of experts production models built on and refined, so its tradeoffs are a reasonable baseline for evaluating any vendor claiming mixture of experts efficiency.
most_cited.explain_practitioner: Switch Transformer replaces the standard Mixture-of-Experts routing, which sends each token to multiple experts, with a simplified top-1 router that sends each token to exactly one expert, cutting communication and routing overhead. Built on the T5 pretraining recipe and evaluated against T5-Base, T5-Large and T5-XXL baselines, the switch routed models delivered up to a 7x pretraining speedup over T5-Base and T5-Large under matched compute, and a 4x speedup over T5-XXL, while scaling a sparsely activated model to a trillion parameters on the Colossal Clean Crawled Corpus. On multilingual mT5-Base comparisons the approach improved results across all 101 languages tested, not just a subset. A key engineering contribution the authors report is stabilizing training enough to use lower precision bfloat16 arithmetic for large sparse models, something earlier Mixture-of-Experts work could not do reliably. The tradeoff the authors acknowledge is that these gains come from wall clock and sample efficiency during pretraining, not from a smaller footprint, the trillion parameter model still requires distributed memory across many accelerators to store its experts.

most_cited.note: Organises evaluation into what, where and how, which is a workable skeleton for the testing section of an audit programme.
most_cited.title: A Survey on Evaluation of Large Language Models
most_cited.journal: ACM Transactions on Intelligent Systems and Technology
most_cited.explain_beginner: This paper reviews ways to test large language models. It groups testing around three questions: what abilities or areas to check, in what situations or uses, and with which techniques and test sets. It covers many areas such as general language tasks, reasoning, medicine, ethics, education, science, social science, and agent uses. It also collects examples where models did well and where they failed. The authors argue testing should be a serious field of its own, because better testing helps build better models and understand risks to society. Open problems remain.
most_cited.explain_business: This paper reviews how large language models are tested. It groups testing into what should be checked, in which settings, and with which techniques and test sets. It covers many uses, from language and reasoning to healthcare, ethics, education, science, and agents. It notes both successes and failures. For leaders, the practical message is that model evaluation should be planned as an ongoing discipline, not a one time check. That informs decisions about where models are used, how their risks are understood, and how evaluation supports development. Remaining difficulties exist.
most_cited.explain_practitioner: This survey reviews how large language models are evaluated. It sorts the field into three questions: which abilities or domains are tested, in which situations testing happens, and which techniques and test sets are used. It covers broad language work, reasoning, healthcare, moral questions, learning, physical and social sciences, and tool using agents. It reports both successful and unsuccessful cases across tasks. The key result is a call to treat evaluation as a central discipline that supports better model development. The authors also identify remaining difficulties and keep related open source materials available.
